News.title: Buildings burn & huge blazes in middle of street as rioters clash with cops during anti-government protests in Albania
News.content:
Next

TENS of thousands of students stormed the streets of Albania, burning buildings and hurling rocks at police amid anti-government protests.

Furious pupils torched a government building and two banks as they clashed with cops during protests in Tirana over rising education costs and corruption on Wednesday.



Apocalyptic scenes coming from the capital showed a dark blustering smoke rising to the sky as bright-orange flames licked the ground.

Videos captured masked protesters rampaging through the streets, dressed in black clutching to flares and rocks as police donned riot shields and deployed water ⁠cannon and teargas to disperse the crowds.



Business fronts were shattered, bins overturned and the Education building set ablaze as well as a nearby Raiffeisen Bank branches.

The student-led protest came after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which call for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.



They are the most ​violent of the outbursts against the Prime Minister, who won a fourth term in office ⁠in elections in May last year but has since faced backlash at perceived corruption surrounding top ​officials.

The young demonstrators call for his resignation as well as better university conditions and job prospects.

Lora, a student who declined to give her ​last name as she admitted to throwing rocks at the police, called the action a “revolution”.

She said: “We are tired of peaceful ​protests.



“We will not stop until Rama resigns.”

Others chanted “Resignation” and “Police of crime.”

Albanian media reported that Wednesday’s protests also spread to universities in other parts of the country, namely Elbasan and Shkodra.

Deputy Prime Minister Albana Kociu pleaded with the protesters in a post to Facebook and said: “I call on students and every honest citizen who believes in the right to protest: Distance yourself from violence and vandalism!”



The ⁠police also issued ​a statement calling for peace, warning that violence will be met with a heavy hand.

They said: “Any person who uses violence, burns ​or destroys property, or attacks Police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed.”

The Flamingo Protests were sparked by the proposed development of a luxury resort along Albania’s southern coast.

The unrest comes as part of a broader wave of European student action targeting poor education and rising living costs.

In France, students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and ​better facilities, saying that ​deteriorating school buildings and ⁠overcrowded classrooms are damaging their education.



Last week shocking videos emerged from Paris showing a wall of armed police clashing with student protesters.

Masked pupils were seen hanging off railings as huge projectiles were hurled at police – including fireworks, plants ripped straight out of the ground and the protesters’ own shoes.

The French Interior Ministry said there has been “an increase in urban violence, on the fringes of the peaceful mobilisations of sixth form students, which has marred their legitimate expression”.

On Tuesday, Greta Thunberg joined protestersat the Paul-Eduard Lycée – one of the schools at the centre of the violent protests – in Saint-Denis, near Paris.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Thunberg, 23, condemned what she saw as an “extremely violent” police response.



That day more than 250,000 protesters took to the streets across the country.

News.title: Notorious Scots hood Paul Ferris died when his organs failed after private alcohol abuse battle
News.content:
Next

NOTORIOUS hood Paul Ferris died when his organs failed after a private battle with alcohol abuse, it has emerged.

The 62-year-old’s liver was critically damaged by chronic boozing that took its toll as he was being cared for at University Hospital Ayr.



Official papers reveal the Scots enforcer-turned-author, nicknamed The Wee Man, died from “multiple organ failure” as well as “decompensated alcoholic liver disease”.

And sources told The Scottish Sun that his battle with the bottle was the “one fight he couldn’t win”.



The admission came as it was revealed the once-feared gangster’s liver had been wrecked by chronic boozing.

His death certificate reveals he passed away at University Hospital Ayr on October 6. The document, certified by a medical practitioner three days later, lists the cause as “multiple organ failure, cardiovascular, liver and respiratory” plus “decompensated alcoholic liver disease”.

Prior to his death, his liver was at a critical stage of alcohol related cirrhosis where it could no longer function. He had been admitted to hospital two days earlier.

An insider told The Scottish Sun: “Ferris was always calm and composed in public but he hid a secret battle with the drink.

“Maybe that’s how he fought his demons and now he’s paid the ultimate price.

“He won many battles in his life but not this one.”



The document also reveals his late father William Chalmers Packer Ferris was a bus driver while his mother Janet McGinty was a sewing machinist.

And it describes his occupation as “author” — a nod to his later success as a crime writer.

It emerged ahead of his funeral at Daldowie Crematorium in Glasgow’s east end on Monday.

After his passing, a close family friend said: “News of his death will come as a shock to many who knew him throughout the different chapters of his life.”



The notorious hood, nicknamed The Wee Man, made his name in the city as a heavy for ‘Godfather’ Arthur Thompson in the 1980s.

He became a household name after being sensationally cleared of murdering his boss’s son Arthur ‘Fatboy’ Thompson Jr in 1992. It followed Scotland’s longest and most expensive gangland trial at the High Court in Glasgow.

Ferris and Arthur Jnr worked together but fell out after Ferris accused him of setting him up.

He became the prime suspect and was aged 28 when he was charged with shooting Thompson dead in the city’s Blackhill.



He was filmed smirking on the steps outside court after being acquitted by a jury following the 54-day trial, which featured 300 witnesses and cost £4million.

He was later jailed for seven years in 1998 after being found guilty of gun-running.

Ferris claimed to have turned his back on his former crime links for the past three decades, going on to become a best-selling author.

We told on Sunday how he had been planning to produce a movie about his murder trial, and trying to obtain courtroom transcripts to turn into a script.

PLUSH LIVING By Graham Mann FERRIS was living in a plush lodge in leafy Surrey before he returned home to Scotland to die. The five-bedroomed home worth up to £1.6million, is a mile from Epsom Downs racecourse, and a world away from the tough streets in Glasgow where he grew up. He was relentlessly bullied before becoming an enforcer for Glasgow ‘Godfather’ Arthur Thompson. He would go on to write several books about his gangland past, claiming he had left a life of crime behind him. It is understood he recently returned to Scotland as he battled ill health. He was admitted to hospital as his condition worsened before passing away last Tuesday.



The mooted drama would be a sequel to the 2013 movie about his life, The Wee Man, in which Ferris was played by Line of Duty star Martin Compston.

Ferris’ death comes just over a year after his notorious killer brother Billy also passed away.

We told how a crime expert who grilled Ferris for a 2019 TV documentary suggested his rebranding as an author and businessman was an act — and that he never truly turned his back on the underworld.

Professor David Wilson recalled how the former enforcer showed “no remorse” and speculated about the unanswered questions he now takes to the grave.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “My first impressions were how quietly spoken and thoughtful he was. And I wondered if that was performative.



“He deliberately undermined the public reputation as a hardman.”

News.title: Child & adult break into pub stealing £20-worth of scrap and flooding cellar as owner left fuming
News.content:
Next

A CHILD and a grown man have broken into a pub – nicking only £20 worth of scrap but flooding the cellar and leaving its owner devastated.

CCTV footage captured the bandits scaling the wall of the Ernehale Pub in Arnold, Nottinghamshire before leaving shortly after with a copper pipe.



Shocking CCTV footage shows a hooded man and the youngster approaching the pub on Sunday evening at around 7.30pm.

The man appears to encourage the child to climb the wall before doing so himself with further videos showing the inside of the cellar, with metal pipes missing from various appliances.



Jamie Thomas – who owns and is renovating the former Wetherspoon pub – said the items taken will only be worth about £20 to the thieves.

However, the cost to repair the damage done will likely cost the business thousands, telling the BBC the ordeal had been “very stressful”.



The 30-year-old – who took over the pub in July – also claims the pair had tried to take the water tank, but likely gave up as it was too heavy.

They did, however, get away with nicking lanterns from the beer garden and flooded the cellar.



The landlord slammed the heist but insisted he will re-open the pub in November as originally planned.

He said: “It wasn’t even worth doing. They’ve done more in damage than they’ve got.

“It’s irritating, just as I’ve got the inside done ready. Now I need to go back in and do it all again.”

“Everything in life has hurdles, and it tests everyone’s strength,” he added.

Thomas also revealed it wasn’t the first time his pub had been targeted, claiming teenagers had previously broken in to film TikTok videos.



Cops have said there is a burglary investigation currently underway, but that no arrests have yet been made.

The Ernehale – the Anglo Saxon name for Arnold which means “Eagle’s Nest” – is a historic pub that operated as a popular Wetherspoon until it closed in July.

Nottinghamshire Police have been contacted for comment.

News.title: Parents arrested after NINE siblings found in ‘appalling’ home where ‘kids were placed in cages & lived in a shed’
News.content:
Next

TWO adults have been arrested after cops found nine children living in what they described as appalling conditions.

Police alleged some of the children may have been kept in cages inside a tiny shed, while others lived inside with a grandmother.



The Licking County Sheriff’s Office executed a search warrant on the home in Etna Township, Ohio, on Tuesday afternoon after being referred to the residence by child services.

“The referral outlined physical abuse, including failure to provide food and water, insufficient living space, and juveniles being forced to stand for hours with nails between their toes and locked behind cages or barriers,” read an arrest warrant obtained by The U.S. Sun.



When deputies searched the home, they discovered a bug infestation, “deplorable living conditions,” and “inadequate sleeping arrangements and bedding” for the kids, the warrant alleged.

“Some of the things I can tell you is that the living conditions were horrific, disgusting, and there was nine children living in the house with three adults,” Captain Jay Cook said at a press conference on Wednesday.

The children, ranging in age from one to 13, have since been removed from the home and placed in CPS custody.

Two of the adults, Jonathan Parr, 37, and Jacqueline Coleman, 32, have since been arrested on child endangerment charges.

Parr and Coleman are not married, but share four children together. Coleman additionally has two of her own children, and Parr has three, Cook said.

The third adult living on the property is a 64-year-old grandmother.



“Upon executing the search warrant, detectives encountered appalling and unsafe living conditions that raised serious concerns for the health, safety, and well-being of the children residing in the home,” the Licking County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement.

At least four of the children allegedly live inside a shed on the property with Parr and Coleman.

Parr was inside the shed while deputies executed the search warrant, whereas Coleman had left with two of the kids shortly before, but was later held at a traffic stop.

Cook described the shed as “not very big,” adding it was “just like a little out building type [of] shed.”



Officials believe the other children were living inside a trailer.

“It was disclosed that maybe some of the kids were placed in cages,” Cook said, saying the cage they found went about halfway up a doorway.

“The way it was explained and what we saw was not necessarily a cage like an actual big size dog cage, but there was like a cage that kind of folds.

“There was no door onto the room, and they used that cage to cover the doorway.”



The children allegedly disclosed the kind of abuse they would face inside the home, Cook said.

“Sometimes it was punishment. Sometimes it was – for no good reason at all – where they would have to stand with their back against the wall, like a wall-squat type situation.

“It was reported that they would sometimes stand there all day.”

Cook said there were also nails in the floor, which were allegedly put there “like a marker to put their feet.”



Several animals were found inside the home, including at least three dogs who had to be removed so deputies could search the property.

Cook declined to comment on whether the grandmother would be facing charges.

Coleman and Parr are being held on a $150,000 bond and were arraigned in court on Wednesday.

Parr has a history of weapons charges in Wisconsin, in which in 2016 he had a charge of operating a firearm while intoxicated dismissed, but was found guilty due to a no contest plea on an endangering safety with a weapon and carrying a concealed weapon, per court records reviewed by The U.S. Sun.



He is due back in court on October 23, and has been ordered not to have contact with the alleged victims and Coleman.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He is also not allowed to have unsupervised contact with anyone under the age of 18 and will be subject to a GPS monitoring device, records revealed.

The discovery comes just a few months after officials in Hamden, Ohio, located about 71 miles from Etna Township, removed 16 children from a home and arrested four adults on child endangerment charges.

News.title: Moment US helicopters blow up Iranian spy boat in huge blaze after sea mine sinks container ship carrying iPhones
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment US helicopters strike an Iranian spy boat with missiles sparking a huge onboard fireball.

The strike came before a cargo ship carrying 2,500 containers hit an Iranian sea mine – the first vessel to be sunk by one since the war broke out.



In the clip of Washington’s latest boat strike near the Strait of Hormuz, two US choppers can be seen in the skies launching a barrage of missiles at the dhow.

Moments later, the spy boat erupts into a massive blaze as the projectile hits.



Plumes of thick black smoke were seen roaring over the ship following the blitz.

US Central Command (Centcom) said the boat was “conducting surveillance and targeting U.S. Navy ships in the Gulf of Oman”.





They said: “Over the past seven months, Iran‘s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has continued to indiscriminately target thousands of civilian mariners transiting regional waters in addition to U.S. Navy warships.

“Crew members were safely removed prior to destruction of the dhow. Repatriation efforts are ongoing.”

The strike took place on October 6 – just days before a UAE-owned cargo ship carrying luxury perfumes and iPhones was blasted by a sea mine.

Iranian authorities confirmed the hulking vessel exploded and sank on Wednesday morning in the Omani corridor of the Strait of Hormuz.

It is the first time Iran reported a ship sinking after hitting a mine during the war.



Shocking footage showed an array of goods laid out on the surface of the water following the blast.

Several smaller boats reportedly rushed to the site before selling the luxury items on the spot.

Meanwhile, shipping officials said two Singapore-registered cargo vessels were hit by “unknown projectiles” as they went through the strait on Tuesday and Wednesday.



One sank, while the other reached safety.

No injuries were reported.

It comes amid a spiralling conflict between the Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia.

Escalating missile and drone attacks by the Iran-backed terror group have left the gulf kingdom reeling and oil prices surging across the world.

At least 20 people, including a US national, were killed in four Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s main airport last week.



The deadliest came on Saturday when the militia unleashed a barrage of missiles at King Khalid International Airport, killing 13 and injuring 300.

Saudi Arabia’s crown prince Mohammed bin Salman, 41, has fled into hiding as parts of the Saudi capital have been transformed into a conflict zone.

With attacks targeting multiple fronts, Saudi Arabia has been pleading for offensive and defensive support from the US, Europe and the Middle East.

A former Nato commander told The Sun Britain should put boots on the ground in the Middle East to defeat the bloodthirsty Houthi rebels before global trade collapses.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Over the weekend Trump said he “may” join Saudi Arabia in strikes on the pro-Tehran militia.



In response, the Houthis threatened “swift and painful” retaliation against the US and its regional interests.

News.title: Pope’s brother – who also has cancer – says Leo’s disease ‘caught early’ as Pontiff recovers from surgery
News.content:
HEALTH BATTLES Pope’s brother – who also has cancer – says Leo’s disease ‘caught early’ as Pontiff recovers from surgery







Next

POPE Leo’s lung cancer was caught in its early stages as his brother – who is also fighting the disease – says he remains optimistic following the pontiff’s surgery.

Doctors discovered a lung adenocarcinoma – a common form of cancer – in a planned procedure on Tuesday, the Vatican announced.



Pope Leo XIV’s, 71, brother, Louis Prevost, said he is encouraged by the outcome of the operation on the lower part of his right lung and says he’s hopeful for a recovery following the recent cancer diagnosis.

He told Newsmax: “They caught it early enough, and he’ll be able to heal from the surgery and go on with his papal ministry.”



Louis, who is undergoing cancer treatment himself, said it was a shock to learn his brother also had cancer, saying “to hear that he had that nodule on his lung, that was kind of nerve-wracking.”

While he has yet to speak with his brother directly, a close aide offered him a promising update.



He said: “I got a message from his right hand that he was out of surgery, awake, feeling good, and was in no pain.

“So, we were all in high hopes and high spirits hoping for the best.”



Louis said his faith and the prayers offered for both brothers have been a source of strength, saying there is “no doubt that the power of prayer goes a long way”.

His wife, Deborah, told CBS News, their family were “going through a lot”.

She said her husband was being treated for multiple myeloma as part of a clinical trial at a hospital in Florida where they live.

He was first diagnosed with cancer in 2017 and had undergone treatment in 2019, but “fell out of remission” three months ago.

Her comments came after The Vatican announced on Tuesday that the first US-born head of the Catholic Church had undergone a successful surgery where a cancer diagnosis was made.



The small nodule on his right lung was discovered during a recent checkup, the Pope said on Sunday.

Louis said his brother described the planned procedure as relatively simple and minimally invasive, helping ease the family’s concerns.

Announcing the news, The Vatican said: “The Holy Father underwent thoracic surgery as scheduled.

“To ensure a complete resection, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique.

“Intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from preoperative tests.



“Following the surgery, the Pope woke up normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the 10th floor.

“The procedure was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He is expected to remain in hospital for a week.

His diagnosis marks the first major health issue of his 17-month tenure.

News.title: ‘He treated me like an animal’…Every claim made at Brand ‘rape’ trial as he ‘abused 6 women to satisfy sexual appetite’
News.content:
Next

RUSSELL Brand’s rape trial began today with allegations of “Basil Fawlty silly walks” and the comic being painted as a “ruthless and manipulative” predator.

Brand, 51, is accused of forcing six women into sexual acts and kissing and groping them in an “obsessive” campaign to sleep with 5,000 women.



He allegedly preyed on the complainants between 1999 and 2009 in a bid to satisfy his “voracious” sexual appetite.

Some of his accusers claim he laughed at them after they had tried to repel his advances, while members of his entourage have been accused of failing to step in to stop him.



Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC also dubbed the comedian a “sexual predator” who was “ruthless, calculated and manipulative”.

She also said women have told police he was “childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met”.



Brand has denied three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault against six women.

Here are the allegations made by each of the six women on the first day of the trial…

‘Basil Fawlty silly walks’ before Labour conference ‘rape’

Prosecutors alleged Brand stripped half-naked and performed silly walks “like Basil Fawlty” before raping a woman he met at the Labour Party conference.

The court heard the woman initially thought Brand was gay and invited him to her hotel room to continue their conversation after a cabaret show in 1999.



She alleged he emerged topless from the toilet and “was prancing around the room, a bit like an ostrich, doing silly walks like Basil Fawlty”.

She asked him why he had taken his clothes off and he allegedly replied: “It’s okay, it’s just how I am, don’t worry…. I’m mostly naked at home.”

The woman, who was aged in her 20s at the time, claimed he pushed her onto the bed and left her struggling to breathe before allegedly raping her.



The court heard from a former friend Mark Pinheiro, who said Brand returned to his entourage’s flat after allegedly raping the woman and told them to “pack up their stuff” because they “had to leave town immediately”.

He later said that “things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand, and he thinks that maybe he did go a little bit too far”, jurors heard.

‘Bewildered and shocked’

The second complainant worked at MTV at the time of an alleged incident in 2001.

While showing Brand where the toilets were he allegedly said to her “come in, go on, come in” and grabbed her hard by her forearm, prosecutors say.

The court was told he beckoned her into the toilets with a “desperate wild-eyed look on his face”.



She managed to pull herself away, and to release his grasp, it was claimed.

The MTV worker was left feeling “bewildered and shocked” by the alleged assault by Brand.

‘Lunged’ at while talking about Big Brother

One alleged victim said Brand “lunged” at her and grabbed her breasts when they were talking about Big Brother in a Soho bar in July 2004.

Prosecutors allege the comedian had a “big, weird grin” on his face.

The woman says Brand “quite strongly” pulled her into the toilet and orally raped her, despite her saying “I don’t want to do this”.



The prosecutor told jurors: “He just said ‘Oh come on don’t be a spoil sport, you want to’ or something along those lines”.

‘Complete disbelief that no one helped’

The fourth alleged victim was in her 20s and working at a radio station in 2004 or 2005 when Brand allegedly sexually assaulted her after she had left a room at work.

Brand, who the court heard was with a woman and some men at the time, allegedly “grabbed her by the face with both hands” before pushing her against a wall.



Jurors heard he then kissed her “sloppily and aggressively” and also allegedly grabbed at her body, her breasts, sides and buttocks in a “rough, fast and frenzied” way.

The woman said she looked to members of Brand’s entourage, “hoping they would intervene”, but she claims they took no action.

“She finally managed to push him away, saying words to him to the effect of ‘f*** off’”, Ms Karmy-Jones added.

“Mr Brand stumbled backwards at that final push and just sniggered – like it was a joke.”

Treated ‘like an animal’

Brand apologised to one of the women after she told him he treated her “like an animal” during an alleged rape, the court was told.



The fifth alleged victim met Brand after seeing his show at the Hammersmith Apollo in London with a friend in 2009.

He allegedly told her his age range was from “16 to death” before she was invited to a backstage bar where they kissed and had a threesome.

The woman claims she went to his home the next day where Brand told her: “Your hair smells funny”.

He then made her take a shower and wash her hair while he watched through a glass shower cubicle, it was said.

Ms Karmy-Jones said once in the bedroom, they had consensual sex but afterwards Brand “flipped” the woman on to her front and on all fours and allegedly penetrated her anally.



Afterwards, jurors heard the comedian told her to “clean up the mess you have made”.

Ms Karmy-Jones KC said Brand texted the woman the following year after seeing each other in a chance encounter in Scotland.

She said she messaged Brand: “Why are you even messaging me?”, and he replied: “Because you’re dirty, and I wanna push you further.”

The court heard she replied: “I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal”, before Brand replied: “I’m sorry.”

‘Startled and incredibly uncomfortable’

The sixth woman worked for Channel 4 when she met Brand while he was filming a project.



She said she was informed Brand was “unhappy” and the situation would not improve unless she gave him a massage, jurors were told.

The woman claimed he walked up to a chair she was sitting on and placed his head directly into her groin area.

Ms Karmy-Jones said: “He was kneeling at the side of her with his forehead on her right thigh and his shoulders pressed against her left thigh.

“(The alleged victim) was given no time to react – she ‘froze.’

“The defendant’s face was pressed deep in her groin area and when he spoke she could feel his breath.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

He allegedly said “come on then, do it”, leaving the woman feeling “startled and incredibly uncomfortable”, the court was told.

The trial continues.

News.title: Brit soldier who had ‘medieval’ cannon & explosives at home among huge range of weapons is jailed
News.content:
COOKER'S CACHE Brit soldier who had ‘medieval’ cannon & explosives at home among huge range of weapons is jailed







Next

A SOLDIER has been jailed after cops found a “homemade cannon” and explosives at his home while promoting extreme right-wing views.

British Army chef, Mark Broadhurst, was arrested in 2024 after a range of weaponry and explosive substances was found at his home.



When police raided his quarters at the barracks and his home address in Derbyshire, they found gunpowder and a home-made cannon, described by an expert as “crude” and similar to a 14th century gun.

The 28-year-old was also found to have crossbows and bolts, six large knives and a baseball bat.



Broadhurst was then jailed for 46 months after the soldier admitted possessing explosives and a firearms offence.

The ex-soldier initially denied the offences were terror-related, but the judge found that he was trying to impress other members of extreme right-wing groups and encourage them in their violent, racist and anti-authority ideology.

Matthew Donkin KC, prosecuting, said most of the activity surrounding the offending happened before he joined the army.

Counter terror police became aware of Broadhurst while carrying out investigations on other members of extreme right-wing groups and saw his messages on two online forums.



Mr Donkin said: “The things he was posting were hateful, racist, aggressive and they demonstrated clear, extreme right-wing beliefs and views.”

The messages demonstrated a hatred of “black, Asian, Muslim and Jewish people”, the prosecution said.

He made references to anarchy, the end of society and his preparedness to bring this about, the Crown said.



He wanted to be “in history books and criminal records” for terrorism and killing police officers, the court heard.

And he shared the online order he made for the ingredients to make gunpowder.

Jim Littlehales, defending, read a reference from a superior officer which described the chef as “excellent at mentoring junior members of the catering team” and said he worked to the highest standards.

Mr Littlehales said the firearm he made was not used to threaten anyone.

The judge sentenced Broadhurst on the basis that he made the weapon and gunpowder so he would be taken seriously by other members of the extreme right-wing groups.



After the sentencing, Detective Chief Superintendent James Dunkerley, head of Counter Terrorism Policing North East, said: “Whilst Broadhurst pleaded guilty to these offences, he did not accept that his intent had a terrorist motivation.

“A thorough investigation was conducted which uncovered an extreme right-wing mindset and he was engaging in extensive conversations online with other individuals who hold similar views.

“He was proactively ordering components to make explosives, plus he amassed multiple weapons including firearms.

“After hearing the extensive evidence compiled throughout our investigation, the judge was satisfied his offending had a terrorist connection.

“I welcome the sentence handed down to Broadhurst which reflects his mindset and the danger he posed to the public.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Frank Ferguson, head of the Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said: “Mark Broadhurst was clearly interested in violence and developing weapons that had the ability to cause untold harm to innocent people.

“He was immersed in extremist material and maintained close contact with three now-convicted terrorists inspired by SS tactics and supremacist ideology over a prolonged period.”

News.title: Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed President Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday, as the Ukrainian leader looks to shore up his European allies five years into Russia's war on Ukraine.

Burnham told Zelensky that Britain "would forever stand by you" and that he was accelerating the delivery of air defences to Ukraine.

Burnham previously told MPs that he would try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States and that Ukraine won't leave "empty-handed".

The two leaders met at No 10 Downing Street where Zelensky was welcomed with a military ceremonial guard - thought to be a first for a foreign leader.

BBC World News correspondent Joe Inwood explains what we know about the meeting.

Read more about the meeting in London.

News.title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
News.content:
The fourth complainant says Brand pushed her up against a wall at Capital Radio in 2004 or 2005 and kissed her "sloppily and aggressively", and "grabbed her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks, aggressively".

She was able to push him away and he "just sniggered, like it was a joke", the prosecutor said.

The jury then heard how the fifth complainant says she met Brand when he was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009.

The prosecution said their encounter began with consensual activity, but that he raped her anally on a later occasion.

The jury heard how the woman "spent months and years blaming herself", becoming anxious and unwell.

They were told Brand texted the woman after seeing her at an event the following summer, saying: "I wanna push you further."

She is said to have replied: "I think you pushed me far enough â you treated me like an animal." He allegedly replied: "I'm sorry."

The sixth complainant - who has accused Brand of sexual assault - says he demanded a massage when she was on a work assignment in 2009.

He "fell to his knees and placed his head directly into her groin area", the prosecution said.

After the accounts of the final two women were heard, the prosecutor said Brand told police in 2023 "he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting".

On Wednesday afternoon, Brand's former flatmate Mark Pinheiro was the first witness to give evidence.

Pinheiro told jurors that Brand had told him he may have gone a "bit too far" with a woman when visiting the Labour Party conference in 1999.

"He said that things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand, and he thinks that maybe he did go a little bit too far.

"Those were his words - 'I think I may have gone a bit too far'."

Pinheiro was pressed under cross-examination about whether he accurately remembered the comment, but he told the court he was sure Brand had said "things may have gone a little bit too far" or "I may have taken things a little too far".

The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

Brand was accompanied by his wife Laura to the court on Wednesday.

He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

News.title: Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support
News.content:
Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action.

The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.

In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books in the UK.

"I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said.

Ebook editions have already been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock of physical copies.

Waterstones confirmed to the BBC that Faber had advised there were no restrictions on booksellers keeping their current copies on the shelves.

Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData.

Normal People was released in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones.

Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You.

Publisher Faber told BBC News: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work.

"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format."

Faber added: "We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories."

News.title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
News.content:
Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years.

Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from Â£7 to Â£10.

Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from Â£6 to Â£8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from Â£5 to Â£8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City.

The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".

The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives".

News.title: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments
News.content:
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.

Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast undercover filming, gathered over a year, of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform,, external a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".

Labour described the investigation as "truly sickening" adding: "Nigel Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples."

A Reform spokesman said: "Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced" and that in some cases there had been suspensions.

The spokesman added that the party had improved its procedures but some individuals who did not share their values would occasionally make it through vetting.

ITV's filming involved eight figures in Reform â the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total.

Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.

ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.

These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, having defected from the Conservative Party in 2025.

He told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites".

Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than one per cent of British population can be non-white."

The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons," and would be continuing as an independent councillor.

Reform Party leader Nigel Farage has repeatedly said he wants to get rid of those he has called "bad apples."

Two years ago he said he didn't want Reform to be "a sectarian or racially based party in any way at all".

"I'm going to be absolutely ruthless about it," he said.

In a statement released after ITV's film was broadcast, Reform said the party "had improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting".

The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."

A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

News.title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
News.content:
On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in the quiet Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.

Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"

Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.

The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (Â£11,000).

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.

In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".

Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.

It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.

They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.

"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.

"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."

News.title: UK threatens to ban Eritreans over migrant return policy
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders.

From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs.

Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans.

Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June - accounting for 18% of arrivals, external, according to figures from the House of Commons Library.

The Eritrean embassy in London has been contacted for comment.

"Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused," said Mahmood.

She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate".

The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.

The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission.

The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.

Earlier this year, the UK threatened bans against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Restrictions were announced against the DRC last year, but the Home Office said these have been lifted after co-operation on returns improved.

Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced.

When announcing changes to the UK's asylum system in November, Mahmood said visa penalties would be applied to countries that failed to co-operate with returns policies.

Penalties included an "emergency brake" on visas for countries with high asylum claims until they take back citizens in the UK illegally.

According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year.

There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year - an 8% increase on the same period last year.

Of those who had been returned, less than 6,000 has been convicted of a criminal offence.

News.title: What we know about the Pope's lung cancer diagnosis
News.content:
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had a successful surgery to remove part of his right lung, the Vatican has confirmed.

The Pope, 71, underwent a 90-minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where he is expected to stay for about a week.

BBC Southern and Eastern Europe Correspondent Sarah Rainsford is in St. Peter's Square in the Vatican as people sent their well wishes to the pontiff.

News.title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
News.content:
The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging".

William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication".

His family added: "It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process."

City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death.

The park remains closed and a reopening date has not yet been confirmed.

"William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said.

The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time".

"The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued.

"The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."

News.title: We are behind you and that will not change, PM tells Zelensky
News.content:
"We are behind you and that will not change," Andy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelensky, as he hosted the Ukrainian leader in Downing Street.

Zelensky was in London as part of efforts to reinforce backing from allies after Donald Trump called for him to go and lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.

The prime minister said Ukraine was willing to discuss an energy ceasefire proposed by the US president but said Russia's response had been "further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine".

Zelensky said: "Our people, we survived and continue to do this because we have strong partners and I'm very proud that we have one of the strongest partners in our history and it's your people, Andy."

The Ukrainian president was greeted with a hug from Burnham, cheers from civil servants and a rare honour guard as he arrived in Downing Street.

Ahead of Zelensky's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.

News.title: I do not have confidence UK is safe from Russian threats, says Swinney
News.content:
Asked about the MI5 chief's comments, the first minister said he was "very worried" about a "lack of coastal and offshore protection".

He identified waters north of Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity.

"I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News.

"There's an obligation on the United Kingdom government to make sure that the country is safe. And I don't think the defence posture of the United Kingdom enables me to have that confidence."

Scotland is home to the UK's nuclear submarine fleet at Faslane, west of Glasgow. The SNP wants those weapons to be removed, but is in favour of an independent Scotland joining Nato.

Swinney insisted that independence would not hamper Scotland's security, but rather give the country "more choices".

The SNP leader said he had "always been a believer in defence co-operation between Scotland and other countries", citing Canada joining the EU's SAFE defence programme, external.

Responding to the first minister's comments, a Ministry of Defence Spokesperson said:

"The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe, and this government is investing Â£298bn over the next four years to ensure we can tackle rising threats.

"The Navy is helping to patrol Nato's northern flank, with this year's carrier strike group deploying to the Arctic and the high north.

"To tackle these threats, we're also investing in new frigates for the Navy and high-tech uncrewed vessels as part of our Hybrid Navy, backed by Â£1.5bn in funding."

Delivering a speech at the UN General Assembly, external last month, Burnham said his government would invest in defence and build up the UK's "hard power and deterrence".

He added: "But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric. Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation."

News.title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
News.content:
On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.

The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.

It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".

But the statement did not specify that this referred to, external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.

A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at Â£300 for hospitality.

Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately Â£699.

Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a Â£150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.

But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.

BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.

Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman.

But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount.

Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City.

"This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football."

And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners".

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester".

"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."

Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me."

With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club".

When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement.

The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned.

In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations.

The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than Â£830m into their football operations.

Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict.

Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).

Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report.

News.title: Teen shot friend by mistake, inquest told
News.content:
A teenager told an inquest he fatally shot his friend with an air rifle at a house party after mistaking the trigger for the safety catch.

Connor Bell, 17, from Tadley, had been drinking with friends at a house in Chineham, near Basingstoke, on 8 November 2025 when he was hit by a pellet fired by Jack Beechy, the Winchester inquest heard.

The pellet entered through his right eye socket, causing an "unsurvivable" brain injury and cardiac arrest. He died at Southampton General Hospital two days later.

Coroner Jason Pegg recorded a conclusion of accidental death, exacerbated by a lack of weapons-handling skills.

The inquest heard Joshua Brown, now 18, had agreed with his parents that only a couple of friends would come round and the air rifle would stay locked in a cupboard.

But he said more friends came than he had told his parents about, and the group drank vodka, cider and beer.

He took out the .177 calibre rifle and it was used to shoot at bottles in the garden from the conservatory.

Beechy, now 18, said he was "a little bit drunk" when Brown asked him to put the rifle away.

He fired off the remaining pellets from the conservatory because he "thought it would be safer", believing the gun was then empty.

Beechy said that as he walked into the kitchen, with Bell standing nearby, he fired the rifle by mistake.

News.title: 'Dark day for Lewis' as one fisherman dead and two missing
News.content:
Police say a body has been found in the search for three men who were onboard a fishing boat that has gone missing off the Western Isles.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) said the alarm was raised about 21:20 on Tuesday when it emerged the boat, called the Kilda, was overdue from Lewis.

A plane, two helicopters, two lifeboats and volunteers searched off the Port of Ness in north Lewis. Police have warned the public not to make their own searches due to bad weather.

Local councillor Kenneth Macleod said it was a "very dark day" for islanders, and their thoughts were with the families of the three men, and First Minister John Swinney said his heart went out to those involved.

Police Scotland said the man's body was found about 02:45, but the remaining two men and their boat remained unaccounted for.

News.title: Swimmer Archie Goodburn thanks prime minister as brain cancer review announced
News.content:
Swimmer Archie Goodburn has been successful in his efforts to improve brain cancer care for patients as the UK government announce new measures.

The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham after making a tearful TV appeal for more investment to be put into brain cancer research.

After the meeting, Burnham announced a new national brain cancer clinical lead and promised a review of brain cancer progress and action to get patients treatment sooner.

Goodburn, 25, thanked the prime minister and said all three of his requests have been "promised to some extent" but "fleshing out" needs to be done on the details.

The prime minister described the swimmer an "inspiration to us all" and said he was "delighted" to welcome him to Downing Street.

Burnham said: "He has spoken passionately about the need for change on brain cancer, and he's right: progress hasn't been good enough, here or anywhere else.

"Families facing this disease can't afford to wait."

Goodburn reached the final of the 50m breaststroke at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

He said he went for medical tests after suffering from numbness and seizures during training for the 2024 Olympic trials.

He was diagnosed with three large oligodendrogliomas, a rare type of cancer which can affect the brain and spinal cord.

The Edinburgh-born athlete underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy to treat the tumours, but surgery to remove them was found to be impossible.

News.title: Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
News.content:
A civil servant is accused of earning almost Â£350,000 by juggling five full-time public sector roles - using sick notes and working from home to cope with the workload.

Kashim Chowdhury allegedly held multiple government jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning Â£350,000 overall.

The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told he wore white make-up during a video call with his boss to try to look ill, but the make-up began peeling off his skin.

Chowdury, a 55-year-old from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The jury was told that Chowdhury got jobs by making ''false representations'' about his employment status whilst applying. Over three years he held overlapping jobs at Tower Hamlets Council in east London, the Home Office, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency and the Department of Health and Social Care.

The jury was told that in 2023 his manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him to discuss his sick leave.

Ms Adams claims Chowdhury was wearing make-up on his face to appear ill - and that during the meeting the make-up started to separate on his forehead showing his real skin underneath. At the time of the call he is alleged to have been paid for five full time jobs.

Lucy Organ, for the prosecution, told the court: "There could be no doubt about it, the defendant had applied make-up to his face for this Teams meeting to try and pretend to his line manager that he was unwell.

"This almost laughable incident demonstrates, we say, quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit."

Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work from home culture that began during the Covid pandemic. The court was told that Chowdhury had told his employers that he had to work from home to care for his "unwell" mother.

But the prosecutor, Ms Organ, said his workload eventually became "too much to cope with" and his performance suffered.

The court heard that he was signed off work from some jobs due to "mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder", but he did not hand his sick note to all his employers.

Jurors heard that the alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra to them.

The trial continues.

News.title: Scaramucci deadpans over Trump fixation with Husted’s butt: ‘Could say he’s bi-curious’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Anthony Scaramucci, Donald Trump’s one-time communications director, has thoughts about the president’s fixation with Senator Jon Husted’s butt.

Trump made headlines earlier this week for some odd comments he made about Husted’s looks as he stumped for the Republican in Ohio ahead of November’s midterm elections.

“I'm standing over here, and I don't do this with men very often. I started examining his body because I didn't know he was a great athlete, and I looked, and I watched up and down,” Trump said of Husted, a former college football player, at a rally Monday night in Youngstown. “I looked at his a**, and I looked at the whole, and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He's got these like claws.”

When CNN host Kasie Hunt asked Scaramucci Wednesday about Trump’s current headspace, he said with a straight face, “Well, you could go with two tracks with that. You could say that the president’s bi-curious by the way he’s talking about the guy — it was sort of awkward and weird.

“Or you could say that the president is an entertainer and he thinks his job is to go to those things and make people laugh.”

open image in gallery Anthony Scaramucci, Donald Trump’s one-time communications director, has joked about the president’s fixation with Republican Senator Jon Husted’s butt ( Getty Images )

Bi-curious is a term coined for people who are exploring their potential bisexuality.

Trump —who has been married to his third wife, Melania Trump, for two decades — has been known to make colorful comments about other men. Scaramucci specifically alluded to the president’s fascination with golfer Arnold Palmer’s phallus.

During a rally in Pennsylvania in the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, Trump said, “Arnold Palmer was all man, and I say that in all due respect to women, and I love women.”

"I refuse to say it, but when he took the showers with other pros, they came out of there. They said, 'Oh my God. That's unbelievable,'" Trump said with a chuckle. "I had to say.”

open image in gallery 'I'm standing over here, and I don't do this with men very often. I started examining his body because I didn't know he was a great athlete, and I looked, and I watched up and down,' Trump said of Husted, a former college football player, at a rally Monday night in Youngstown, Ohio ( Getty Images )

Scaramucci spent just 11 days as Trump’s communications director in 2017 during the president’s first term before being fired.

He has recently been in the news after an awkward and short press briefing by the new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia.

Zacharia’s dismal performance at the podium Tuesday prompted jokes that she may not last as long as Scaramucci.

Scaramucci, now a Trump critic, even chimed in, writing on X, “The clock is running. Thus far 1/11th of a Scaramucci.”

open image in gallery ‘You could say that the president’s bi curious by the way he’s talking about the guy,’ Scaramucci said in reaction to Trump’s bizarre remarks. ‘Or you could say that the president is an entertainer and he thinks his job is to go to those things and make people laugh’ ( Getty Images for Vox Media )

Despite prediction market Polymarket already taking bets on when Zacharia, who previously served as senior communications advisor for Trump’s Truth Social platform, will be out of the White House, Scaramucci told Hunt on The Arena Wednesday, “I don’t think she’s going to get fired.”

“People that are talking about her getting fired, I think, don’t understand the current White House, and she’s done nothing wrong to deserve to be fired,” Scaramucci said. “Will she get to the podium any time soon? Probably not. She probably needs media training.”

While Scaramucci doesn’t think Zacharia will be forced out, he doesn’t think she’s a right fit for the job either, saying she “comes across as too nice of a person.

“You got to have mendacity in your spirit to work for Donald Trump in that position.”

News.title: Even after explosive diarrhea outbreak Trump’s FDA looks to ease food requirements
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

As federal health officials work through the aftermath of a major Cyclospora outbreak, the Food and Drug Administration under the Trump administration is moving to ease food safety record-keeping requirements for thousands of smaller restaurants.

The nationwide outbreak of the parasitic infection, tied to contaminated iceberg lettuce from a Taylor Farms facility in Mexico, had hospitalized hundreds and recorded two deaths in Michigan — the hardest-hit state — following exposures earlier in the year. The microscopic parasite, which spreads when human waste contaminates irrigation water or crops, causes severe nausea, dehydration and explosive diarrhea. Symptoms often do not appear until two weeks after consumption, leaving health officials to trace contaminated produce long after it has cleared restaurant kitchens.

Yet despite those supply-chain tracking hurdles, the FDA is proposing to exempt food businesses generating between $250,000 and $1 million in annual food sales from detailed supply-chain tracking regulations, as reported by Restaurant Business Magazine.

Passed during the Obama administration under the 2011 Food Safety Modernization Act, the traceability framework gives the federal government broader authority to mandate recalls and track contaminated ingredients back to their source during foodborne illness investigations.

Full enforcement of the Food Traceability Rule was scheduled for 2028, but expanding the exemption would relieve many independent restaurant operators from the cost and work of tracking high-risk inventory, such as leafy greens, soft cheeses, eggs and nut butters.

open image in gallery The Food and Drug Administration is moving to exempt thousands of smaller restaurants from detailed food safety tracking rules ( Getty Images )

Agency officials said that the proposed flexibility was not final and that additional adjustments remained under consideration.

The proposed rule comes amid several other regulatory shifts across the restaurant and food production sectors.

In New York City, Council members introduced a bill requiring third-party delivery services to deploy tracking technology on courier e-bikes to monitor traffic infractions.

The system would track speeding, sidewalk riding above 4 mph and wrong-way travel on single-direction streets. Couriers receiving three notifications within seven days would be temporarily barred from accepting deliveries until completing a road safety course, and delivery apps would need to file quarterly safety reports with the city.

open image in gallery Under the proposed policy, independent food businesses making between $250,000 and $1 million annually would be spared from tracking high-risk items such as leafy greens, eggs and soft cheeses ( Getty Images )

In food manufacturing, the FDA finalized a rule permitting producers to use sodium substitutes, including potassium chloride, yeast extracts or MSG, in standard food formulations that previously required table salt. Designed to support national efforts to reduce sodium consumption, the measure gives manufacturers more flexibility to reformulate packaged goods while offering restaurants expanded options for low-sodium menu items.

And in municipal infrastructure, Philadelphia unveiled two prototype outdoor dining enclosures at LOVE Park, developed by local design firms under Mayor Cherelle Parker’s PHL Open for Business initiative.

The city plans to evaluate public feedback on the structures, which feature customized aluminum frames and recycled plastic paneling, before offering both designs as free downloadable templates for local restaurant owners. The prototypes will remain on display through November 23.

News.title: Costa Rica opens a Bukele-style mega-prison. Here's how it got here
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Costa Rica, considered for decades a peaceful enclave in turbulent Central America, has now made fighting drug trafficking one of its main goals. And it is turning to one of its Central American neighbors for inspiration in its hardline crackdown.

On Wednesday, President Laura Fernández inaugurated a mega-prison that emulates the Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT) that has become a symbol of Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele's security strategy.

Bukele has managed to reduce murders to a historic low in El Salvador but faces accusations of abuses during the state of emergency that began in 2022 and has imprisoned more than 91,000 people.

Costa Rica is not the first to turn its attention to the man who has proclaimed himself the “coolest dictator in the world.” Ecuador has done it. So have the new presidents of Peru and Colombia. From Honduras to the Southern Cone, these countries are joining the hardline security strategy also endorsed by U.S. President Donald Trump.

Now, Costa Rica says it will incarcerate its most dangerous criminals in the High-Containment Center against Organized Crime, with a capacity for 5,100 inmates and a cost of $35 million. Here's how the country that was once the region's most stable got here.

The cocaine route to Europe

For decades, Costa Rica was a “passive” transit zone for drugs from South America, according to the organization Insight Crime. But without an army, and with extensive jungle and ports on both coasts, it began to attract Mexican and Colombian cartels.

At the end of the last decade, a new cargo terminal transformed the Caribbean port of Limón into a storage and transshipment point for cocaine destined for Europe, according to the U.S. State Department, which, in a 2025 report, also detected fentanyl distribution in the Central American country.

Now, the two major Mexican cartels, Sinaloa and Jalisco, are present in the country, as are the Colombian Clan del Golfo, the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua — all considered terrorist organizations by the United States — and Italian mafias, while local cartels proliferate, explained Vanda Felbab-Brown, an organized crime researcher at the Brookings Institution.

Homicides raise alarms

The cartels’ interest in new routes and the rivalry between the two major Mexican cartels “pushed local proxies to fight with each other and then drove homicides up” in Costa Rica, Felbab-Brown noted. Payments to these gangs in drugs developed local markets that further increased the violence, and the authorities felt overwhelmed.

The alarm was raised in 2023 when the country registered a record 907 homicides — a figure that has decreased, but only slightly — and the government acknowledged that they were mostly due to organized crime.

Insecurity, although far from that of Ecuador or Mexico, became the biggest concern for Costa Ricans and was a key factor in Fernández’s election.

It was then that Fernández’s predecessor, Rodrigo Chaves, sought out Bukele, whose success in cutting down killings have led his counterparts in the region to turn to him for inspiration on security policy. Chaves bestowed him with a diplomatic honor, and sent his security minister to visit the CECOT. The Salvadoran president, in turn, donated the design for the prison to the Costa Rican government.

The CECOT has become a symbol of Bukele’s security policy and is increasingly being imitated. Ecuador’s Daniel Noboa opened a similar prison last year. Honduras planned something similar on an island, though it has not yet been built. And Peru’s Keiko Fujimori has just announced a trip to El Salvador in response to the rise in homicides and extortion.

The measures tend to be popular, and a large portion of the Costa Rican population supports the new mega-prison.

“Many people are afraid,” said Carlos Ávila, a business administrator. “I think it’s good that they’re building a prison and isolating the criminals.”

But it remains to be seen how criminal gangs and society will react to Costa Rica’s new prison, said Felbab-Brown.

“Orchestrating mass arrests at the scale that we see in El Salvador might be both politically unpopular (in Costa Rica) and opposed and challenged also in terms of intelligence,” she said.

Extraditions, the other way to fight crime

Chaves opted for another tool against crime: in 2025, he carried out a constitutional reform to allow Costa Ricans to be extradited for drug trafficking and terrorism offenses.

In March of this year, the first extraditions to the United States took place, including that of Celso Gamboa, former security minister and Supreme Court justice, accused of drug trafficking.

In recent months there have been high-profile arrests, such as that of Alejandro Arias Monge, alias “Diablo,” the country’s most wanted drug trafficker, and the president announced investigations into two hundred police officers.

Meanwhile, Costa Rica remains a staunch ally of Trump, with agreements to receive deported migrants and participation in the Shield of the Americas, which involves maritime patrols.

___

Verza reported from Mexico City.

News.title: Reform suspends members after undercover investigation exposes councillors making racist remarks
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in
