In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Mike Tyson admits he suffered near-fatal overdoses at lowest point of his crippling drug issues... and reveals unusual remedy that saved him
Sports.content:
Mike Tyson admits he suffered near-fatal overdoses at lowest point of his crippling drug issues... and reveals unusual remedy that saved him

Mike Tyson has claimed he was saved by a powerful psychedelic from the toxin of a toad after suffering near-fatal drug overdoses.

The legendary boxer, 60, opened up on the terrifying health scares in a new Netflix docuseries, TYSON.

The former heavyweight champion detailed how he nearly died after battling alcohol and drug addiction, claiming: 'When I think about a low point, I think about this — OD'ing. I'm bleeding out, my nose is bleeding and I'm hysterical. I'm sweating.

'I OD'd, I've done it plenty of times but this one was a little more extreme than others.'

But Tyson survived after a shaman gave him 5-MeO-DMT, a substance found in the secretion of the Bofu alvarius toad. Early studies suggest it could help treat anxiety and depression.

The boxer claimed he has used the psychedelic 'over 100 times' and it helped him come off cocaine and alcohol.

Mike Tyson has claimed he was saved by a powerful psychedelic from the toxin of a toad

The legendary boxer, 60, opened up on near-fatal drug overdoses in a new Netflix docuseries

A shaman gave him 5-MeO-DMT, a substance found in the secretion of the Bofu Alvarius toad

'At the time we had this friend, he knew a shaman who does this thing called 5-MeO-DMT, it comes from the Bufo alvarius toad,' his third wife, Lakiha 'Kiki' Spicer, explained.

'Whatever kind of addictions or things that you're going through, it helps level them in your mind.'

According to the UC Berkeley Center for the Science of Psychedelics, 5-MeO-DMT - which is also known as 'Bufo' or 'God molecule' or 'The Toad' - is 'usually inhaled through vaporizing or snorting.'

The drug, which is illegal to use recreationally in the United States, 'induces feelings of awe, visual and auditory hallucinations, and other sensations' with effects 'starting just a few seconds after ingestion and lasting about twenty to thirty minutes.'

In the new series, the 60-year-old is filmed smoking the drug at a treatment center.

'It blew my mind. I’ve done it over 100 times,' Tyson claimed. 'Any time I have to make a big decision about anything, I take the toad. I haven’t used cocaine and drink since.'

Sports.title: Frank Warren calls on Oleksandr Usyk to return and make more boxing history as he plots huge 12 months of heavyweight mega-fights in the United States: 'My door is open'
Sports.content:
Frank Warren is ready to cross the Atlantic on his tidal wave of thunderous world heavyweight title fights.

Having established Queensberry as the dominant boxing promoters in the UK, Warren is primed to pitch for big fights in the US. Not least in New York’s fabled Madison Square Garden.

This Saturday’s Slugfest II between Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley at the O2 and December’s Battle of the Aged between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua in Cardiff - both for versions of the world championship - will be the prelude to a 2027 crammed with sell-out battles at sky-high prices.

They will involve the winners – and possibly the losers – of those fights, plus Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic, the Croatian iron man who beat him for one of the titles, and Agit Kabayel, who will shortly defend another of the belts in front of a 50,000 stadium crowd in Germany.

‘After 12 months putting on the big fights the fans love,’ says Warren, 'we are looking at a year chock-full of multiple heavyweight events involving all these guys and more.’

If Wardley gets revenge over Dubois by regaining his WBO title one of those happenings could be a trilogy match. Fury v Dubois is on the hob. As is the conquering of America., To which end Queensberry have signed Jared Anderson, the only heavyweight over there who looks remotely capable of coping in this company. Says Warren: ‘Jared will be a key part of our US expansion.’

Frank Warren is plotting a huge 12 months of heavyweight mega-fights in the USA next year

The promoter has invited Oleksandr Usyk to return and 'make even more boxing history'

That move will pitch Warren into a promotional rivalry with Dana White, the UFC boss whose new boxing company Zuffa has muscled into a share of the Fury-Joshua action – and a war of insults with AJ’s promoter Eddie Hearn.

Warren has watched those bitter exchanges with amused interest as well as reflections on his own disputes with Hearn down the years and says: ‘Nobody pays good money to watch promoters squabbling. The fans only have eyes for the men in the ring. I get on fine with Dana. Like me, he relishes competition.

'As far as Queensberry is concerned we are enjoying fabulous times the like of which has never been seen this side of the Atlantic.‘

Their heavyweight roster will be supplemented further by the return to action of popular Kiwi Joseph Parker from the positive drugs test which cost him a world title.

Most intriguingly of all, Warren is keeping tabs on Oleksandr Usyk. The Ukrainian genius who is the greatest boxer of two generations vacated all his undisputed heavyweight titles ‘to give the new generation their chance.’

But he has never triggered the retirement which would have had him join Rocky Marciano as the only heavyweights to hang up the gloves undefeated. Instead he has been keeping active in crossover combat while reviewing other options. Such as returning to the squared ring, in which he defeated Joshua, Fury and Dubois twice each.

‘If Oleksandr wants to make even more boxing history, ’ says Warren, ‘then Queensberry is the only place for him to come. The door to all our heavyweights is not just open. It’s off its hinges.’

The return of the Cat of Kyiv would be one of Uncle Frank’s greatest coups.

Sports.title: Floyd Mayweather Jr to fly with Trump on Air Force One and attend President's Arizona rally as he continues to turn to A-list athletes before crunch midterms
Sports.content:
Floyd Mayweather Jr to fly with Trump on Air Force One and attend President's Arizona rally as he continues to turn to A-list athletes before crunch midterms

Boxing legend Floyd Mayweather Jr. will join Donald Trump on Air Force One on Wednesday as the President jets from Las Vegas to a rally in Arizona, The Daily Mail can reveal.

Mayweather, 49, a Vegas native, who happens to have strong business ties in Arizona, is expected to attend the rally with Trump in Bullhead City as the President looks to boost Republican candidates ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.

It is unclear whether the undefeated fighter is expected to take the stage alongside Trump following recent onstage appearances from fellow athletes.

Dennis Rodman, Mike Tyson, Jake Paul, Roger Clemens and Jon Gruden have all made appearances at recent rallies in support of Trump.

Mayweather has long been an outspoken supporter of Trump, hailing him the 'best president in US history' last year.

He attended Trump's first inauguration as president and supported him throughout his first term in the Oval Office.

Boxing legend Floyd Mayweather Jr. joined Donald Trump on Air Force One on Wednesday

Policy-wise, Mayweather and Trump have been aligned on a few issues, including in the Middle East. Mayweather is a staunch supporter of Israel and donated $1million to the United Hatzalah of Israel in 2024.

'We had Trump before, we didn't appreciate him,' Mayweather told Fox Business in February of last year. 'I think Trump is a great president, actually he's the best president in my eyes, he's the best president we've ever had. Great business man and that's what it's about.'

'Trump has done an amazing job and a lot of people around America are upset. But no matter who goes into the White House, we're always upset. And I think Trump is the man for the job, he's the best president in my eyes.'

Mayweather's fellow boxing icon Tyson also joined Trump on the Presidential aircraft last week, making the journey from the White House to Syracuse, New York.

During his speech at the rally, Trump spotted Tyson in the crowd and invited the former boxing champion on stage.

'I think we have to call him up, Mike Tyson, will you get up here?' Trump said.

Fellow boxer Mike Tyson also joined the President at a rally in Syracuse, New York last week

As the President's athletic guest of the day, Tyson praised Trump in front of the Syracuse crowd, thanking him during a brief moment on stage.

'Thank you, thank you very much. I'm just happy to be up here with my president, President Trump. There's no way in the world I would ever be here if it wasn't for a president like Donald Trump,' Tyson said.

Trump was also joined by NBA icon Rodman in Durant, Oklahoma, and former NFL coach Gruden and influencer-turned-boxer Paul in Youngstown, Ohio.

He announced his intention to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to MLB legend Clemens when the former pitcher joined him at a rally in San Antonio, Texas.

Sports.title: He took a trip to Vegas with Elvis, wore a Man United scarf gifted by George Best and took Muhammad Ali the distance (twice)... now a new book lays bare the astonishing life of Joe Bugner
Sports.content:
Joe Bugner Jr is charting the occasions when his late father called someone ‘a f****** idiot’. It’s a conversation that finds room for both Elvis Presley and Russell Crowe.

‘I might have even been there when the Elvis one happened,’ says the son, aged 56. ‘I would have been tiny but I was definitely on that trip to Vegas.’

The occasion behind the tale was fairly spectacular – Joe Bugner, the Greek God of British heavyweight boxing, was in town for his first of two fights with Muhammad Ali, The Greatest. The year was 1973 and Elvis, The King, happened to be staying at the same hotel, so he invited both men to his suite for a gathering of divine beings.

‘Elvis gave Ali a robe with “People’s Choice” on the back for the ring walk,’ Bugner Jr recalls. ‘My dad asked something to the effect of “Where’s mine?” and Elvis then said something my dad didn’t like. I gather dad called him a “f****** idiot”. Or it might have been “d***head”.

‘He called a few people “f****** idiots”, actually. One of them was Russell Crowe. This was years later. He had originally hired my dad as a boxing consultant for Cinderella Man but then he went with someone else. My dad lost the plot on that!’

There’s a lot of laughter down the phone in this chat. But there’s also some sadness for Bugner Jr, because it was a year ago last month that his father passed away at 75 in Australia, which he had called home for four decades.

As a man who had once ranked among the most colourful, recognisable and contentious personalities in British sport, Bugner had incurred the erosions of dementia in the latter stages of his life.

‘It still hurts,’ says Bugner Jr. ‘I miss him. Dementia is terrible, it really is, but I’d say he had a good version of it. By that I mean he was happy.

Joe Bugner, pictured in 1972, finished his 32-year boxing career in 1999

Bugner tangled with Muhammad Ali for a second time in Kuala Lumpur in 1975

The pair appeared at a press conference to promote the fight and remained close

‘In his head, he was still 38 years old and getting ready for a boxing fight. The next day he might think he was doing an interview in the newspapers. In reality, he was just sat in his room at in the care home, but he was happy up until the last days of his life. And it was some life.’

The legacy of that life is why we are talking. Bugner Jr and the respected author David Tossell have collaborated on an excellent new book, The Bugner Identity, that dives into the enduring riddle of its title character.

That being the boy who fled Soviet-occupied Hungary on foot aged six, went the distance with Ali (twice) and Joe Frazier as a man, played football most Saturdays with Rod Stewart, golfed with Dean Martin, named a son after James Hunt, deployed Tom Jones as best man for his second wedding, and later blew his fortune on a wine business.

Showbiz types loved him, allowing a level of celebrity in the United States rarely matched by British athletes in subsequent decades, but boxing fans were far harder to convince, which was the cost of winning British, European and Commonwealth titles from the nation’s darling, Henry Cooper, in 1971.

Bugner was never forgiven for the receiving the favourable side of a razor-thin verdict. As Bugner himself once put it: ‘When I beat Henry Cooper I was no longer British. I was a Hungarian refugee.’

‘There was so much resentment from the Cooper fight,’ says Bugner Jr. ‘I spoke to my father about it so many times and probably watched it back even more.

‘The thing is, it was a close fight. In the Seventies and Eighties, if the champion was down by a point, he would still get the verdict, but if fight happened nowadays, I do believe he would have got the decision 100 per cent. Back then he became the villain for it.’

Older generations will be better placed to understand the tighter grip boxing possessed in that golden era. Likewise, they will likely know Bugner was hardly reluctant to lean into his role as the bad guy.

Rebranding himself as ‘Aussie Joe’ after emigrating to Australia in 1986 only widened certain rifts and he repeatedly claimed that he was hounded out of this country by the press. The truth probably lay somewhere in the middle.

Bugner pictured with second wife Marlane and their son Joseph Jr in 1972

Joe Bugner beat Henry Cooper in 1971 - and the British public never forgave him

‘Look, my dad was not above saying things for publicity!’ says Bugner Jr. ‘But he wasn’t a villain. He was a really nice, caring guy, and he always loved England. I can promise you, behind closed doors, he was always grateful for what he had in this country after arriving with nothing from Hungary.

‘The villain reputation stuck for some people, I suppose. I’ve thought about that a lot in the past year, but I’ll tell you what gave us a lot of comfort after he died – there was genuine warmth in what people wrote about him a year ago.

‘It was really touching and actually quite surprising. I think it would have surprised my dad a bit as well.’

The book will perhaps go some way to shifting perceptions further. The merit of Bugner’s sporting accomplishments has always been underrated, which seems bizarre in review of a career that spanned 1967 to 1999 and saw him take Ali to the cards in 1973 and 1975. In between those bouts, he contested the full 12 rounds of a classic with Frazier, but didn’t landed a credible world title.

‘One thing I won’t forget is Ali on Michael Parkinson’s show and really stuck up for dad,’ says Bugner Jr. ‘Parky had laid into him and Ali goes, “He's the only man that took me took me 15 rounds and took me 12 rounds, and you are telling me that he's a crap boxer. Does that mean you’re saying I'm a crap boxer?”

‘It’s strange to look back now and think how normal it felt for me to be around Ali growing up, but dad and Ali spent a lot of time together in and out of the ring. They were good friends.’

The subject leads Bugner Jr onto the other side of his father’s life – the remarkable cast of people in his orbit. Frank Sinatra and Oliver Reed were among those who fell in with Bugner during his LA years in the late Seventies and it was at Joan Collins’s house that he met his second wife, Marlene Carter.

Bugner dancing with USA's Miss World, Marjorie Wallace, in 1973

‘It’s only as an adult that you look back and realise it was quite unusual,’ says Bugner Jr. ‘I’d see them at the house and, like with Ali, it all seemed normal! I remember asking dad years ago why he supported Manchester United, because there wasn’t any obvious connection, but he had this United woolie hat and scarf. It was because George Best had given them to him.

‘I mean, Christ, my brother is called James because he was friends with James Hunt. He would play a bit of golf with Dean Martin, play football with Rod Stewart on a Saturday, Tom Jones was his best man – the way I saw it was he was a kind of a David Beckham figure in the Seventies. But he was a warm and funny guy, nice to anyone on the street, and people liked him.’

With the possible exceptions of Elvis and Crowe, of course. And many Cooper fans. But the book at least offers a wider context that might have been missed by some in the first telling of Bugner’s complicated life.

‘He did well for a for a for a kid that walked from Hungary to England and didn't have a pot to p*** in,’ says his son. ‘I’m super proud of him. He wasn’t a villain.’

The Bugner Identity, published by Pitch Publishing, is available now

Sports.title: Fabio Wardley admits he 'feels more natural' NOT being world champion ahead of Daniel Dubois rematch after being stopped in first bout
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley is delighted to be the white collar underdog rather than the recognised holder of a world title as he goes into Saturday's second slugfest with Daniel Dubois.

That unusual juxtaposition of psychological status gives the businessman disrupter of the ring order belief that he can spring a second upset on Dubois, the two-time champion.

Their first war for Wardley's WBO belt started with Dubois being knocked down early and Wardley being battered to a stoppage late.

'I've always been regarded as the underdog since I turned professional,' says Wardley as he opens the fight week conversation.

Then he adds: 'I love it. Honestly, it's great. It feels more natural for me. Weightless.

'Yes, it's fantastic being a world champion. That and having an undefeated record going in with such a good fighter as Daniel carried a level of weight.

Fabio Wardley (right) is relishing being the underdog the second time around against Daniel Dubois (left)

'But now I just feel free. Free of pressure. Talk around the fight has changed. I'm back to being expected to lose with things going bad for me. I'm the challenger and I'm the chaser.

'But for me it's just... "Ah, this is it". This is the nice bit I enjoy and still love however many years I've been on my way up. It feels great.'

Have any fighters had more fun being in a succession of brutal battles? But how does that improve his chances second time around with Dynamite Daniel?

'A relaxed fighter is a comfortable and confident fighter,' he says. 'That's always beneficial.

'It was funny how the pendulum swung in our first fight. Suddenly everyone was saying, "Oh this is the one you're going to win". And I end up losing. Seemingly for me it's better being underdog.'

When this philosophy was relayed to Dubois he smiled and responded: 'Tell you the truth, I also prefer being the underdog. That's how we are. Like being backs to the wall and coming out biting. That's always my mentality. Champion or not.'

Whoof whoof. May the loudest bark win.

Sports.title: The £13,128 ticket: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua is sport's most expensive standard seat EVER as fans complain they are half a million places back in online queues
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua tickets have reached £13,128 at the top end of the scale, as more than half a million fans joined an online queue for one of the most eagerly anticipated fights in boxing history.

The most expensive seats for the December 11 showdown in Cardiff cost more than those for some of the world's biggest sporting events, eclipsing the top face-value price of £6,300 for the 2026 Super Bowl and World Cup ticket prices of £8,333.

Tickets for Fury vs Joshua went on sale at midday on Friday, with Saudi Arabia's Turki Alalshikh keen to ensure fans had an accessible entry point, reflected in the starting price of £88.50 including fees.

The top-tier tickets, priced at £13,128, sold out within just 45 minutes, underlining the extraordinary demand for the December 11 showdown.

The figures do not include VIP packages, hotel and travel packages, group bookings or concession prices, and all tickets remain subject to availability.

Demand for the fight was immediately apparent, with more than half a million people waiting in the online queue as fans raced to secure seats for the long-awaited clash.

Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua tickets have been priced from £88.50 to a staggering £13,128, as fans prepare to snap up seats for the long-awaited heavyweight showdown

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on December 11 in Cardiff with the showdown set to begin at 1am so Netflix subscribers can stream it at peak time in America

The fight will take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on December 11, bringing an end to years of speculation over a meeting between the two former world heavyweight champions.

Fury and Joshua have been linked with a blockbuster contest for more than a decade, with negotiations repeatedly failing to produce the long-awaited clash.

Now, the British rivals are finally set to share a professional ring in a contest that could prove defining for both men's careers.

Fury, 38, returned to the ring in April after another retirement announcement, beating Arslanbek Makhmudov on points. The former WBC heavyweight champion has won 36 of his 39 professional contests, with two defeats and one draw.

Joshua, 36, won Olympic gold at London 2012 before becoming a two-time unified heavyweight world champion. He has recorded 30 victories, including 27 knockouts, alongside four defeats.

Joshua's most recent high-profile outing came in December 2025, when he stopped Jake Paul, before returning to the ring in July 2026 to defeat Kristian Prenga by second-round knockout.

The December showdown will give both men the chance to settle their long-running rivalry and claim a defining victory in front of a huge crowd.

The Principality Stadium can accommodate up to 80,000 spectators for major events, while Netflix is set to stream the contest globally.

The December showdown will give both men the chance to settle their long-running rivalry and claim a defining victory in front of a huge crowd

Fury against Joshua was almost the fight that got away, with the heavyweights now set to sort out differences that should have been settled a decade ago

Main-event ring walks are expected at approximately 1am local time on Saturday, December 12, although the final schedule remains subject to confirmation.

As for those in attendance, Turki Alalshikh had been keen to ensure there was an accessible entry point for fans, with tickets starting at £88.50 including fees.

At the top end of the scale, tickets cost a staggering £13,128, putting them among the most expensive publicly listed prices for a major boxing event.

The figure is not without precedent in a sport where premium seats can command eye-watering sums.

When Floyd Mayweather and Manny Pacquiao met in 2015, official tickets cost up to $10,000 (£6,700), while resale listings subsequently reached around £94,000 after the initial allocation sold out in less than a minute.

Meanwhile, a premium hospitality package for Mike Tyson's 2024 bout with Jake Paul was advertised at $2million (£1.57m) for 10 tickets and an exclusive ringside experience.

Some individual ringside seats were also listed on the secondary market at $50,000 (£39,000).

The highest-priced ticket previously listed for a British boxing event was a VIP ringside seat for Anthony Joshua's 2017 showdown with Wladimir Klitschko at Wembley, which was advertised for £202,400 on resale platform Viagogo.

However, that figure was an asking price rather than a confirmed sale. Around 90,000 fans attended the fight, which saw Joshua stop Klitschko in the 11th round.

Meanwhile, face-value prices for inner-ringside seats at Tyson Fury's 2022 fight against Dillian Whyte at Wembley reached £2,250.

Sports.title: Mike Tyson says he delivered letter to Trump from Diddy from behind bars in bombshell claim as he opens up on friendship with disgraced rapper
Sports.content:
Mike Tyson says he delivered letter to Trump from Diddy from behind bars in bombshell claim as he opens up on friendship with disgraced rapper

Boxing legend Mike Tyson revealed that he hand delivered a letter from his friend Sean 'Diddy' Combs to President Donald Trump in a recent meeting.

In an appearance on SiriusXM radio show 'Andy Cohen Live,' the former fighter spoke at length about his friendship with the disgraced music mogul who is serving a 50-month prison sentence for a sex-crimes conviction.

Tyson said he is 'friendly with Puff' – using one of Combs' many stage names – before Cohen asked him if the boxer was 'surprised by what happened with him?'

'Listen, I was surprised that they went through so many lengths to get him,' the athlete replied.

'They used a 110-year-old rule to get him – that case 110 years ago, but they used it to get him. Can you imagine that?'

After being convicted on this charge, Tyson said that he spoke with Combs from jail – where he asked 'Iron Mike' to deliver a message to the President.

Mike Tyson says he was asked to deliver a letter from Diddy to President Donald Trump

Diddy - born Sean Combs - wrote Trump a letter from jail asking the President for a pardon

'And did you give a letter to the president from him?' Cohen inquired, to which Tyson replied: 'I did what he told me to do, yeah.'

In January, President Trump confirmed that he received a letter from Combs asking for a pardon. Trump did not reveal how he received the letter, but said that he wouldn't grant the request.

The '110-year-old' rule Tyson referred to was the 1910 Mann Act, a law that criminalizes the transporting of 'any woman or girl for the purpose of prostitution or debauchery, or for any other immoral purpose.'

Combs faced accusations of leading a criminal enterprise where he allegedly coerced victims to participate in debaucherous sex parties – nicknamed 'freak offs' – which occasionally involved travel across state lines and international borders.

After a two month trial, Combs was acquitted of trafficking and racketeering, a jury cited the Mann Act when finding him guilty of two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution.

Combs has denied all allegations of sexual misconduct and has attempted to appeal his conviction.

He is currently being held at FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey and still faces upwards of 70 civil lawsuits throughout the country.

In January, Trump said he got a letter from Combs but said he wouldn't pardon him

Combs is serving 50 months in prison on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution

Join the discussion Should celebrities be able to use their connections to seek pardons for serious crimes?

Combs' release date has moved multiple times since his incarceration due to his alleged misdeeds behind bars.

An NBC News report revealed it was pushed back from January 21, 2028 to March 2, 2028 after he allegedly made fellow inmates cook and clean for him, give him massages and received access to outside alcohol and a cellphone.

In an August 2025 interview, Trump addressed Combs' conviction in an interview with Newsmax.

'I was very friendly with him. I got along with him great,' the President said at the time.

'[He] seemed like a nice guy,' Trump continued. 'I didn't know him well, but when I ran for office he was very hostile.'

Sports.title: 'He's not a p***y President': Mike Tyson launches wild defense of Trump and says president has overcome problems only 'black' people face
Sports.content:
'He's not a p***y President': Mike Tyson launches wild defense of Trump and says president has overcome problems only 'black' people face

Donald Trump is 'not a p***y President,' according to his longtime friend and boxing legend Mike Tyson.

Speaking on the latest episode of Piers Morgan Uncensored, Tyson discussed his history with Trump, whom he first met as a young heavyweight in the 1980s as the future President was making a name for himself in New York and Atlantic City real estate.

'I voted for him,' the 60-year-old Tyson told Morgan. 'I ran the streets for him. You know, me getting votes… I'm very proud of him. He's somebody that everybody should be proud of.'

Tyson doesn't have many remaining personal ties to his early days in the ring. The boxing legend's famed trainer, Cus D'Amato, died in 1985, his turbulent marriage to actress Robin Givens ended four years later and Tyson's fragile business relationship with promoter Don King finally ruptured in the late 1990s.

But for all of the turnover surrounding Tyson, Trump has been a constant for the former heavyweight champion. Not only did Tyson fight at Trump's hotels and casinos, later adding the real estate mogul to his unofficial entourage, but the two remained friends throughout the ups and downs of their later lives.

And it's those obstacles that make Trump an admirable figure in the eyes of Tyson: 'Listen, if you didn't know who Donald Trump was and you didn't know his name, you would think he's Black.'

Speaking on the latest episode of Piers Morgan Uncensored, Mike Tyson discussed his history with President Trump, whom he first met as a young heavyweight in the 1980s

Trump and Tyson attend the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) 287 in April of 2023

Donald Trump and Mike Tyson attend March of Dimes Gourmet Gala Benefit in 1989

According to Tyson, it's Trump's perseverance in the face of multiple bankruptcies and sexual misconduct allegations that have made him a formidable figure.

'When he went for President, he was bankrupt... He owed taxes, he owed so much money,' Tyson said, somewhat erroneously.

While Trump's businesses did declare bankruptcy six times, the last filing came in 2009, well before his successful 2016 White House run.

But it's not just the financial problems that give Trump credibility in Tyson's eyes. Tyson was also impressed with the way Trump survived multiple waves of sexual misconduct claims.

'All this sex abuse and all that stuff that he went through,' Tyson continued. 'People don't normally go that well. They normally have a nervous breakdown. He handled it. And that's why everyone has to respect him. Just from the way he handled his court procedures… I don't care if you hate his guts… you have to respect that. Just off the bat.'

Trump has never been convicted of any sexual misconduct, although in May of 2023, a federal jury found him liable in a civil trial for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll. A later trial resulted in a federal jury ordering Trump to pay an additional $83.3 million on top of the initial $5 million penalty he was ordered to pay Carroll.

Previously, Trump supported Tyson in the face of sexual misconduct claims. When Tyson was convicted of rape in Indiana in 1992, the future President told NBC the boxer was 'railroaded in the case' and questioned the victim's story.

While heavyweight champ Mike Tyson steals a kiss from his wife Robin Givens (R), real estate developer Donald Trump and Givens' mother Ruth Roper (L), talk to the media in 1988

Tyson chats with an attorney during a court hearing aimed at ending his contract with manager Bill Cayton. Sitting with Tyson's wife Robin Givens and her mother Ruth is Donald Trump

Donald Trump, Mike Tyson and Fred Trump attend a press conference at the Plaza Hotel

Donald Trump, Mike Tyson and Don King attend Gourmet Gala Benefit for March of Dimes on November 21, 1989 at the Plaza Hotel. King and Tyson later broke their business ties

Trump went so far as to publicly suggest Tyson should be allowed to dodge prison by giving 'millions and millions' of dollars to the victim.

'What has happened to him, the conviction, is already punitive,' Trump told the New York Post in 1992. 'The victim has had the satisfaction of humbling him and being vindicated.'

Speaking with Morgan, Tyson did not address the support he received from Trump in 1992.

He did, however, discuss the assassination attempt Trump survived in Pennsylvania on the campaign trail in 2024 by explaining he is 'not a p**** President.'

As for his immediate future, Tyson's planned exhibition with Floyd Mayweather Jr. is currently on hold after the former heavyweight broke his hand in May. Another complicating factor is a lawsuit against Mayweather by the promoter, CSI Sports.

In his previous return to the ring in 2024, Tyson was easily defeated by cruiserweight Jake Paul, who scored a unanimous decision victory that was watched by an estimated 60 million households on Netflix.

Sports.title: Mekies extends contract as Red Bull's F1 team boss
Sports.content:
Laurent Mekies has extended his contract as team principal of the Red Bull Formula 1 outfit with a new deal that takes him through until the end of 2031.

That will see the Frenchman spend at least six seasons leading the Austrian outfit after joining in July 2025 to end Christian Horner’s 20-year tenure as Red Bull team boss.

Mekies joined from sister squad Racing Bulls, who the 49-year-old took over at the start of the 2024 campaign following six years at Ferrari - first as sporting director and then racing director.

“I am incredibly proud to continue this journey with Oracle Red Bull Racing,” said Mekies.

“I would like to thank Chalerm [Yoovidhya, shareholder], Mark [Mateschitz, shareholder], and Oliver [Mintzlaff, CEO], the entire team and everyone involved for the trust they have placed in the project.

“What makes this team special is the way everyone comes together in pursuit of the same goal, and I feel privileged to work alongside such a talented and committed group every day.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Laurent Mekies, Red Bull Racing Team Principal Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

“Together, with Pierre Wache’s and Ben Hodgkinson’s teams playing a central role in shaping our future, we have a strong platform for the years ahead.

“We genuinely believe this is only the beginning. As we look ahead, we will continue to embrace the principles that define us: being free in our thinking, fast in our actions and bold in our decisions.”

This news comes at a good time for Red Bull as it has responded to its slow start to the 2026 regulation change by fitting continuous car upgrades, leading to a late resurgence.

World champion Max Verstappen has won the last two grands prix - Malaysia and Singapore - from pole, with Red Bull now only seven points off third-placed McLaren with six rounds left.

Verstappen also recently tied his future to Red Bull in August by signing a new deal through to the end of 2030, extending on his original deal that was set to expire in 2028.

That put an end to any mounting speculation over his future and in 2027 the Dutchman will partner impressive sophomore Isack Hadjar, who was confirmed last month.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“Laurent has demonstrated outstanding leadership since returning to the Red Bull family,” said Mintzlaff.

“He combines technical expertise, strategic thinking, and a deep understanding of what makes our team successful.

“Just as importantly, he embodies the values and mentality that define the Red Bull way: courage, teamwork, determination, and an unrelenting desire to compete at the highest level.

“Continuity in leadership is a key ingredient for sustained success, and we are delighted that Laurent will continue to lead the team through the next chapter of our journey.”

Sports.title: Five key takeaways from F1's big African Grand Prix reveal in Rwanda
Sports.content:
Tuesday's launch of the new African Grand Prix at Kigali's BK Arena in Rwanda was attended by Rwandan president Paul Kagame and both F1 boss Stefano Domenicali and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

But following the official presentation, several key questions were still outstanding and Autosport has now heard from the key people behind the race to fill in some of those blanks.

When will Rwanda actually join?

Rwanda will officially join in the "early 2030s", leaving the door open for plenty of wiggle room to actually join the calendar. It is quite curious for a new race to be officially announced in 2026 without a clear entry point, especially when the earliest possible date is four years into the future.

But the reality is that the project hinges on a number of critical infrastructure projects to get done. The big ticket item is the brand-new Bugesera international airport, which is currently just a runway with a concrete apron while early work has started on the terminal building. The airport isn't due to open until the second half of 2028.

Then there is the ambitious 6km track itself, which runs south of the future airport up and down two steep hills and alongside a lake. The circuit design itself is finished, with the project handled by Tilke Engineering & Architects, engineering consultancy DAR and Wurz Design now entering the engineering phase, and the Rwandan government will also have to figure out how to get 100,000 fans in and out of the track smoothly.

While there is every chance of racing there by 2030, by not pinning an exact entry point on Rwanda, the local authorities have less pressure and more time to complete all the required works on time and to the right standard. With Kigali set to become F1's anchor point in Africa for at least a decade, the sport is keen for the race to be executed as well as possible, rather than as early as possible.

Rwanda African GP Photo by: Formula 1

"There aren't really limiting factors other than key milestones that we keep in mind," Jean-Guy Afrika, CEO of the Rwandan Development Board, said when asked about the flexible start date. "One of the major ones is the completion of the international airport which is set to be completed in early 2028. The other one was more to retain the flexibility to finalise what must be done in relation to the racetrack, before a final decision is made on where we would fit exactly on the calendar. That decision is driven and coordinated by F1, but it is a decision that we prefer to postpone to the future."

At the same time, after over three years of talks and planning it was still important to make a public announcement well ahead of time to get the project out of the conceptual stage and into something that will actually happen. "We needed this moment, because we were in a sort of chicken-and-egg moment," said F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali.

"We're talking, having everything almost ready, and I said: 'Listen, if we don't start, we're [not] going to get it [done]."

Why is it called the Africa Grand Prix and not the Rwandan Grand Prix?

Curiously, the race isn't named after its host country or city but after the entire continent, which organisers say is a gesture of goodwill towards Africa as a whole.

"Rwanda has always been a champion of regional integration," said Afrika. "We are a member of the East African Community, of the Common Market for Eastern Africa. We abolished visas on arrival for Africans. So, it's really part of that spirit to bring the sport to the continent.

"We want to make it bigger than just Rwanda. We want to make it the moment when the sport came back to Africa and then never left. So that's why we felt that calling it Kigali Grand Prix or Rwanda Grand Prix would have felt slightly exclusive. It's much easier if you call it an African Grand Prix to approach partners in this wider effort."

Afrika also believed Rwanda would open the floodgates for more races on the continent. "We foresee a future where we look back at this moment and we see a critical juncture from where multiple races eventually end up happening in Africa. You've already seen that the interest [in Africa] was very high. We weren't the only ones bidding, and we expect that after the first race, there probably would be many more races."

What kind of circuit will Rwanda get, and will it be good for overtaking?

Rwanda F1 track for African GP Photo by: Formula 1

The Rwanda Motodrome is a permanent, purpose-built facility, rather than a street or urban track. The 6km, 17-corner layout is built from the ground up to make full use of the natural features of the Bugesera site, especially the two hills the circuit will be going up and down. The total elevation change per lap is 197m, which is almost twice as much as the current number one - Spa Francorchamps (102).

As well as fast and flowing corners that will get the drivers excited, there's also a 1km back straight followed by a hairpin to promote overtaking. TILKE managing director Carsten Tilke said the site chosen for the venue was a "dream location" because the undulating topography did a lot of the heavy lifting to come up with a challenging circuit as well as an arena-like vistas for fans.

"When we design a racetrack, of course we need to always work with the site we have," Tilke said. "We were very, very lucky because it's a very hilly topography. We have a lake. We have everything you dream of when you design a track. This also gives the character of the track; very flowing, very fast. It's really shaped by the natural features and beauty of the site. And this is why we also have a lot of elevation changes. It's really is a roller coaster track with a lot of banking. It goes up and down 12% to 13%."

Wurz is perhaps in a slightly awkward position as he is also the chairman of the F1 drivers association GPDA, so there is no place to hide for him if the track isn't a big hit. But when asked about his design, the former F1 driver was bullish about its potential to be both beloved by the drivers, by the spectators and by fans watching on TV because of the overtaking opportunities baked into the design. And he revealed several current drivers and FIA world champions had already tried his design in the simulator.

"The circuit is not designed for specific rules or categories, so you will see some corner combinations, which work perfect for touring cars, for motorbikes, where you can have really sneak attacks, or if you are up on your tyre degradation and you can stay very close, even on downforce [heavy] cars, whether that's World Endurance Championship cars or Formula 1 cars.

"We will have long straights, the hairpins and all the attack corners within the simulator. We are playing heavily with slight camber changes at times where you have degradation on the front or the rear, we consider what tyre temperatures are coming into the tyres on certain corners, so that the defending driver actually is at a disadvantage for the next long straight.

"There's a lot of science as well as knowledge from the years of driving and designing tracks going in, and I hope that this circuit is the cherry on the cake on everyone's list. More than a dozen FIA World Championship titles eyes have seen the circuit, have seen the onboard videos, and I think everyone is sharing great excitement."

What does F1 get out of Rwanda?

Stefano Domenicali at African GP announcement in Rwanda Photo by: Filip Cleeren

Domenicali called Tuesday's announcement "one of the most significant days in the history of Formula 1." Even for a man who generally embraces hyperbole, that's quite a statement to make. But it's true that finally breaking into the African market could well be one of Domenicali's biggest achievements when everything is said and done.

F1 hasn't been back to the African continent since leaving South Africa after 1993, and given the impressive list of requirements for a Liberty Media era grand prix, for the longest time it has felt like it just couldn't be done.

But as pointed out by Lewis Hamilton, who was praised by Rwandan sports minister Nelly Mukazayire as a "very strong voice about F1 in Africa", F1 can't call itself a truly global championship without setting foot on African soil. The hope is that Liberty Media has now found the right, credible and stable partner to do so, one that doesn't underestimate the huge workload ahead.

Domenicali claimed Africa's rapidly growing market "is home to more than 100 million fans of Formula 1", who will now get to watch a race on their own continent.

What does Rwanda get out of F1?

Attracting the latest high-profile sporting property has landed Rwanda fresh accusations by Amnesty International of using F1 for sportswashing, drawing attention away from significant human rights issues.

Domenicali, however, called Rwanda "one of the world's great success stories" and "a nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past", referencing the devastating 1994 genocide. F1 maintains that sport can be a positive force for good.

Long-time president Paul Kagame explained hosting elite level sports on home soil was a first step towards reversing the one-way traffic of Africa delivering some of the biggest global stars in football, basketball, athletics and other sports, but not getting any economic benefit from them.

"For decades, African athletes have been a pillar of the global sports economy, adding significant commercial value to top leagues, with the continent receiving almost nothing in return. Partnerships like the one we are building help break this cycle because they serve as a catalyst for sports infrastructure development. This is not just about building venues. It's about creating a sustainable economic model where different revenue streams across hospitality, tourism, and entertainment are generated and anchored into local communities. Sports is a great equaliser, but we have to be intentional about delivering this promise."

F1 also offers the next step in Rwanda's development as a tourist destination and business hub, fresh off hosting the 2025 road cycling world championships. Unlike that one-off event, Rwanda has signed up for a 10-year period which gives it time to write off investment, which is said to be an undisclosed mixture of public and private investment.

"I think it's critical to highlight that F1 is part of a much bigger picture and long-term strategy to position Rwanda as a hub for tourism investment and services," Afrika said. "F1 was a natural continuation of this effort. The track will have a capacity of around 100,000 spectators. Over a weekend, we're talking close to 300,000 people consuming everything from retail products, restaurants, hotels, accommodation infrastructure. Massive demand that generates growth for our existing businesses. And that means more in terms of what we can collect in terms of sales taxes, increases in corporate income taxes, and so on. We also anticipate an increase in terms of investment in new businesses and that means more jobs and so on."

The Rwanda Development Board is keen to make the venue a multipurpose facility that can be used year-round for events like concerts and conferences, with a karting track, off-road facility and handling track also built in to further boost grassroots motorsports. After launching the FIA cross car at the FIA General Assemblies in Kigali two years ago, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem vowed the governing body would step up efforts to support karting in the country.

"The arrival of Formula 1 in Rwanda will send a very powerful message to young people across the continent. It will tell them that the highest levels of international motorsport are within their reach, that Africa can not only participate in the future of our sport but help shape it," Ben Sulayem said.

Sports.title: Why McLaren cannot fix its F1 car handling until 2027
Sports.content:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has conceded it cannot improve its Formula 1 car handling characteristics ‘without fundamental changes’ that will not be possible until 2027.

While every F1 driver has needed to adapt to the new generation of cars and engines in order to extract the maximum performance, often applying unnatural or unusual techniques never used in their entire careers, McLaren has also been battling a car handling issue in greater depth all season.

As Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have attempted to adapt their driving styles to suit the V6 turbo hybrids with the increased electrical power elements from this year, the added complication of car handling has hamstrung the team’s overall progress relative to its frontrunning rivals.

A problem that has seemingly struck Piastri harder than his team-mate due to their different natural driving styles, it is a matter the team cannot fully solve until it can make major technical changes with an all-new car in 2027.

Stella explained: “I don't expect that what's coming to the car will improve this characteristic. I think we need something more fundamental than simply adding some downforce to the car like it's happening in the coming races.

“Without fundamentally changing some further aspect which we are addressing longer term and at the earliest I would say with the MCL41 for 2027.”

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

After the Singapore Grand Prix Norris went into detail on the subject, explaining he needs to “force” his McLaren F1 car into what he wants it to do rather than finding a balance he is comfortable with.

“It's [the car] just on a knife edge on every single corner,” Norris said. “You've just got to drive it within an exact percent, and you have to force the car in every single way. You can't let the car do any work. You can't just let the front do the work, or the rear do the work. You have to force the front; you've got to force the rear.

“You've got to drive it in a way that takes so much concentration and so much ability. It's just full-on and mentally draining because of how hard you have to work behind the wheels.

“It's just too difficult and it makes it impossible to put laps together in qualifying, which just shows how good of a job we were able to do when we were getting on pole and things like that and how rewarding that felt.

“We haven't been quick enough now, it's just too difficult and you can't do anything magical because you're simply not quick enough. You have to force the car, and you can't let the car do any work because it doesn't do it on its own. And that's not what you want from a car at all.”

This driving “intensity” is a feature Stella believes has been a part of McLaren’s F1 car all season which Norris and Piastri have needed to adapt to and something the Australian’s natural smoother and gentler inputs found harder to get to grips with.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

“The fact that the car needs quite a lot of effort to deliver lap time, and it requires a level of intensity in the driving input, which is much superior to last year, this is something that took some time for the drivers to understand,” he explained.

“And it's also one of the reasons why Oscar, at some stage, he almost lost like some of the competitiveness compared to Lando. And we were here discussing, what is happening with Oscar? And I've always said that that was a technical matter. Oscar just needed to understand how to force the car to do some things and sort of abandon the fact that driving fast will not necessarily mean driving clean if that makes sense.

“Which was the signature of Oscar when we have seen him fast in the past. He was like... He was clean, he was really good [with the] data to see he was very repeatable and he was fast. With this car, all these things together they don't seem to happen very often so it's a lot of work for the drivers.”

Sports.title: F1 signs historic 10-year Rwanda deal to host African Grand Prix
Sports.content:
The government of Rwanda and Formula 1 have announced a 10-year deal for a new African Grand Prix in capital Kigali, which will first be held in 2030 at the earliest.

F1 will head to a yet-to-be-built natural road course 40km south of Kigali, next to the Rwandan capital's under-construction Bugesera international airport. The first edition of the race, which is officially billed as 'Formula 1 African Grand Prix, presented by Visit Rwanda', could be held as early as 2030, depending on when construction of the track is completed.

Regardless of the start date, the deal is billed as a 10-year agreement which will see F1 head back to the African continent for the first time since the 1993 South African Grand Prix.

The deal was announced on Tuesday at a press conference in Kigali attended by Rwandan president Paul Kagame, F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

The Bugesera track, the result of a cooperation between Tilke Engineering & Architects, former F1 driver Alex Wurz and his design company WurzDesign, and engineering consultancy DAR, will make full use of the natural terrain, creating a natural arena for fans to watch cars tackle the 6km, 17-corner anti-clockwise challenge - with no less than a 197m change in elevation per lap. It is part of a wider investment plan by the Rwandan Development Board in tourism, infrastructure and commercial development.

Damon Hill, Williams FW15C, leads Alessandro Zanardi, Lotus 107B, Rubens Barrichello, Jordan 193, and Ivan Capelli, Jordan 193 Photo by: Motorsport Images

"Today belongs to Africa. For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement," said president Kagame. "Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.

"This 10-year partnership is also an investment in Rwanda's future. The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."

Domenicali said: "Today is a landmark moment for Formula 1. With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the World Championship closer than ever to fans around the globe. Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact.

"This is about much more than hosting a Grand Prix. Together, we can create lasting economic and social benefits through tourism, investment, skills development and local business growth, ensuring the positive impact of this event is felt for generations. For our fans, this is an especially exciting moment. Africa is home to more than 100 million Formula 1 fans, and that number continues to grow rapidly."

FIA president Ben Sulayem added: "The return of the FIA Formula One World Championship to Africa is a historic moment for our sport and an important step in the continued global growth of motorsport. Rwanda has demonstrated a strong commitment to delivering a world-class event, and the FIA will work closely with FOM and our partners as this new circuit is developed to the highest international standards."

Stefano Domenicali at African GP announcement in Rwanda Photo by: Filip Cleeren

Talks between F1 and Rwanda over a race accelerated in 2024, with the central African nation keen to attract major sporting events to boost tourism and business. Last year Kigali hosted the UCI Road World Championships in cycling, and in 2024 it hosted the FIA's annual Prize Giving Ceremony, with Max Verstappen among the FIA world champions travelling to the country to collect his fourth F1 world title trophy.

Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton has been a long-time proponent of an F1 return to the African continent. "For the past six years I've been fighting in the background to get a grand prix," he said earlier this year. "So, sitting with the stakeholders and asking them the question, why are we not in Africa? We're on every other continent, why not Africa? I know they're really trying.

"The ones that I've enjoyed the most so far [were] Kenya, and Rwanda was particularly spectacular - two places I felt like I could live. And South Africa. I think those are the ones that I think would be good places for us to potentially go to."

Sports.title: The not-so-obvious chance Leclerc missed to usurp Verstappen
Sports.content:
When Charles Leclerc had a better start than Max Verstappen and claimed the inside line for Turn 1, many in the media centre thought the Monegasque should have held his ground to take the lead.

However, Verstappen was on the outside, on the normal racing line that offered slightly more grip, and the Dutchman was prepared to take every risk. Verstappen had already told Autosport a day earlier that second or third place in the drivers' championship would mean nothing to him and that he simply wanted to go all-in for race victories.

In other words, Verstappen was willing to risk everything, although that was not even the main reason why Leclerc was unable to complete the move. The reference points drivers use under braking – such as the 150-metre and 100-metre boards – are on the right-hand side approaching Turn 1, but Leclerc could not see them because he was alongside Verstappen.

The Ferrari driver had to choose his braking point by instinct and tried to judge it as well as possible. As a result, he does not regard it as a missed opportunity, adding: "I would have done exactly the same."

No regrets in that respect, then, although Leclerc admits that he did let an opportunity to pass Verstappen slip away a few laps later.

Verstappen appeared to be managing his pace in the opening stages to preserve his tyres, but the four-time world champion revealed in the post-race press conference that this was not entirely a deliberate choice.

"We had a few laps with some deployment issues, so that's where Charles actually almost got me into Turn 7."

Verstappen managed to keep the lead into Turn 1, despite Leclerc's better launch off the line Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

Verstappen was not getting all the electrical power at the points where he needed it, something Arvid Lindblad at Red Bull's sister team Racing Bulls – which uses the same power unit – also complained about.

"Yeah, I also had issues with the PU, which we're trying to look after. I was getting driven past on the straights and the engine braking was really bad, which wasn't easy to drive", Lindblad said.

For Verstappen, the problem was limited to deployment issues in the opening stages of the Singapore Grand Prix, but Leclerc believes he should have taken advantage of them.

"There were a few opportunities in the first three laps when Max had the deployment issues, but I always thought that it was a one-off, so I wasn't really using my battery, which maybe was a mistake", Leclerc admitted.

Every time Verstappen was slow on the straights, the Ferrari driver thought it would be the last time, meaning he did not anticipate the problem recurring or adjust his own deployment strategy accordingly. By the time the issue occurred again, Leclerc could no longer react.

"When I was realising that he had no power at the end of the straight, I couldn't do anything. It was too late for me to use my power."

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

The question, however, is whether it would have made any difference to the final result. Track position is crucial at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, and in that scenario Leclerc would not have had to spend so long running in dirty air. On the other hand, he acknowledges that Verstappen was simply too strong and that Red Bull managed its tyres better.

"I don't know if it would have changed much. Of course, for the first stint it would have helped, but I think eventually they just had too much pace for us."

Leclerc made another attempt in the closing stages with a different strategy and a second stop under the virtual safety car, but a second win of the season, following his triumph at Silverstone, ultimately proved beyond reach.

"I’m happy, but not super happy. I mean, second place is a good result considering the tendency that we've had lately, where we were lacking just a little bit of pace.

"I feel like, particularly in qualifying yesterday, we had strong pace. Today in the race, Max had a bit more pace than we did, which was expected, but maybe we were a little bit closer than what we expected.

"It was a cool race and I believed in it until the very end, but unfortunately it wasn't quite enough."

Nevertheless, it was enough to secure Leclerc's first podium finish since the summer break and his fifth overall this F1 season.

Sports.title: The hidden factor that gives Verstappen and Red Bull extra hope for 2027
Sports.content:
With two victories in the last three Grands Prix and a deficit of just 0.196 seconds in Baku, Verstappen and Red Bull are firmly back at the front in Formula 1. The resurgence has understandably come too late to play a meaningful role in the title fight, although Verstappen now has a top-three finish in the drivers' championship in his sights.

Verstappen trails Lewis Hamilton by just eight points after the Singapore race weekend, while Russell is only 17 points ahead of the Dutchman. In other words, finishing runner-up in the championship is a realistic prospect.

When Autosport asked whether Verstappen is already starting to worry about 12 December – when the annual FIA gala takes place in Shanghai – a smile appeared on his face.

"Is that the prize-giving ceremony? Well, I was really ill last year! But we'll see what happens."

A second- or third-place finish in the final standings would not mean anything to Verstappen, however, as he told the Dutch media in the Singapore paddock. After the extremely difficult start to 2026 and the turnaround that followed, such an outcome might carry more significance than usual, but Verstappen does not see it that way.

"No, because ultimately you're not winning. You're not becoming world champion, and that's the only thing that matters to me."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

The aspect of 2026 that gives Verstappen the most confidence

While the title is out of reach this season, Red Bull's resurgence does provide confidence for next year.

"The most important thing is to look at where we were at the beginning of the season and where we are now", Verstappen said, referring to the fact that Red Bull was still fighting Haas and Alpine in China and Japan.

"All the upgrades that have been introduced on the car since then, and also the problems we had with certain parts of our car, we've managed to solve all of that. That's very important heading into next year.

"When you see that some teams still have doubts about certain aspects of their new upgrades, everything is working for us, and that's a real positive."

Verstappen has previously explained that certain limitations of the 2026 car can no longer be eliminated, meaning more fundamental changes will still be needed for next season's car.

Asked by Autosport whether the development direction is already 100% clear in that respect as well, and whether it gives Verstappen confidence, he replied:

"You never know fully. It's always very difficult to say that with things you're developing now that have never actually existed in real life, only on drawings.

“But everything we've introduced on the car this year has worked. That's very positive, and hopefully we can use that for next year."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Anni Graf - Formula 1 via Getty Images

What's the latest on Red Bull's long-awaited new wind tunnel?

Verstappen also brought up another, more hidden factor that could help Red Bull as 2027 progresses:

"Of course, we'll also have a new wind tunnel at our disposal next year. That's a separate matter, but naturally we hope it will work properly and help us as well."

The wind tunnel Red Bull currently uses is the oldest on the F1 grid. During his time as team principal, Christian Horner repeatedly described the wind tunnel as “a Cold War relic” and said working with the 70-year-old facility near Bedford was like looking at “two different watches”, highlighting how the correlation between the wind tunnel and on-track performance had failed more than once.

The fact that correlation has proved accurate in 2026 is therefore not something to be taken for granted, although Verstappen added that the new regulations and the dimensions of the cars may be helping as well.

"Those earlier problems might also have been partly down to the width and length of the car [and what you can replicate with the model]. Of course, we have different cars now, but the most important thing is that we'll be able to use the new wind tunnel next year."

Verstappen acknowledged that the new wind tunnel cannot yet be used for the initial development of the RB23 – after all, that development process is already underway – but it can be used for further development of the car throughout the season. That will still be crucial, as the second year under these regulations is also set to feature an intense development battle.

Pierre Waché previously told Autosport that the wind tunnel should be operational in early 2027, possibly in February, as Red Bull indicated in Singapore. However, the exact timing during the first quarter of 2027 will still depend on factors such as calibration, ensuring that Red Bull can have complete confidence in its new facility.

Sports.title: Why Antonelli avoided a penalty despite four track limits incidents in Singapore GP
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli committed what appeared to be four track limits violations during the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix but avoided a penalty.

This left many onlookers puzzled post-race, although the usual five-second penalty would not have changed the result: Antonelli finished third, 15.9 seconds ahead of fourth-placed Lando Norris.

An immediate post-race assumption was that his fourth incident, which occurred on the lap after his pitstop, had not counted. That would have left Antonelli within the permitted limit of three track limits violations.

Read Also: Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix Driver Ratings 2026

An FIA spokesperson has confirmed this was indeed the case. The fourth violation could be explained by braking problems, which had also been discussed over the Mercedes team radio. In the eyes of the FIA stewards, this constituted a "justifiable reason" for leaving the track on that occasion.

This is also how the 2026 Formula 1 regulations address the matter in Article B1.8.5, which states: "Drivers must make every reasonable effort to use the track at all times and may not leave the track without a justifiable reason."

The braking problems therefore saved Antonelli from a penalty, particularly as he gained no advantage by going off track.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff is nevertheless well aware of the fine line his driver is walking during the race: "That stresses us. Half the race we already have three strikes, but it also shows that he's pushing the limits a lot."

The official FIA document listing deleted lap times during the race records track limits violations for Antonelli at Turns 2 (twice) and Turn 19 (once) – all of them in the first half of the race, as Wolff suggested.

The apparent fourth violation, this time at Turn 7, prompted a somewhat irritated response from Antonelli's race engineer Peter Bonnington over the radio.

With a little distance, however, Wolff was able to see the funny side.

"I think he managed his race, he kept his cool – other than a few of the track limits, where I have a good strategy, I'm going to put a pillow from the hotel under his butt, so he can actually see the road. Because I think he can't see it," Wolff joked.

Overall, however, Wolff praised Antonelli's handling of the situation as "mature and good", and added: “We talked about it and he said, 'I've just got to keep my calm here and make sure that I finish the race'. So, handling a difficult car at that stage and trying to develop it and learn, it's good."

Sports.title: Verstappen jokes about coded messages as Red Bull phases in Lambiase’s successor
Sports.content:
There were still two races on the current Formula 1 calendar missing from Max Verstappen's list of victories: the Madring and the Marina Bay Street Circuit. Given that F1 only visited the street circuit in Madrid for the first time this year, that is understandable, but Singapore has proved to be Red Bull's Achilles' heel for years.

Until this season. In 2026, Verstappen was dominant in Singapore, claiming two pole positions and two victories over the sprint weekend. On Sunday, the main focus was on the start – a major headache for Red Bull this year – although Verstappen managed to hold his position this time.

“The start was critical, and it was just good enough. Again, something was not particularly right at the start, so I need to understand what went wrong there”, Verstappen revealed.

“Before releasing the clutch, it didn't feel good. Then we had a few laps with some deployment issues, so that's where Charles almost got me into Turn 7. Once we had cleared the deployment problems, it was fine.”

According to Verstappen, those starting problems were different from what he had experienced in recent weeks. On those occasions, things had gone wrong when he released the clutch, but this time the problem had already emerged at an earlier stage.

“I need to understand what went on with the engine before even dropping the clutch, because I think that did hurt my start. It was again not fantastic, you can say that.”

Afterwards, Verstappen braked late on the outside line and also managed to survive the deployment issues. That meant the threat from his rivals had passed, although the Dutchman still had to deal with another inconvenience for the remainder of the race: his radio was not working properly.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

The four-time world champion could still hear the team, but his responses were unintelligible.

“Maybe GP was happy that it was not working!” Verstappen laughed in the post-race press conference.

“I couldn't really say anything. He did try at one point to ask me a few things in code, and I think he understood well what I meant or what I didn’t want! But it's never nice. I've been having difficulties with my radio already the whole season, and this weekend has been particularly bad.”

It meant Lambiase had to get creative to obtain Verstappen's input. In the closing stages of the race, he asked the Dutchman to remain silent if he wanted to make another pitstop in the event of a safety car, and to press the radio button if he preferred to maintain track position.

Team principal Laurent Mekies clarified that these radio problems were entirely on Red Bull's side and were not related to any wider technical issues in Singapore.

“I don’t think it’s the circumstances, no, I think it’s on our side”, Mekies said on Sunday night.

“It was not the same issue as in FP1, but it was a little bit painful. These cars are complicated and there is a huge amount of dialogue that needs to happen between the drivers and engineers. But as you have seen, GP found his ways to communicate with Max and vice versa when it mattered.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“Of course, it's something that we take seriously like everything else. And I'm sure we will come back with a strong solution for it, because it could cost you decisive time in crucial moments.”

Hart to replace Lambiase as Verstappen's race engineer in Austin

As a reward for all his efforts, Red Bull sent Lambiase onto the podium alongside Verstappen, which also came as a surprise to the four-time world champion.

“Yeah, I didn't expect that. I remember he said to me last year in Vegas, "This might be the last time I'm on the podium." I said, "Don't be silly, we're going to win much more." But I almost jinxed myself there, I guess!” Verstappen laughed.

“It was just super nice that they sent him up. We all know that he is leaving, but I think it was very special to share the podium on a track that we had not won together. So yeah, very nice to see him up there.”

At the same time, Red Bull is planning the transition to Verstappen's future race engineer, Tom Hart. He was initially set to join Williams as Alexander Albon's race engineer, but when Verstappen made his preference for Lambiase's successor known internally, Red Bull did everything it could to reverse that move and retain Hart – successfully.

There is no official date yet for when Hart will permanently take over from Lambiase, although Red Bull is in discussions with McLaren about Lambiase's start date and his gardening leave. The timing of the transition partly depends on those arrangements, with 2027 theoretically emerging as a logical outcome.

Before that happens, Hart and Verstappen will already have several race weekends to become more familiar with working together. Red Bull has confirmed to Autosport that Hart will serve as Verstappen's race engineer in Austin, Brazil and Las Vegas, replacing Lambiase in that role.

The team added that Lambiase will still be present at the circuit during those weekends, carrying out his duties as Head of Racing.

Sports.content:
Red Bull has given a vote of confidence in its team principal Laurent Mekies by extending his contract to run the team until 2031.

Mekies took over from Christian Horner in charge of the team last year. Horner had run Red Bull since it entered F1 in 2005.

Sports.title: Verstappen says Red Bull’s car was “scary” to drive early in 2026 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Red Bull has made huge progress with a car which felt “scary” to drive early in the season, says Max Verstappen.

The four-times world champion has won the last two grands prix in a row and also took victory in the sprint race in Singapore last week. The team’s form has improved significantly since the beginning of the season, when Verstappen only reached the podium once in the first seven rounds.

Verstappen spun out of the British Grand Prix suffered costly spins in qualifying at the Red Bull Ring and Hungaroring as the team struggled to get on top of its car. However their most recent upgrades have transformed its performance.

“The car definitely felt a lot nicer from Baku onwards,” said Verstappen. “It’s just been a lot more balanced. Then naturally, of course, when you can compete a bit further up front without having too many issues with the car compared to the beginning of the year, where it was actually sometimes a bit scary to drive, that makes it a lot nicer.”

Verstappen finished a close second behind George Russell in Baku. He qualified only eighth but was in contention for pole position until his final lap was compromised by a yellow flag.

He has been undefeated since then and expects to remain competitive over the final rounds. “We’re not in a championship fight, and that’s why I think ’til the end we’ll just try to have a good time and try to add more podiums and hopefully a few wins.”

It is the second time in as many years that Red Bull has made a breakthrough with a troublesome car in the second half of a season. “Two completely different cars as well, with the regulations,” Verstappen noted. “Also two completely different problems.

“We had to find lap time. Plus, of course, also this year with the engine side of things, I think for everyone it’s been sometimes a bit complicated to get the most out of it.”

Red Bull needs to ensure they begin next year in better shape, said Verstappen.

“From race one to now, I think we’ve gained a lot of experience. Of course, we’re still not where we want to be, but I guess everyone will say the same thing.

“But we have learned so much and definitely also on the car side have fixed a lot of our weaknesses. We just need to keep improving, keep learning this year that so we can apply that also into next year.”

Sports.title: Spotlight: Cadillac already has better facilities than Mercedes, says Bottas | Brief
Sports.content:
Cadillac remain yet to score a point in their first season in Formula 1 but Valtteri Bottas says their progress is clear to see.

“We are definitely seeing an improvement somewhere every weekend,” he told the Financial Times. “It’s not necessarily in the results yet, but it’s in how we operate as a team in different areas.”

Bottas scored all 10 of his grand prix victories for Mercedes. He drove for the world champions between 2017 and 2021.

Cadillac is based partly at Silverstone, a short distance from Mercedes’ Brackley factory. Asked whether his new team’s facilities are better than the world champions’, Bottas replied: “I would say so.”
