World.title: Image of mournful elephant mom wins 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

(Federico Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

An Italian photographer's "heartbreakingly poignant" photo of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won this year's top Wildlife Photographer of the Year award.

Federico Veronesi captured "The Aftermath" while tracking elephants in the Huab River Valley in Namibia. He noticed unusual drag marks in the sand of the dry riverbed. When he caught up to a family of elephants, he saw an adult female with a calf's leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.

Kathy Moran, chair of the jury for the 2026 competition, described the photo as working on "so many levels."

"Emotionally it's a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant. Intellectually, it's proof that animals have cognition," she wrote in a news release announcing the winners.

In addition to winning the grand prize, the photo also won the Behaviour: Mammals category.

Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the U.K.-based Natural History Museum in London, with a stated goal to share nature's stories and insights about environmental challenges that need our attention.

This year, the annual competition — the 62nd edition — attracted 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories.

It awards top prizes to both an adult photographer and a young photographer under 18.

This year's Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year prize was won by Oscar Whitfield, a young British photographer who grew up in Zimbabwe and frequently returns there during school holidays.

His photo, captured while lying on the ground, shows a close-up of a dung beetle hard at work pushing a ball of dung. It was also the winner in the 11 to 14 years age bracket.

(Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the year)

Officially, there were no Canadian category winners this year. However, Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, who lives in Germany and won this year's Rising Star Award, is a Canadian citizen who has previously told CBC News his parents were both born in Canada, and he has relatives in Ottawa and Nova Scotia.

His featured photo, "Afternoon snack," is a close-up of a robber fly preying on a flesh fly. "The bubbles forming in the victim's eyes indicate that the robber fly has injected digestive enzymes that liquefy its internal tissues before they are sucked out," the photo's description reads.

(Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

Canadians can see the 100-photo exhibition at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto from Nov 7, 2026, to Feb 28, 2027, or at the Royal B.C. Museum in Victoria from Feb. 12, 2027, until April 18, 2027.

It opens at the Natural History Museum in London this Friday.

Here are some of the other category winners.

Amelie Davis, of the U.K., won the 10 years and under bracket with this photo of a common carder bee in southern England, captured with her father's smartphone.

(Amelie Davis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

A California newt lays eggs while clasping vegetation that already contains another newt's egg clutch in the winner of the Amphibians and Reptiles category, captured by U.S. photographer Anton Sorokin. The newt will stay like this until the egg mass swells to a size too large to be eaten by a predator.

(Anton Sorokin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

Greek photographer Agorastos Papatsanis used UV light to make these fluorescent bonnet mushrooms glow brightly on a decaying log on the lower slopes of Greece's Mount Olympus. The image won the Plants and Fungi category.

(Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

A young bull elephant sprays water on a group of zebras at a waterhole in the Chyulu Hills of Kenya in this photo, the winner of the Animals in their Environment category, captured by James Lewin using a camera converted to infrared to soften harsh lighting.

World.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator James Cody Bryant indicted by grand jury
World.content:

A grand jury in Washington state has indicted an alleged co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting.

The indictment of 30-year-old James Bryant for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country means there is probable cause for prosecutors to pursue the case.

Emily Langlie, a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office, said last week that an indictment would mean a preliminary hearing in the case scheduled for Oct. 20 would be eliminated.

Bryant, whose lawyers say uses she/her pronouns and goes by the name Melody , was denied bail a day ahead of Wednesday's indictment.

WATCH | Criminal complaint lists allegations against Bryant: U.S. resident allegedly gave advice, money to Tumbler Ridge shooter | Duration closed caption 8:26

A statement issued by the U.S. Department of Justice says the indictment "details several overt acts that Bryant took to further the school shooting conspiracy."

Eight victims were shot dead in Tumbler Ridge by 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar in February, including five students and a teacher at a secondary school.

The indictment of Bellingham, Wash., resident Bryant lists that she allegedly agreed to record the shooting and broadcast it over the internet, offered the shooter advice on where to attack and what weapons to use and sent Van Rootselaar money to buy a lighter for use in an improvised explosive device.

The Justice Department's statement says conspiracy to murder in a foreign country is punishable by up to life in prison.

It cautions that the accusations against Bryant remain unproven, and says the case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Todd Greenberg with help from the Justice Department’s National Security Division.

Van Rootselaar shot herself dead at the school on Feb. 10.

As a young woman, globe-trotting doctor Kirsten Johnson knew she wanted her life to be adventurous and deeply meaningful. Turns out it is also awe-inspiring. World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.

World.title: Mayor from Colombia’s north claims De la Espriella’s armed men intimidated him
World.content:
The mayor of Sincelejo claimed Sunday that armed men intimidated him during a meeting with Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a video message, Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña said that armed men positioned themselves behind him while the president accused the mayor of corruption and threatened to pull municipal funds.

The accusations were partly published on the social media pages of the president, who accused Acuña of being “a person who, like you, faces 13 corruption charges, has a video in which he explains how to embezzle funds from the PAE, and, on top of that, is set to stand trial in the Supreme Court of Justice on charges of illicit enrichment.”

So let’s see what we do with Sincelejo, but I do not work under your scheme of corruption. And if you think you can continue engaging in those practices, know that someone has arrived who is going to prevent it and that I am going to concentrate on it. This money, mister mayor, I will take care of it, and to take care of it I have to keep it away from your control. President Abelardo de la Espriella

In his response, Acuña claimed that De la Espriella’s video “has been edited and digitally manipulated.”

I ask you, please, to show the full video, where you can see how disciplinary and criminal codes are being violated in Colombia, where you can see how a mayor is being intimidated with rifles in the hands of civilians. How can a mayor be constantly flanked—for the entire duration of an event—by a person armed with a rifle, with the sole purpose of intimidating him? Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

Investigative journalist Laura Ardila said on social media platform X that sources from the province confirmed Acuña’s allegations.

Sources from the department who were present say—fearing they might be named—that they left the scene terrified. They claim that Acuña was indeed surrounded by heavily armed men in civilian clothing, that the president’s office was recording the entire time, and that, based on details like these, they believe it was a scene staged in advance to go viral. Journalist Laura Ardila

The mayor subsequently pointed out that the investigations into his alleged corruption existed before the presidential campaign, during which the De la Espriella campaign may have violated electoral laws, according to Acuña.

Among other things, the mayor said that he had been approached by De la Espriella’s parents to support the far-right president’s campaign and that local print shops may have received unreported campaign funds.

Since this needs to be clarified, mister President, it would be a good idea for the oversight agencies to investigate whether any printing shops in Sincelejo incurred campaign expenses that have not yet been reported to the National Electoral Council, whether there was campaign financing, and where that campaign financing came from, Mister President. Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

The mayor also pointed out that two members of the De la Espriella administration are being investigated on corruption charges and that the president had ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

The president has repeatedly used corruption allegations to target political enemies.

World.title: Colombia’s top corporate lobbyist resigns over reported tensions with president
World.content:
The director of one of Colombia’s most powerful business associations, Bruce Mac Master of the ANDI, resigned amid tensions with President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a letter to the ANDI, Mac Master said that “it is time for me to step down from my role as head of the National Association of Entrepreneurs of Colombia.”

According to the former ANDI boss, “unexpected and troubling circumstances” made working for the association “particularly complex” and ‘multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously.”

In recent weeks, unexpected and troubling circumstances have arisen that have made the Association’s operating environment particularly complex, with potential adverse effects on its members and staff. Multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously. In the face of these challenges, I have sought to act with firmness and prudence, always prioritizing institutional channels and placing the interests of the ANDI above any personal considerations, in an effort to resolve this situation. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master’s resignation followed news suggesting that De la Espriella instructed his cabinet of boycotting the ANDI chief.

According to political news magazine La Silla Vacia, the rift between the ANDI and the government was because De la Espriella’s law firm was never allowed to join the ANDI and the association’s donations in response to the august 10 earthquake bypassed the First Lady’s newly founded and very controversial foundation.

“The General Board of Directors, its Executive Committee, and I did everything in our power to facilitate a solution and create conditions that would allow the Association to fully fulfill its role, seeking to keep channels of dialogue open and to continue contributing,” but “all of those attempts were unsuccessful.”

I deeply regret this, because I have always believed in collective intelligence and in the need for the government, the private sector, and institutions to work together—even in the face of differences—with respect, independence, and a sense of national responsibility. We tried, but we were unsuccessful. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master said that he hoped that his resignation would restore “collaboration between the national government and the business community—as represented by the General Board of Directors, the members, and the various divisions of the Association.”

The former ANDI chief had been trying to represent the business interests of its approximately 1,600 members since 2013.

World.title: Badenoch accuses Farage of trading Chagos for Trump’s silence on the Falklands
World.content:
Badenoch accuses Farage of trading Chagos for Trump’s silence on the Falklands

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 22:05 UTC Full article

“There is no pride in our country in the way he talks about us. This is careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security,” added Badenoch

British Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called “humiliating” a proposal by Reform UK leader Nigel Farage to offer US President Donald Trump the Chagos archipelago in exchange for him to stop talking about the Falklands. “Giving away British territory in return for someone keeping quiet is not a deal. It is humiliating,” she told The Telegraph.

“There is no pride in our country in the way he talks about us. This is careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security,” added Badenoch, who said it was “mad for someone who wants to be prime minister to say we should give away one piece of British territory just to stop an American president talking about another”. “The Chagos Islands are British. And the Falklands are British and will remain British, irrespective of what the American president says. When Donald Trump is right, we should say so. When he is wrong, we should have the confidence to tell him.”

On the US podcast The Benny Show, Farage had suggested offering Trump Diego Garcia “in perpetuity” in return for his silence on the Falklands. “I give him something. I ask for something back. He’d get that. He’s a businessman,” he said. A Reform UK spokesman said he was referring to US use of the base, “not the Chagos Islands as a whole”, and noted that Farage has opposed handing the archipelago to Mauritius.

The deal to transfer sovereignty over Chagos to Mauritius while retaining the joint Diego Garcia base was paused in April following opposition from the US administration, although Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to see it through. According to The Telegraph, the White House even considered buying the archipelago as an alternative.

The same newspaper notes that Trump said in August he was reviewing the US position on British sovereignty over the Falklands, amid a dispute over defence spending. Burnham assured him in September in New York that the United Kingdom would defend “the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British”.

World.title: US lifts sanctions on Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly
World.content:
US lifts sanctions on Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 22:02 UTC Full article

The US Treasury Department on Wednesday removed from its sanctions list Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly and brother of acting president Delcy Rodríguez. The Treasury did not explain the reasons for the decision.

Rodríguez, who has led the Venezuelan parliament since 2021, was taken off the Office of Foreign Assets Control’s Specially Designated Nationals list, which entails the blocking of assets in the United States, a ban on entering the country and a prohibition on transactions with US citizens and companies. He had been designated in September 2018, along with his sister, former first lady Cilia Flores and then defence minister Vladimir Padrino. At the time, the Treasury said Nicolás Maduro had given them “high-ranking positions” in the government to help him “remain in power”.

Rodríguez was removed from the list in April, which allowed her to travel to New York in September for the UN General Assembly, where she met US President Donald Trump. Rodríguez took power after Maduro and Flores were detained in a US military operation in Caracas in January; both face charges in New York of drug trafficking and, since last week, of torture and repression.

Since then, the Rodríguez government has negotiated an oil agreement with Washington, announced in August, which according to El País gives the United States majority control over a fifth of Venezuela’s reserves, the largest in the world. According to Reuters, the Rodríguez siblings pushed legal changes to further open the energy and mining sectors to foreign companies.

Presidential elections remain without a date. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio received in Washington Dinorah Figuera, head of the opposition delegation in talks with the Venezuelan government, with no announcements. Opposition leader María Corina Machado is not taking part in that dialogue and has been unable to return to Venezuela.

World.title: Farage proposes offering Trump Diego Garcia in exchange for his silence on the Falklands
World.content:
Farage proposes offering Trump Diego Garcia in exchange for his silence on the Falklands

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 21:53 UTC Full article

“I’d have gone in and said, ‘Right, you know what mate? Chagos, it’s yours. Diego Garcia, in perpetuity, the most strategic American military base in the world’,” Farage said

Reform UK leader c has said that, if he were prime minister, he would offer US President Donald Trump the use in perpetuity of the Diego Garcia military base, in the Chagos archipelago, in exchange for him to stop talking about the Falklands. The proposal sparked a clash with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who called it “humiliating”, and prompted the White House to come to Farage’s defence.

“I’d have gone in and said, ‘Right, you know what mate? Chagos, it’s yours. Diego Garcia, in perpetuity, the most strategic American military base in the world’,” Farage told the US podcast The Benny Show. “In return, just please stop talking about the Falkland Islands. I know you like Milei, but this really matters to us. And there’s a trade, you see.”

Badenoch responded in The Telegraph: “Giving away British territory in return for someone keeping quiet is not a deal. It is humiliating.” She added that “the Chagos Islands are British, and the Falklands are British and will remain British, regardless of what the American president says”, calling Farage’s remarks “careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security”.

Farage didn't say that Trump/USA could use the Chagos Islands in perpetuity. In his interview he literally said he would trade the Chagos Islands for the Falklands. Reform officials and Farage can deny it all they like, but the evidence is right there and cannot be altered. https://t.co/84HYJw12sf — Thomas Evans @Renewal2030 (@ThomasEvansAdur) October 14, 2026

Farage replied on X that Badenoch “is lying again” and said he would offer the United States the use of Diego Garcia, not sovereignty over the archipelago, in return for America going “quiet on the Falklands”. A White House official quoted by The Times agreed: “He was obviously referring to the use of the Diego Garcia military base, which is critical to countering threats from China and Iran,” and accused Badenoch of peddling fake news and undermining the Anglo-American relationship.

The agreement signed by the British government in 2025 to transfer sovereignty over Chagos to Mauritius, with a 99-year lease for the base, is on hold following Trump’s opposition. The row comes amid an escalating dispute over the Sea Lion oil project: on Tuesday, Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran told the House of Commons that Prime Minister Andy Burnham had raised with Trump the islanders’ wish to remain British.

World.title: What are the red notices Argentina has sought from Interpol over Sea Lion
World.content:
What are the red notices Argentina has sought from Interpol over Sea Lion

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 21:45 UTC Full article

The chief executive of the islands’ government, Andrea Clausen, acknowledged that the use of Interpol poses a threat

Argentina has requested Interpol red notices against individuals linked to the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, and the United Kingdom has asked the organisation to reject them as “politically motivated”, according to the British newspaper The Guardian. Interpol responded by reaffirming Article 3 of its constitution, which prohibits any intervention or activity of a political character.

A red notice is a request to police worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. It is not an international arrest warrant: Interpol reviews each request before circulating it, but each state decides whether to act. According to the newspaper, British officials are concerned that Argentina could persuade other countries that its requests are based on domestic law rather than political motives. It has not emerged how many people are affected or whether any notice has been issued.

The chief executive of the islands’ government, Andrea Clausen, acknowledged that the use of Interpol poses a threat. “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action,” she said. “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.” Workers in the oil and fishing sectors fear being detained if they travel, particularly to South America.

Argentina has launched criminal proceedings against Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, the project’s partners. British officials quoted by The Guardian describe Argentina’s campaign as the most serious since the 1982 war. On Tuesday, London announced measures to shield its companies from Argentine sanctions, and Argentina asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order a halt to Sea Lion.

World.title: HMS Protector breaks down and leaves UK without an Ice Patrol
World.content:
HMS Protector breaks down and leaves UK without an Ice Patrol

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 21:10 UTC Full article

HMS Protector at Devonport Dockyard, Plymouth

Britain has been left without its Ice Patrol after HMS Protector on Tuesday suffered engine problems and had to be towed back to Plymouth, according to reports in the media. This could speed the Royal Navy’s assessment as to whether the vessel originally built in Norway and now with 25 years of rough seas in both poles has to be replaced.

The breakdown comes at a critical moment, when world powers are rushing to take advantage of navigation opportunities in the Arctic, particularly Russia, and in the southern seas, with as ever aggressive Argentina threatening the Falkland Islands development of its resources.

The Telegraph reports that Royal Navy sources admitted the situation as a “catastrophic failure”. And Commander Tom Sharpe, who commanded HMS Endurance, Protector’s predecessor, said it would be “poor timing” to remove the ship from service.

In March, Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord, admitted that the Navy was not ready for war. It has five active frigates, six destroyers and two aircraft carriers, alongside a submarine fleet of six Astute-class attack boats and four Vanguard-class subs, which carry the UK’s nuclear weapons.

Both carriers, HMS Prince of Wales and HMS Queen Elizabeth, have reported mechanical problems since their maiden voyages.

Military chiefs are waiting for the spending review for details about how the Government will meet a long-term Nato pledge of increasing the core defense budget to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2035.

HMS Protector underpins the UK’s presence in the British Antarctic Territory, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

In 2008, HMS Endurance, the Navy’s previous icebreaker, suffered a flood caused by “poor engineering standards”. At the time, the Navy insisted that she would be repaired and returned to sea. However, she was not and was eventually replaced by HMS Protector after around three years.

HMS Protector was originally named MV Polarbjørn, meaning Polar bear in Norwegian, before being leased in 2011 by the Navy for £8.7m a year. The UK government paid £51m to own the ship outright in 2013. Later refurbished, HMS Protector should expect to have another decade of use before being withdrawn from service.

With a crew of 88, she is typically lightly armed carrying machine guns, but often carries a detachment of Royal Marines. Although classed as a Royal Navy warship, the vessel has retained her original red and white paint scheme. The Royal Navy website says she is affectionately referred to as the “Swiss army knife – red, versatile, and always there when you need her!”

Last month, Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, described HMS Protector as an “essential presence” and confirmed she would be replaced at the end of her service life. He said the Ministry of Defense would replace HMS Protector with “a more modern variant” to ensure support for government activities in the Arctic and around the British Antarctic Territory would continue.

A Royal Navy spokesman said: “HMS Protector has returned to her home port of Devonport while investigations into a defect take place. As part of the defense investment plan, HMS Protector will be replaced with a more modern variant to maintain the ice patrol capability.

World.title: A tornado and an unusual spring hailstorm overwhelm Santiago, Chile
World.content:
A tornado and an unusual spring hailstorm overwhelm Santiago, Chile

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 07:01 UTC Full article

An electrical storm with hail, unusual in the middle of spring, flooded streets, homes and businesses in Santiago, Chile, on Tuesday and produced a tornado that the Chilean Meteorological Directorate preliminarily classified as EF0, the lowest intensity category. The national disaster prevention and response service declared a red alert in the Metropolitan Region, five days after the mudslide that hit the Las Condes district.

The tornado struck a bus terminal in Estación Central, in the west of the capital, where the gust lifted dozens of zinc sheets into the air. The storm began around 3:30pm, as students and workers were leaving schools and offices, and within minutes flooded avenues, underground car parks and buildings, in some cases with water coming through the roofs. According to regional governor Claudio Orrego, around 20 millimetres fell in about two and a half hours, and districts such as Independencia and Providencia recorded some 18 millimetres in one hour.

Some 22,000 homes were left without electricity, according to the Superintendency of Electricity and Fuels. Classes were suspended at municipal schools in Santiago, Providencia and Ñuñoa, and Las Condes extended its restricted-movement perimeter because of the risk of further landslides. Interior Minister Claudio Alvarado said “all emergency institutions” had been activated and that the rain was expected to ease overnight.

“Because of global warming, weather processes are intensifying. And we have just had an electrical storm like none ever seen in Santiago,” climatologist Alejandro Vial told the newspaper El País, linking the episode to El Niño.

Last week, an atmospheric river intensified by El Niño made this the wettest October on record in the Chilean capital and caused the October 8 mudslide in San Carlos de Apoquindo, which left six people injured and around 2,000 homes damaged.

World.title: New US Hemp Rules Take Effect December 11, Shifting Demand for South American Exporters
World.content:
New US Hemp Rules Take Effect December 11, Shifting Demand for South American Exporters

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 00:10 UTC Full article

When new US hemp rules take full effect on December 11, the products with the clearest path forward will be non-intoxicating goods made with THC-free ingredients.

One example: The USDA-certified organic CBD gummies sold by Colorado-based Joy Organics, which uses third-party lab testing to confirm non-detectable THC. For hemp growers and extractors in Uruguay, Colombia, and Argentina, that is where US demand is now likely to concentrate.

The change comes from Section 781 of Public Law 119-37, signed in Washington in November 2025, which rewrites the federal definition of hemp for the first time since the 2018 Farm Bill. Compliance moves from delta-9 THC alone to total THC, which also counts THCA, and finished hemp-derived cannabinoid products are capped at 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container.

The law was due to take full effect on November 12. A short-term funding bill signed on September 2 pushed most of it to December 11, although cannabinoids that the plant cannot produce naturally still lose hemp status on the original date.

Flower shipments face the steepest test

South American exporters have sent raw hemp north for several years. Uruguay recorded its first hemp export in 2020, a shipment to Switzerland, and in 2023 a Uruguayan company sent 10 tonnes of CBD flower to the United States, the largest such shipment from the country to date.

Under the new standard, laboratories calculate total THC as delta-9 THC plus 0.877 times the THCA content. Flower that passed the old delta-9 test can fail the new one once THCA is counted, which makes raw plant material the most exposed part of the trade.

The wider US market faces a similar squeeze. The US Hemp Roundtable, an industry group, has estimated that the new definition would eliminate about 95% of existing hemp-derived cannabinoid products, and stakeholders expect the per-container cap to rule out most full-spectrum CBD products as well.

Where demand is likely to move

What remains is a narrower but steadier category: CBD and other non-intoxicating cannabinoids in finished products that stay under the cap. That favours THC-free inputs, chiefly CBD isolate and broad-spectrum distillate from which THC has been removed, over whole flower and full-spectrum oil.

Paperwork will matter as much as the product. US brands selling gummies, softgels and tinctures already publish lab reports for their own goods, and they are expected to demand the same from suppliers. Joy Organics, for example, makes its THC-free gummies in 10, 25 and 50 mg strengths under USDA organic certification and posts batch lab results online. An organic label in the US depends on certified organic ingredients, so that kind of documentation has to travel back up the supply chain to whoever grew and extracted the hemp, which gives growers with organic certification an opening.

The region starts from different positions. Colombia has permitted hemp production for medical and scientific purposes since 2016 and built a licensing system aimed at export. Argentina passed a law in 2022 creating a framework for medical cannabis and industrial hemp. In Brazil, rules issued by the health regulator Anvisa earlier this year allow authorised companies to grow hemp for medicinal and research purposes, including cultivation aimed at exporting plant material. Brazilian trade press has also reported Uruguayan suppliers turning toward Brazil's import market as the US tightens.

December 11 is not necessarily the last word. The delay is tied to the US funding bill, so the date coincides with the next government funding deadline in Washington, and industry groups are lobbying for a regulated framework rather than a ban.

For exporters, the practical reading is simpler. Shipments built around THC-free ingredients and batch-level testing fit the rules as written, while raw flower depends on what Congress does next.

World.title: Argentina asks the law of the sea tribunal to halt Sea Lion and bar new oil permits
World.content:
Argentina asks the law of the sea tribunal to halt Sea Lion and bar new oil permits

13th Tuesday, October 2026 - 23:03 UTC Full article

The measures are sought pending the constitution of the arbitral tribunal under Annex VII of the Convention, proceedings Argentina launched with a notification to the United Kingdom on September 28

Argentina has asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order the United Kingdom to prevent the development of the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands and to refrain from granting new permits to exploit the resources of the disputed continental shelf, according to a statement published by the Hamburg-based tribunal. The hearing will be set “at the earliest possible date”.

The request, submitted on October 13 under Article 290(5) of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, lists four provisional measures: that the United Kingdom prevent “the commencement or continuation” of hydrocarbon exploitation through Sea Lion; that it refrain from using information obtained from exploring the disputed areas “to the detriment of the rights” of Argentina; that it stop preventing Argentina from complying with its obligation to protect the marine environment of those areas; and that it refrain from any measure that might aggravate the dispute, “in particular the granting of new permits”.

The measures are sought pending the constitution of the arbitral tribunal under Annex VII of the Convention, proceedings Argentina launched with a notification to the United Kingdom on September 28. Before that tribunal, Argentina asks for a declaration that the United Kingdom, by unilaterally authorising the exploration and exploitation of resources in the waters around the South Atlantic archipelagos, is in breach of its obligation to respect Argentina’s “sovereignty and sovereign rights” over those maritime areas; of the obligation to refrain from unilateral measures in areas subject to a dispute “within the framework of the decolonization process” of the UN; of the obligation to protect the marine environment; and of the obligation to settle disputes by peaceful means.

To prescribe provisional measures, the tribunal must consider that the arbitral tribunal would have prima facie jurisdiction and that the urgency of the situation so requires. In previous cases, such as Chagos in 2015 and Crimea in 2020, tribunals under the Convention have declined to rule on questions of territorial sovereignty.

The United Kingdom has said it will engage with the process and challenge any attempt to use it to settle sovereignty. Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran said on Tuesday that London’s position is that provisional measures are binding on the parties. Sea Lion, operated by Navitas Petroleum with 65% and Rockhopper Exploration with 35%, expects first oil in 2028.

World.title: Space debris on Mexico’s Bagdad Beach might be from a launch by SpaceX
World.content:
High tides are slowing efforts to remove suspected SpaceX debris found on Playa Bagdad — a stretch of Mexican coastline in the northeastern border state of Tamaulipas — where environmentalists reported collecting more than 200 fragments in the first 400 meters of a cleanup.

The conservation nonprofit Conibio Global said on Facebook it had delivered another bag of suspected space debris to Mexico’s federal environmental protection agency (Profepa).

🚀 #EsNoticia | ¿Qué está llegando del espacio a las costas de #Tamaulipas? En Playa Bagdad, reportan nuevos fragmentos que presuntamente provienen de cohetes de #SpaceX. La ONG Conibio Global pide investigar su origen y posibles daños ambientales. Mira esto. #OnceNoticias 🔻 https://t.co/TTke3t14Se — Once Noticias (@OnceNoticiasTV) October 10, 2026

The organization suspects the fragments came from SpaceX’s 14th Starship flight, launched Sept. 28 from Boca Chica, Texas — just across the border from Bagdad Beach, which takes its name from a historic port destroyed by hurricanes in the late 1800s.

However, the origin of individual pieces has not been confirmed.

Concerns about the debris harming marine life echo earlier discoveries.

In June 2025, President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico’s Environment Ministry (Semarnat) and other ministries would investigate debris reported on Bagdad Beach. At the time, hundreds of metal and plastic fragments had washed ashore following a Starship test flight launch.

In response at the time, SpaceX said tests of Starship materials found no chemical, biological or toxicological risks, and that it had offered Mexico resources and assistance to help recover debris.

As for the most recent cleanup, the newspaper Milenio reported that Conibio Global aimed to survey 50 kilometers of coastline, about 31 miles.

The group said tides had blocked access to some areas and that collection would resume when conditions dictate.

Inspections so far have identified insulation and coating materials. Environmentalists said waves, rain and currents could carry more fragments ashore.

Conibio Global warned that turtles, dolphins, birds and other marine animals could ingest debris or become entangled.

It called on authorities to identify the fragments, investigate potential environmental harm and require those responsible to repair any confirmed damage.

It also sought investigations into reported structural damage to homes and schools and declining fishing catches. However, reports do not establish causal links to SpaceX launches.

Playa Bagdad lies on Mexico’s Gulf coast, south of the Rio Bravo’s mouth. Known as the Río Grande in the United States, the river originates in Colorado and forms the entire 2,018-kilometer border between Texas and Mexico.

With reports from Uno TV, Once Noticias, Milenio and La Razón de Tamaulipas

World.title: Healthcare workers protest in virtually every state over pay, shortages and staffing
World.content:
Listen to this article

Thousands of Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) workers took to the streets of Mexico City and other cities across Mexico on Tuesday to demand higher pay, better work conditions, increased funding for healthcare and an end to shortages of medicines and medical supplies.

In the capital, around 7,000 workers, including doctors, nurses, orderlies, social workers and administrative staff joined a so-called megamarcha (mega-march), which set off from the IMSS-run Siglo XXI National Medical Center in the Doctores neighborhood at 4 p.m. and made its way to IMSS offices on Paseo de la Reforma, the tree-lined boulevard that runs into the historic center.

🔴“¡Presente!” Con un pase de lista, manifestantes mencionan a los estados donde trabajadores del IMSS se movilizan para exigir un aumento salarial, mejores condiciones laborales y el abasto de medicamentos e insumos médicos en las unidades de salud. https://t.co/hOiEVTO42z — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) October 14, 2026

“Don’t get sick because there are no supplies” and “Listen up people, this is your fight too” were among the slogans chanted by the protesting workers.

IMSS workers protested in virtually every state across Mexico on Tuesday, and additional demonstrations were held on Wednesday, including in Mexico City. Among the cities where protests were held on Tuesday were Monterrey, Guadalajara, Tijuana, León and Mérida. Some IMSS derechohabientes (beneficiaries) and other supporters of healthcare workers, including members of various unions, also participated in the protests.

IMSS is a major healthcare provider in Mexico, running hospitals and clinics across the country. Some 78 million people have healthcare coverage through IMSS, a figure that accounts for around 60% of Mexico’s total population. IMSS has more than 520,000 employees, around 80% of whom work in healthcare-related roles.

A 10% pay rise among workers’ demands

Thousands of IMSS workers have made it clear that they reject an offer of a 2.9% pay rise coupled with a 3.9% increase in benefits. Instead, they are demanding a 10% increase to their base pay.

IMSS workers reportedly turned out in large numbers to vote on the proposed pay rise on Wednesday. The newspaper Reforma reported that workers “fear the result might not reflect the will of the voters because the union is the judge” — i.e., members of the National Social Security Workers Union are overseeing the voting process.

At Tuesday’s protest in Mexico City, workers said they were formerly considered “heroes” because of their work during the COVID pandemic, but have now been “forgotten on the payroll.”

In addition to higher pay, IMSS workers have a range of other demands. They include:

The adequate supply of medications and medical supplies in IMSS hospitals and clinics.

The hiring of additional healthcare personnel in order to ease excessive workloads.

The allocation of resources equivalent to 7% of GDP to healthcare. (Mexico’s public and private expenditure on healthcare was below 6% in 2024, according to the OECD.)

Respect for their labor rights, including their right to speak out about problems in IMSS healthcare facilities.

Modifications to the Social Security Law to guarantee the ongoing financial viability of IMSS.

Changes to their pension system.

Additional upgrades to IMSS healthcare infrastructure. (The government has been modernizing hospitals.)

IMSS workers are also calling for the resignation or dismissal of Rafael Olivos Hernández, head of the National Social Security Workers Union. Workers have accused Olivos of pressuring them to accept the 2.9% pay rise on offer and violating union statutes. Some workers also called for the dismissal of IMSS chief Zoé Robledo.

Outside the IMSS offices on Paseo de la Reforma, disgruntled IMSS workers said that their fight for better pay and conditions is just getting started. They pledged to keep up the pressure with future protests if their demands aren’t met.

Vinicio Martínez, a spokesperson for protesting IMSS workers, told Reforma that protests could be “intensified” and that “activities that are a little bit more drastic” could be carried out “until our voice is heard.”

‘There are no syringes, [rubbing] alcohol or diapers. We’re short-staffed, too’

Workers who protested in Mexico City on Tuesday offered firsthand accounts of the conditions they face in IMSS healthcare facilities.

A nurse from the No. 30 General Hospital in the Mexico City borough of Iztacalco told the La Jornada newspaper that no one is called in to cover for staff who are on vacation or off sick.

“We don’t know why,” said the nurse, who asked to remain anonymous.

“We’ve had deficiencies for years and the quality of [medical] supplies has declined significantly,” she said.

The same woman rejected the proposed 2.9% pay increase, saying that it would only increase her fortnightly salary by 109 pesos (about US $6).

“That would be my raise if the union proposal is supported,” she said.

“I’m a single mother, I have a son at university and a daughter at primary school. It’s an insult to the work we do.”

José, a nursing student who works at the No. 32 General Hospital in the capital’s Coyoacán borough, told La Jornada that basic supplies are lacking.

“There are no syringes, [rubbing] alcohol or diapers. We’re short-staffed, too,” he said.

José also denounced the heavy workload medical personnel face, saying that it affects the quality of care they can provide.

América Barragán, a nurse from Jalisco who traveled to Mexico City to participate in Tuesday’s megamarcha, told Reforma that the public healthcare system lacks funds, medicines, medical supplies and personnel. She said that hospitals are overwhelmed by patients, who face long waits to receive specialized care.

“The demand to treat more patients in less time affects both working conditions and the quality and timeliness of medical services,” Barragán said.

She said that the problem won’t be resolved by demanding greater productivity from healthcare workers. Instead, more resources need to be allocated to healthcare, more workers need to be hired and hospital infrastructure needs to be upgraded, Barragán said.

She called on authorities to respond to IMSS workers’ demands with concrete solutions.

Sheinbaum: Workers’ ‘legitimate demands’ are being addressed

Asked about IMSS workers’ protest at her Wednesday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum initially responded by showing aerial footage of the Mexico City march.

“We took it from social media; it’s not filmed by the government or anything, but rather …by people who had drones,” she said.

“It’s important for everyone to reach their own conclusions,” Sheinbaum said before presenting footage that showed that the march stretched for quite a distance, but the crowd was relatively thin.

“That was the protest,” she said, adding that everyone could do “their own count of how many people participated.”

Sheinbaum went on to say that IMSS workers’ “legitimate demands” are being addressed. She conveyed the same message at her Tuesday morning press conference, during which she said resident doctors’ salaries would be increased and acknowledged that the government has work to do to improve the distribution of medications and medical supplies to public hospitals.

On Wednesday, Sheinbaum said that Robledo, the IMSS director, has been instructed to draw up an “action plan” to “immediately” address “all the legitimate demands of IMSS workers.”

“… When there is a legitimate demand, we’re listening,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that IMSS workers would vote on the proposed pay rise on Wednesday.

“A union consultation is taking place today to see whether [the pay rise] offered by IMSS management is approved or not. It was already approved in Congress, but as there were people who didn’t agree an open consultation is taking place,” she said.

“I asked the Mexican Social Security Institute to ensure that it is totally free,” Sheinbaum said. “… We’re going to wait for the results.”

A day after she outlined a range of government achievements in the area of healthcare, Sheinbaum said that her government is working hard to improve Mexico’s public healthcare system.

“We’re doing better [but] there are still challenges and we have to solve them,” she said.

With reports from La Jornada, Sin Embargo, Reforma, El Financiero and El Economista

World.title: The IMF casts doubt on Mexico’s chances of cracking the top 10 of world economies by 2030
World.content:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has thrown cold water on Mexico’s ambitious plan to return to the world’s Top 10 economies by 2030 by declaring in its latest World Economic Outlook, released on Tuesday, that the goal is unlikely to be reached until at least 2031, if then.

Citing underinvestment as a major factor, the IMF indicated that the expected maximum GDP growth rate over President Claudia Sheinbaum’s first term (ending in 2030) is 2.2%, not enough to reach 10th place among world economies. Sheinbaum had announced that goal shortly after her first 100 days in office two years ago in presenting her Plan México, which has guided Mexico’s economic policy since.

The IMF expects the average annual rate to reach 1.7% during President Sheinbaum’s term, compared with 0.9% under her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador and 1.9% under Enrique Peña Nieto (2012-2018).

On October 2, the IMF revised its projections for Mexico’s economic growth to 1.5% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027. It is projected at 2% in 2029, 2030 and 2031, which is lower than the average for Latin America and the Caribbean, which is is expected to exceed 2.5% in those years.

Mexico had held a top 10 position from 1999 to 2004, but by 2025 it had slipped to 15th. It is expected to rise to 13th this year, overtaking Australia and Spain, and is likely to remain there until 2030, when it will displace Russia to reach 12th place.

What Mexico needs to do to move up

In its report, the IMF stressed Mexico’s need to increase private investment by closing infrastructure gaps, reducing regulatory burdens and uncertainty and strengthening trade integration. It also highlighted the need to improve security, combat corruption and reduce informality.

The director of analysis and strategy at the Mexican financial institution Kapital, Alejandra Marcos Iza, cited a lack of investment, moderate consumption and the ongoing United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) negotiations as limiting factors for economic growth, suggesting that ongoing uncertainty surrounding trade fragmentation and U.S. tariffs has hindered new productive projects.

Meanwhile, a Bank of Mexico survey published in July, which assessed the opinions of 42 economic analysis groups from the national and international private sectors, highlighted governance issues as a major hindrance to economic growth, including public insecurity, the lack of the rule of law, internal political uncertainty and corruption.

With reports from El Universal and Puente Libre

World.title: El Jalapeño: US man who applied for Mexican citizenship confirms he now somehow knows the lyrics to ‘El Rey’
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Naturalization officials confirmed Thursday that a 34-year-old applicant who submitted his final paperwork for Mexican citizenship was immediately, involuntarily infused with the complete lyrics, pitch-perfect phrasing, and emotional gravity of José Alfredo Jiménez’s ranchera classic “El Rey.”

According to witnesses inside the Secretariat of Foreign Affairs (SRE) office, applicant Mark Miller was signing the final page of his administrative petition when his posture visibly shifted. Miller then closed his eyes, tilted his head slightly backward, and spontaneously articulated the nuanced vocal differences between Jiménez’s original 1971 recording and Vicente Fernández’s iconic 1973 cover version.

“I went to hand the clerk my residence card, and suddenly I was overcome by an absolute certainty regarding the exact moment to hold out the syllable in ‘re-e-ey‘,” said Miller, who had previously required a smartphone display to navigate basic verse structures at social gatherings. “I also felt a deep, ancestral understanding that while ‘Chente’ brought unmatchable vocal power to the track, José Alfredo’s version remains the definitive one.”

SRE officials stated that the phenomenon, colloquially referred to by immigration lawyers as the “subliminal cantina effect,” is a standard bureaucratic side effect of the naturalization pipeline. While native-born citizens absorb the complete national songbook passively during childhood family gatherings, naturalized residents typically receive the entire catalog in a single, concentrated neurological download upon biometric verification.

“It is a completely standard administrative outcome,” said SRE spokesperson Ana Luisa Peralta. “Once the background check clears, the applicant’s mind and body automatically integrate ‘Por Tu Maldito Amor,’ the mandatory world-weary vocal inflections for ‘Camino de Guanajuato,’ and the emotional capacity to belt out ‘Querida’ as though they were personally as heartbroken as Juan Gabriel back in 1984.”

Department sources noted that Miller’s files have been cleared for final processing, provided he can successfully complete the mandatory exit physical, which tests an applicant’s ability to distinctly trill their r’s without warm-up exercises.

World.title: Sheinbaum signs decree blocking violent and hostile content from minors’ social media feeds: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📱 Sheinbaum signs decree to curb harmful online content for minors: Social media sites and online forums will be barred from displaying or recommending content to minors that “generates or promotes” hate speech, violent extremism, self-harm, eating disorders, cyberbullying and illegal conduct. Platforms must also verify users’ ages, classify content by age group and offer parental supervision tools. The decree, drawn up after an Oct. 1 machete attack at a school in Torréon, Coahuila, takes effect one month after its publication in the government’s official gazette today.

🚓 Sheinbaum orders CNDH probe into alleged police torture in Guadalajara: The president said the National Human Rights Commission must conduct a “very thorough investigation” into allegations that Jalisco police tortured people detained at Sunday’s water contamination protest. “How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she asked.

⚖️ Sheinbaum defers to judges on ex-INM chief Garduño’s exoneration: Asked about Francisco Garduño’s exoneration over the 2023 Ciudad Juárez detention center fire that killed 40 migrants, the president said, “It’s what the judges determined.” Lawyers for the victims will challenge the ruling.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum signed a decree that will bar social media sites and other online forums from displaying or recommending content to minors that “generates or promotes” hate speech, violent extremism, sexual exploitation or violence, suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, cyber-bullying and illegal conduct in general.

The government drew up the decree after a fatal Oct. 1 machete attack at a school in Torréon, Coahuila, that was allegedly perpetrated by twin 18-year-old brothers who authorities say were exposed to violent content and extremist ideology online.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s response to allegations that Jalisco state police tortured people who were detained in Guadalajara on Sunday during a protest against contaminated water. One woman said that police beat her and stepped on her bare feet, causing fractures.

Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus said Tuesday that all 39 people detained during Sunday’s protest had been released. He said that police used excessive force and made “unjust arrests.”

He also said that “serious mistakes that must be investigated and sanctioned” were made.

“… No one should have been exposed to violence,” Lemus said.

Sheinbaum signs ‘safe digital environments’ decree

Presidential legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde told reporters that she and other officials met with representatives of social media and other tech companies to discuss the “decree to guarantee safe digital environments for girls, boys and adolescents,” which was presented by the government last Friday.

“Far from demonstrating resistance, they perfectly understood the need for an instrument of this nature,” she said.

Alcalde said that the decree will be published in the government’s official gazette today and take effect one month later.

The decree will oblige social media sites to detect and “immediately” remove “accounts and content that promote or generate violent conduct,” she said.

📲 SHEINBAUM FIRMA DECRETO PARA QUE PLATAFORMAS DIGITALES EVITEN DIFUNDIR CONTENIDOS VIOLENTOS La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum da un mes a las plataformas digitales para avanzar en la regulación de contenidos que inciten a la violencia, contra niñas, niños y adolescentes. ⚠️ Advirtió que, si las medidas no funcionan, se promoverá una reforma legal que establecería SANCIONES. Aclaró que no se trata de censura, sino de garantizar espacios digitales seguros. 📱🫡🫡 — Isabel Uribe (@Isa_Uribe) October 14, 2026

Alcalde said that social media sites will also have to “classify content” by its appropriateness for different age groups, verify the age of their users and “establish supervision tools” for mothers, fathers and legal guardians of minors.

Before signing the decree, Sheinbaum noted that social media and “digital platform” companies agreed with the government’s initiative.

“The only thing they asked for was a month to prepare their platforms so that this is a reality,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the government’s Digital Transformation and Communications Agency will monitor social media sites to ensure that companies are complying with the decree.

“If we see they aren’t complying, we would move onto a law which would involve sanctions for the platforms,” she said.

Sheinbaum orders investigation into allegations of police torture in Guadalajara

Regarding allegations that police tortured people who were detained during a protest against water contamination in Guadalajara on Sunday, Sheinbaum said that the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) has to conduct a “very thorough investigation.”

“Yesterday I was asked about the issue of torture in Jalisco. … What happened in Jalisco can’t be allowed,” she said.

“… In addition to the use of streams of water and tear gas [against protesters], the issue of torturing young people is something that has to disappear in our country,” Sheinbaum said.

“A police force cannot torture anyone,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the CNDH investigation should examine “who gave the order” to torture detainees and interview “the victims.”

“… How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she asked.

“… We, who came from the fight against [government] repression, cannot allow there to be police forces in Mexico that repress and torture,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum responds to exoneration of former INM chief

A reporter asked the president her opinion about the exoneration of former National Migration Institute (INM) chief Francisco Garduño, who faced a charge of improper exercise of public service in connection with a 2023 fire in an INM detention center in Ciudad Juárez that killed 40 migrants.

“It’s what the judges determined,” Sheinbaum responded.

Garduño, head of the INM between 2019 and 2025, was exonerated at a court hearing in Ciudad Juárez on Tuesday. Lawyers for the victims said they will challenge the decision.

Sheinbaum said that “a very thorough investigation” that examined “the responsibilities of each person” in connection with the fire was carried out. She then reiterated that the exoneration of Garduño was a decision made by “judges.”

According to authorities, the fire started when two detained migrants set a mattress alight to protest poor conditions in the INM detention center. Those two men survived the blaze and face homicide charges.

The Federal Attorney General’s Office began criminal proceedings against Garduño in April 2023, alleging that he failed to fulfill his duty to “supervise, protect and provide security to the people and facilities” under his control.

In September 2025, the former INM chief issued an apology to victims and relatives of the deceased.

There were “human rights violations that never should have happened” due to “omissions by personnel of the [INM],” he said at the time.

The Associated Press reported that Garduño “called for ‘those responsible’ to be punished and for reparations to be made without recognizing his own responsibility in the tragedy.”

To date, no one has been convicted of criminal wrongdoing in connection with the deadly fire.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Helping out after hurricanes, planning for Día de Muertos
World.content:
By the time you read this, Puerto Vallarta will be recovering from its third consecutive hurricane in the last few weeks. First came Polo, then Rachel, and now Simón — a Category 3 storm currently making its way up the Pacific coast. Luckily, the storms’ eyes stayed offshore, sparing the city the worst impacts. Still, our malecón and beachside resorts have taken a beating from intense tidal surges and waves; many neighborhoods have flooded, and we haven’t been able to safely enjoy the beach since Sept. 23, when the first red flags were raised.

Needless to say, many residents — myself included — are feeling a bit of a hurricane hangover these days and are thinking less about going out on the town and more about helping our communities recover.

So instead of entertainment listings, this week’s events roundup highlights a few volunteer opportunities and organizations that provide disaster relief and organize cleanup efforts after major storms and throughout the year. Whether you live in Puerto Vallarta permanently, seasonally, or just vacation here from time to time, there are ways you can help residents recover through these groups.

We’ve also thrown in what we know so far about Día de Muertos happenings. Even though we’ve been thrashed around by storms lately, this is still Mexico, so the celebrations will go on come hurricanes or high water.

Disaster relief, cleanup and community support organizations

Vallarta Cares

Vallarta Cares is a local charity that mobilizes food, water, hygiene and medical supply distribution to communities affected by natural disasters, including hurricanes, floods and other emergencies. The organization also operates a year-round soup kitchen that serves hundreds of meals daily, provides weekly medical services, including free dental services, and organizes medical brigades throughout the year.

Vallarta Cares was also recently awarded first place in the interior of Jalisco category for the 2026 Premio a la Generosidad Jalisco. You can inquire about volunteer opportunities and make a donation through its website.

Limpia Tu Mar

Limpia Tu Mar organizes trash cleanups along Vallarta’s beaches, rivers and at sea. Since its inception in 2017, the group’s cleanup brigades have removed more than 900 kilograms (1,984 pounds) of plastic, 125 kilograms (275 pounds) of styrofoam, 350 kilograms (771 pounds) of glass and 5,000 kilograms (11,023 pounds) of general garbage from the sea. Each week, volunteers set sail on boats from Puerto Vallarta to remove floating trash from the ocean.

Limpia Tu Mar also hosts one of Mexico’s largest environmental awareness events, the annual International Trash Fishing Tournament. This year’s tournament is coming up Oct. 18, and registration is still open if you want to participate or help sponsor the event. With all the recent storms washing tons of trash and debris into the bay, we could use all the help we can get to clean it up.

Local collection centers and cleanup brigades

If you are in Puerto Vallarta during hurricane season (June through November), local collection centers (centros de acopio) are often set up at community centers, fire stations and churches on short notice to organize relief efforts. Joining local community and business groups on social media is one of the fastest ways to find pop-up volunteering needs immediately following a storm.

One such brigade I join regularly is the Banderas Bay Project, started by local real estate agent Luis Salazar, which organizes monthly trash pickups around Boca de Tomatlán, one of the harder-hit areas from the recent storms.

Planning for Día de Muertos

Día de Muertos — Mexico’s annual celebration honoring departed souls — is around the corner, and that means Puerto Vallarta will again be pulling out all the stops.

This year, the city is participating in the statewide Festival de Las Almas (Festival of the Souls), featuring more than 350 free events across 11 municipalities in Jalisco from Oct. 24 through Nov. 2.

In Vallarta, the city is planning 28 free events and experiences Oct. 31 through Nov. 2 along the historic center, Los Arcos, Muelle de Los Muertos, Isla del Cuale, and, of course, the Malecón, which will again feature a monumental Catrina. The giant beauty has adorned the Malecón for the past several years, each time designed by a different Mexican artist. According to the Puerto Vallarta Tourism Board, this year she will be adorned with waves, whales, manta rays and bougainvillea.

If you do plan on heading downtown for the festivities, I recommend going early before the crowds get too big. Last year, we waited until after dark to go see the Catrina and were stuck in traffic for more than an hour trying to drive from the Marina to the Malecón.

Concierto de Día de Muertos

The Vallarta Symphony Orchestra will perform with the choirs of Puerto Vallarta and the University of Brasília for special Día de Muertos concerts on Oct. 30 at the Iglesia Reina de la Paz in Marina Vallarta at 9 p.m., and on Oct. 31 at the Haramara Auditorium at Universidad Tecnológica de Bahía de Banderas in Nayarit at 7 p.m. Tickets can be purchased from IAMPV.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: US congressional candidate says Mexico is where he gets healthcare as high costs dominate midterm debate
World.content:
Bobby Pulido, a singer and Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in Texas’s 15th District, recently said that he does not have health insurance and has had to go to Mexico to receive medical care.

Pulido, who is running against Republican Mónica De La Cruz, made the unexpected remark to Council President and CEO Javier Palomerez during a virtual discussion on Monday with the U.S. Hispanic Business Council.

“I’m going to start off by telling you that I don’t have health insurance, Javier. And I’m embarrassed to tell you that I’ve had to go to Mexico for my health care,” Pulido said, as cited by news outlet Border Report, reportedly the only journalism outlet that accessed the meeting.

Pulido, 52, whose full name is José Roberto Pulido Jr., lives in Edinburg, a border city located in southern Texas. According to Border Report, he also owns a home in Mexico.

During the conversation, Pulido contrasted U.S. President Trump’s reported plans to boost military spending with the difficulties U.S. residents face in obtaining affordable medical care.

“I live in the richest country in the world. Now the president wants to give a million and a half trillion dollars for our military budget when we cannot provide affordable health care to our people,” he said.

Pulido’s statements did not describe what specific illness, procedure or medical emergency has brought him to seek care in Mexico. Nor does the information shared by Border Report specify which Mexican city he visits for treatment, how much he pays or the reasons why he lacks insurance in the United States.

However, this isn’t the first time Pulido has publicly shared that he has traveled to Mexico for healthcare. On Sept. 27, he told Univisión he sought medical services in Mexico due to high costs in the U.S., while questioning the power of insurance companies in that country.

Before turning to politics, Pulido had a renowned career as a Tejano singer, with a fan base spanning Mexico and the U.S. Over the course of a three-decade career, he won two Latin Grammy Awards for Best Tejano Music Album — one of which he won in November 2025.
