World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Chief ministers unite to press federal government on devolution
World.content:
Chief ministers unite to press federal government on devolution

Their two-day meeting ended Wednesday with an agreement to form a joint forum to push for greater provincial powers, fiscal autonomy, and a clearer division of responsibilities with the centre.

In the Koshi Declaration-2026 issued at the end of the conference on Wednesday, the chief ministers identified incomplete devolution of powers, limited provincial fiscal autonomy, and delays in transferring administrative structures as major obstacles to the effective implementation of federalism. Partbat Portel/TKP

World.title: Deuba faction presses ahead with parallel Congress convention
World.content:
Deuba faction presses ahead with parallel Congress convention

The rival camp has completed constituency conventions in 112 of 165 federal constituencies, but thousands of ward and local-level gatherings remain outstanding.

Members of the Sher Bahadur Deuba-led faction of the Nepali Congress attend the joint ward convention in Kathmandu Constituency-1. Nepal Photo Library

World.title: Parliamentary panel rejects two ambassador nominees, clears 10
World.content:
Parliamentary panel rejects two ambassador nominees, clears 10

The committee rejected Giri Bahadur Sunar and Chudamani Kharel over concerns about their suitability, while questions over the Japan nominee’s residency status prompted the panel to adjourn its meeting until after Dashain.

Lawmakers at the Parliamentary Hearing Committee meeting at Singha Durbar, Kathmandu, on Wednesday. RSS

World.title: Father cannot afford last rites for son missing in Bhotekoshi floods
World.content:
Father cannot afford last rites for son missing in Bhotekoshi floods

Forty-seven days after 25-year-old Pradip Sapkota went missing, his family has yet to recover his body and is struggling to pay for his funeral rites.

Baburam Sapkota, whose son Pradip went missing in the Bhotekoshi floods, visits the Makawanpur District Administration Office on Monday to seek financial assistance for his son’s last rites. Post Photo

World.title: Makawanpur begins process to declare 58 missing people dead
World.content:
Makawanpur begins process to declare 58 missing people dead

Authorities have begun verifying the status of those missing since the August 26 Bhotekoshi floods under a special government procedure, with local units required to collect applications and check claims.

World.title: Army chief Sigdel returns from official UK visit
World.content:
Army chief Sigdel returns from official UK visit

General Sigdel met senior British military officials and honoured Nepali soldiers who won gold at an international military exercise.

Lieutenant General Pradip Jung KC welcomed General Ashok Raj Sigdel at Tribhuvan International Airport on Wednesday. Sigdel had been on an official visit to the UK on October 5. Photo: Courtesy of Nepali Army

World.title: A timber bridge reopens route to Upper Manang after three weeks
World.content:
A timber bridge reopens route to Upper Manang after three weeks

A wooden deck laid over the steel girders of a submerged bridge has restored access for jeeps and motorcycles, but heavier vehicles remain barred.

A temporary wooden deck has been laid over the steel girders of the existing truss bridge in Chame, allowing light vehicles to cross the river again. Aash Gurung/TKP

World.title: India boat capsizes, drowning 13, mostly children
World.content:
India boat capsizes, drowning 13, mostly children

Police are ​investigating the ​cause of the incident, regional police ​officer Subodh Kumar ​told Reuters on Wednesday, giving the tally of those ​rescued.

World.title: Japan to invest up to $21 billion in two U.S. chip factories to be run by GlobalFoundries
World.content:
Japan will invest up to $21 billion in two chip factories in New York state that will be jointly owned by the U.S. government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries, the company said on Wednesday.

The move is part of a deal for Japan to invest $550 billion in the U.S. struck by President Donald Trump’s administration last year in return for the U.S. lowering tariffs on Japanese cars and other imports from at least 25% to 15%.

The U.S. will take a stake in the new chip factories, but Japan will provide all of the investment capital, GlobalFoundries said.

World.title: Saudi crown prince faces Houthi menace in one of his biggest crises
World.content:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is facing one of the biggest crises of his tenure as the Houthis, whom he tried to crush a decade ago, attack the kingdom while his allies hold back.

The Houthi drone and missile campaign has killed at least 18 people and shut the country’s main airport, stretching the kingdom’s defenses. Hundreds of Saudi flights remain grounded, schools have moved online and the capital’s financial district has shifted to remote work — less than two weeks before Riyadh hosts its flagship gathering of global investors.

That leaves the crown prince, who has spent years and billions of dollars courting world leaders and financiers, in need of allies more than at any time since he became the de facto ruler in 2017. But with the Houthis hitting deep inside the kingdom from their base in Yemen, Crown Prince Mohammed may find Saudi Arabia has few options.

World.title: AFC open to postponing Asian Cup as attacks in Saudi Arabia disrupt sports calendar
World.content:
The “Six Kings Slam” tennis tournament originally scheduled for October has been postponed to December 27 to 30, organizers said on Wednesday after the recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, while the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) is open to postponing the Asian Cup to 2028.

A strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement claiming responsibility for the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

“The decision reflects Riyadh Season’s commitment to delivering sporting events to the highest standards, following an assessment of the organizational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament and their potential impact on the quality of the audience experience,” organizers said in a statement.

World.title: Ukraine accuses U.S. of helping Russia as missiles hit Kyiv
World.content:
Ukraine on Wednesday accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv’s military response through changes to the Starlink system it uses on the battlefield.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on U.S. tech billionaire Elon Musk to restore Starlink, which Kyiv says has been slowed down.

“I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem,” Zelenskyy told U.K. journalist Piers Morgan. “I don’t know, but we are asking to do it, to switch (it) on.”

World.title: Kobe sees off Jeonbuk to claim second Asian Champions League win
World.content:
Vissel Kobe maintained a perfect start to the eastern league phase of the Asian Champions League Elite on Wednesday with a 2-0 victory over South Korea’s Jeonbuk Motors to register the team’s second win in a row.

Yuya Osako gave the home side the lead in the 12th minute when he peeled away from his marker to convert from Katsuya Nagato’s corner and Yuya Kuwasaki hit the second midway through the second half.

“I think it’s extremely important to earn three points at home,” said Osako, whose goal was his first in this season’s competition.

“I’m happy we were able to get off to a good start and begin our home campaign on a positive note.”

Kobe had dominated the opening exchanges and deserved to take the lead when Osako struck but as proceedings wore on Jeonbuk’s threat increased.

Brazilian winger Italo cut the home defense open repeatedly after the interval, setting up Bruno Mota to hit the woodwork before substitute Lee Seung-woo headed inches wide of the Kobe goal.

Choi Woo-jin then struck the crossbar from distance before Kobe pounced on the counterattack, with Yoshinori Muto setting up Kuwasaki to sweep his 68th minute shot past Song Bum-keun.

The win moved Kobe level with compatriots Kashima Antlers and Gamba Osaka as well as China’s Beijing Guoan on six points.

Kashiwa Reysol picked up its first win of the campaign with a 5-1 thrashing of Thailand’s Port FC as the Japanese host took a five-goal lead inside the opening half hour.

Tojiro Kubo put Kashiwa in front in the third minute before goals from Yuki Kakita, Riki Harakawa, Koya Yuriki and Hinata Yamauchi gave the home side an unassailable advantage by the 28th minute.

The first eight finishers in the 16-team league phase in both east and west Asia will qualify for the last 16 with the quarterfinals, semifinals and final due to be played in Saudi Arabia in April and May.

World.title: Hitachi eyes small nuclear reactors in Japan as power costs rise
World.content:
Hitachi is exploring developing small modular reactors in Japan as high energy costs have started shifting public opinion toward nuclear power, according to the company’s energy business head.

Hitachi Energy is developing SMR technology with partners, Chief Executive Officer Andreas Schierenbeck said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi. Building a new reactor from scratch could take five to 10 years, he said, while playing down concerns that new projects could face opposition rooted in memories of the Fukushima nuclear disaster more than a decade ago.

“The public opinion is changing slightly,” Schierenbeck said in an interview. “High energy prices are changing these positions.”

Japan relies heavily on imported natural gas and coal for electricity and has faced elevated fuel costs from disruptions linked to the Strait of Hormuz and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Nuclear power, when operating, is among the country’s lowest-cost sources of electricity.

Small modular reactors, having capacity of 300 megawatts or less, are increasingly seen as a way to decarbonize energy, especially in hard-to-abate industries. Only three such reactors are currently operating across the world — in the U.S., China and Russia — and about 70 projects are at different stages of progress, according to the World Nuclear Association.

The Japanese government has been pushing to restart reactors idled after the Fukushima disaster and build new units to replace aging plants, seeking to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. But strict regulation and local opposition have slowed the revival, with only 15 of the country’s 33 operable reactors currently online.

World.title: Program helps children with developmental issues through theater
World.content:
An after-school program in Kobe is helping children with developmental issues build confidence and independence through theater activities, a relatively unusual approach in Japan.

The provider of the after-school program, Hokagorubi, offers creative activities through improvisational plays. It was established by Masatoshi Odaira in 2020 after he gained experience in theater as a university student and later taught drama to students at a special-needs school.

According to Odaira, children who had difficulty maintaining posture or speaking clearly often became more confident and expressive after performing on stage. This made him believe that theater can “have a therapeutic effect.”

In late July, ahead of a stage performance, nine students at Hokagorubi rehearsed a play set at an airport and centered on a young travel enthusiast. Although some forgot lines or encountered difficulties, the participants communicated with and supported each other.

Currently, Hokagorubi has 39 students ranging from elementary school first-graders to high school seniors, including those with autism spectrum disorder or attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. Some refuse to attend school.

It holds three performances a year, with participants divided into six groups. Each group is responsible for writing scripts, directing productions and creating props.

A 14-year-old participant said, “I enjoy improvisational performances as they allow me to express myself freely” and “I hope to continue taking part.” When he feels anxiety, he impersonates an anime character and talks to himself in the bathroom. His mother said that the theater program “helps foster self-esteem by providing a place where participants can take on roles and express themselves.”

Nabi Ito, a lecturer specializing in contemporary theater at the University of Osaka, said that theater can make communication easier for children who struggle with conversation because scripts provide a framework and such children can act as someone else.

Odaira said that a performance should be considered a success as long as it reaches its conclusion, even if participants encounter difficulties on stage.

“I hope children will gain positive experiences in conversation and communication while acting and develop confidence in interactions with others,” he said.

World.title: ‘Zen and Ghibli’ doesn’t lecture. It teaches contemplation.
World.content:
For more than four decades, Toshio Suzuki has shaped Studio Ghibli from behind the scenes as a producer, working alongside directors Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata. In “Zen and Ghibli: Life Lessons for Lasting Happiness from the Legendary Studio,” Suzuki reflects on his career through a series of conversations with three Buddhist priests about uncertainty, ordinary life and the ways in which anime can illuminate Zen thought.

The book, originally serialized in the monthly Japanese magazine Nagomi, is part film commentary, part spiritual reflection and, at its best, a reminder that the studio’s appeal has always depended on negative space: what its stories leave unexplained as much as what they show.

World.title: ‘Not tailor-made for us’: Hongkong Post staff say transfer scheme too narrow
World.content:
Hong Kong postal workers denied permanent contracts have criticised a special government transfer scheme as too narrow, calling for more pathways into roles that match their experience, such as workman and artisan positions.

Several affected workers told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday that the concessions offered insufficient support and failed to reflect their skills or circumstances.

One postal worker, who asked not to be named, said that while the government had offered priority hiring for other civil service jobs, suitable vacancies were limited.

“I checked the government vacancies system; most of the openings are for doctors, nurses, aircraft engineers and marine officers, which are not suitable for postal staff,” he said. “We cannot get an offer.”

World.title: Hong Kong extends smart fire alarm scheme to another 6,000 old buildings
World.content:
Hong Kong’s Fire Services Department has extended a scheme allowing property owners to install smart fire alarm systems rather than traditional safety equipment to another 6,000 old buildings, but conceded that no installations had been completed although the policy was rolled out over five months ago for 3,600 blocks.

Lai Kin-mo, acting deputy chief fire officer for building improvement, said on Wednesday that while 300 buildings had expressed interest in installing the system, which can send alerts within 10 seconds of detecting smoke, owners were still trying to reach a consensus on related issues.

“Different service providers will provide different installation plans that involve work fees. I think it’s mostly prices that they are negotiating as the technology is already there and space is not a concern,” Lai said.

World.title: Exhibition of pioneering Hong Kong school for national talent in early 1940s opens
World.content:
A new exhibition about a pioneering school that nurtured talent for the country has opened at a Hong Kong history museum as part of the government’s efforts to promote national education, with many exhibits shown in the city for the first time.

“National Development and Achievements Series: Cultivation and Renewal – The Education Legacy of Hong Kong’s Ta Teh Institute”, a free exhibition presented by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, will run at the Hong Kong Museum of History in Tsim Sha Tsui from Wednesday to February 15 next year.

Ta Teh Institute was a liberal arts university established in Tuen Mun in 1946 during the Chinese Civil War. It was the second university to be established in the city after the University of Hong Kong. The institute closed down in 1949.

World.title: Nearly 1 in 3 unattended dogs captured in Hong Kong euthanised this year
World.content:
Roughly one in three unattended dogs captured by Hong Kong authorities had been euthanised as of May this year, a sharp rise from 18 per cent in 2021, according to the latest legislative documents.

The proportion of captured unattended dogs later reclaimed by their owners or transferred to animal welfare groups for rehoming has also fallen over the past five years, the Environment and Ecology Bureau told lawmakers on Wednesday.

In a written response to the Legislative Council, Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan said 617 unattended dogs had been euthanised between 2021 and May this year.

World.title: 3 Hong Kong taxi drivers banned for 3 months under demerit points system
World.content:
Three Hong Kong taxi drivers have been disqualified from driving cabs for three months after accumulating 15 demerit points or more under a penalty system in place for two years, the transport chief has said, disclosing such figures for the first time.

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said on Wednesday that since the mechanism took effect in September 2024, 229 taxi drivers had incurred demerit points as of October 2, with 125 cases involving a refusal to accept a hire.

In a reply to a question from lawmaker Chris Ip Ngo-tung, Chan said the three drivers had been disqualified for three months after incurring 15 demerit points or more on the Taxi-Driver-Offence points system - the first time authorities revealed this figure.

Under the system, taxi drivers will receive three, five or 10 demerit points for each of the 11 types of misconduct and can be disqualified from driving a taxi for three months if they accumulate 15 points or more within two years. Repeat offenders face a six-month suspension.

World.title: Hong Kong police hunt suspect who stole HK$80,000 necklace from jewellery store
World.content:
Hong Kong police are searching for a man who stole a gold necklace worth nearly HK$80,000 (US$10,193) from a Chow Sang Sang jewellery store in Tai Po on Wednesday afternoon.

According to a source, the suspect, described as a man in his forties, entered the shop on Kwong Fuk Road around 3.10pm.

After asking to try on the necklace, which weighed more than a tael (37.5 grams or 1.3 ounces), he snatched it, fled towards Kwong Fuk Lane and boarded an airport-bound bus.

Initial investigations revealed that the suspect did not appear to be armed, and no property was damaged during the incident.

World.title: Hong Kong urged to add online safety briefings, penalise no-shows at public gyms
World.content:
Hong Kong should make better use of its public gyms by allowing online safety briefings and penalising no-shows, an industry leader and a lawmaker have urged after the ombudsman identified management loopholes.

The Office of the Ombudsman launched the inquiry into public gym management on Tuesday, noting that rigid mandatory training requirements combined with a severe shortage of places were creating significant barriers to public participation and leaving facilities underused.

The watchdog also flagged booking loopholes for monthly ticket holders, including late cancellations and the absence of penalties for no-shows.

Gordon Yau Yick-chung, chairman of the Hong Kong Fitness Guide, on Wednesday described the briefing and training requirements as outdated.

World.title: In Hong Kong, accountability must be more than a slogan
World.content:
When news broke last week that three newly completed housing blocks were to be demolished without ever having been occupied, I suffered an immediate attack of deja vu. In early 1974, I was in the first wave of recruits to the Operations Department of the newly established Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

As luck would have it, my first posting was to the team dealing with the old Public Works Department. That was my introduction to the wide world of corruption and shoddy work in the local construction industry. The terrible thing is that some practices seem to have hardly changed at all despite half a century of efforts to eradicate them.

Common problems we found in those days were foundations not dug deeply enough or concrete not up to strength . There seemed to be a particular issue with steel reinforcement bars: there were not enough of them, or they were too short, too thin or in the wrong place. Sometimes they were deficient in all four aspects.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019121/Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.title: Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019121/Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.content:
Popular Chinese TV drama “Against the Current” has sparked debate about power dynamics between divorced male characters and their female counterparts after featuring a romantic plot between a low-ranking young woman and a high-status divorced man.

The discussion began after the 48-episode drama premiered Sept. 11 on Tencent Video, its international platform WeTV, and Disney+, and was bolstered by this month’s release of a similar drama also featuring a divorcé, “Irreplaceable.”

Set in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), “Against the Current” follows Shen Jialan, whose privileged life is upended when her grandfather, a renowned academician, is falsely accused of treason, endangering the lives of her entire family.

In exchange for a previous act of kindness, a couple allows Shen to take on the name of their late daughter, Xu Lanxiang, to escape execution. Under her new identity, Shen goes to work as a maid for her former fiancé, Lin Jinqi, who has since married another woman. Lin eventually divorces his wife to marry Shen.

After its release, the series became the most popular series on Disney+ in markets including North America and Spain, and topped WeTV charts in the U.S. and at least seven Asian countries outside China. Domestically, it currently tops analytics platform Yunhe Data’s long drama most-viewed list, with over a third of market viewership on Oct. 12.

Though the drama has been applauded for its storytelling and nuanced character development, some viewers have criticized Lin’s characterization, arguing that the show romanticizes unequal relationship dynamics, fueled by his status as a male divorcee. Lin, who divorces his wife after she cheats on him, curries favor with the King, asking him to force Shen to marry him against her will.

The debate has spread to other Chinese romance dramas that increasingly feature divorced and remarried male leads, from past hits such as “The Story of Minglan” (2018) and “The Glory” (2025), to dramas like “A Splendid Match” and “Irreplaceable” released this year.

Viewers have critiqued the imbalanced power dynamics in these series, which feature powerful, wealthy divorcés who offer protection, stability, and emotional guidance, often to younger, naive heroines from lower social statuses.

The recent popularity of remarried male leads marks a departure from the decadeslong shuangjie, or “purity on both sides,” trope in Chinese romance dramas, which favors depicting couples with no prior romantic or sexual experience before they fall in love.

In these stories, male leads are usually portrayed as successful, devoted figures whose affection belongs exclusively to the heroine, while female leads are frequently portrayed as innocent and kind.

Social media users have linked the shift to changing social realities, including rising divorce rates and the growing visibility of divorce and second marriages. Others have criticized it as a cheap way to create attention-grabbing plot twists, adding that the trend risks turning divorced males into a symbol of maturity and status while reinforcing unequal relationship dynamics.

Viewers point to the gender gap commonly found in romance narratives between divorcés and their female counterparts. When dramas instead feature divorced female protagonists, the corresponding male leads are often single or younger, and the story follows them as they “catch up” to their female counterparts professionally.

In the modern drama “Sniper Butterfly,” for instance, divorced protagonist Cen Jin reunites with a younger man who later becomes a successful professional in his own right as well as her business partner.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “Against The Current.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019117/Zheng Qinwen’s China Open Win Swamps Her Sponsor’s Tea Shops
World.title: Zheng Qinwen’s China Open Win Swamps Her Sponsor’s Tea Shops
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019117/Zheng Qinwen’s China Open Win Swamps Her Sponsor’s Tea Shops
World.content:
A daylong, nationwide buy-one-get-one-free promotion by Chinese milk tea brand Chagee, launched in honor of Zheng Qinwen becoming the first Chinese woman to win the China Open title on Sunday, saw its online ordering systems crash amid inundated orders.

The company made the announcement via its official account on microblogging platform Weibo the night of Zheng’s win, saying the sales promotion would run throughout Monday, calling it a “new (moment) in history worth raising a glass to together.” The tennis player has been a Chagee brand ambassador since 2024.

The sudden traffic surge beginning around 8 a.m. Monday crashed the brand’s mini program on super app WeChat, leaving many users unable to place orders. The crash sparked heated discussion online, with a related hashtag on Weibo attracting over 180 million views as of Tuesday and rising to the platform’s trending topics list. A check by Sixth Tone later on Monday found the problem had been resolved.

At the China Open, Zheng defeated Russia’s Mirra Andreeva, the French Open champion, in two straight sets, catapulting her to the 23rd-best women’s tennis player in the world. Last June, Zheng ranked world No. 4, a career high, but injuries over the past year forced her to stop competing and caused her ranking to drop to No. 160. She entered this year’s China Open as a wildcard, invited directly by the organizing committee.

After the win, several photos of Zheng lifting the China Open trophy were posted on her official Weibo account. A caption alongside the photos reads: “The weight of this trophy is the weight of a dream, dedicated to the younger me who always worked hard for that dream.”

According to domestic media outlet ChinaStarMarket.cn, Zheng currently holds 14 brand endorsements spanning cosmetics, sportswear, luxury accessories, cars, and technology, among others. Her endorsements include international brands such as Nike, Dior, Rolex, and Wilson, as well as Chinese brands such as Chagee, Alibaba-owned digital payment system Alipay, and large language model Qwen, also owned by Alibaba.

During Zheng’s break from competition, none of her brand endorsements were terminated, according to domestic media outlet Jiemian News. Instead, many companies increased their support, with Chagee upgrading her title from Global Health Ambassador to Global Brand Ambassador, and Wilson launching a Zheng-inspired signature tennis racket.

According to Forbes’ world tennis player earnings list, released in August and covering the 12 months prior, Zheng was the only Chinese player in the top 10, ranking seventh globally with $22.6 million — with over 97% reportedly coming from brand endorsements.

Zheng also earned roughly 474 million yuan ($71 million) in prize money and endorsements between 2024 and 2026, matching in three years what Chinese tennis legend Li Na made over her entire 15-year career.

Zheng’s commercial breakthrough came in 2024, when she finished runner-up at the Australian Open, her best Grand Slam result and the second-best by a Chinese player after Li Na. She went on to win the Paris Olympics women’s singles title that year, becoming China’s first Olympic tennis singles champion.

At the Guangzhou Auto Show in November 2024, Audi’s Chinese sub-brand AUDI named Zheng a brand ambassador. In January 2025, Dior selected her as its global brand ambassador, making her the first Chinese athlete to hold the role.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: China’s Zheng Qinwen poses with the trophy after defeating Mirra Andreeva in the women’s singles final of the China Open at the National Tennis Center in Beijing, Oct. 11, 2026. Fred Lee/Getty Images/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019102/She Is Chinese Opera’s Greatest Star. And Its Most Divisive.
World.title: She Is Chinese Opera’s Greatest Star. And Its Most Divisive.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019102/She Is Chinese Opera’s Greatest Star. And Its Most Divisive.
World.content:
For Chinese opera fans, 2026 will surely be remembered for one thing: Mao Weitao’s triumphant return to the stage.

Few outside China may have heard of her, but the 63-year-old is a titanic figure in her chosen discipline, Yue opera, and part of that rare group of artists who transcend their field to achieve crossover fame.

Over her nearly 50-year career, Mao has fearlessly reinvented the traditional art form, dragging it back into China’s cultural mainstream through a series of daring — and often provocative — creative choices.

From shaving her head to play Kong Yiji, the poor male scholar and eponym of Lu Xun’s classic short story, to producing “The New Dragon Gate Inn,” hailed as China’s first immersive opera show, she has continually pushed the boundaries of what a Yue opera can be.

The innovations have helped her achieve unprecedented commercial and critical success. But they have also made her a polarizing figure: even today, she jokes that she feels like she should wear “a bulletproof vest” whenever she premieres a new work.

Mao’s journey began at 17 with her first bow in Yue opera — one of around 300 regional varieties of traditional Chinese opera, originating in the city of Shaoxing in eastern China’s Zhejiang province.

Yue opera is known for being the only Chinese opera style in which female performers play every role — including male characters — and Mao quickly stood out for her rare ability as a kunsheng: an actress able to infuse male roles with beauty and elegance.

Within five years, she became the first ever Yue opera performer to receive the Plum Blossom Prize, China’s highest honor for theatrical performance. She has since won the award twice more — the only Yue opera actress in history to receive the so-called Plum Blossom Grand Prize, given to those who win the honor three times.

Yet she has also sparked plenty of outrage. Her raw, stripped-back portrayal of Kong Yiji in 1998 — which saw the 36-year-old Mao appear onstage with a buzzcut and dressed in rags — violated every norm of Yue opera, which traditionally seeks to delight audiences with lavish costumes and graceful performances.

A heated debate over the merits of tradition versus modernization followed, as critics accused Mao of sacrificing Yue opera’s soul for the sake of her creative vision. But ticket sales were excellent — and Mao continued to forge her own path.

After stepping back from performing in the mid-2010s, she co-launched her own production company — Baiyue Cultural Creative — with partners including the Chinese tech giant Alibaba and a Zhejiang Yue opera troupe. More experimentation followed.

In 2023, Baiyue debuted “The New Dragon Gate Inn” — an immersive Yue opera based on a hit 1992 Chinese martial arts movie. The first Chinese opera show of its kind, it followed a format similar to immersive stage shows like “Sleep No More,” letting the audience move freely through a recreation of the inn as the actors performed around them.

When the show became a massive commercial success — turning lead performers Chen Lijun and Li Yunxiao into stars — it felt like Mao was passing the baton to the next generation. Mao, however, had other ideas.

Earlier this year, she unexpectedly returned to the stage for the first time in nearly a decade in the new show “Su Dongpo” — an opera based on the life of one of China’s most beloved poets.

With Mao in the title role of Su, it is one of her most avant-garde productions yet. The show ditches Yue opera’s traditional linear narrative structure, instead leaping from one episode in Su’s life to another in a style Mao likens to Christopher Nolan’s movie “Inception.”

Critics have complained that “Su Dongpo” looks more like a Broadway musical than a Yue opera. But Mao has grown used to such comments: after decades in the spotlight, she knows she’ll never please what she describes as “traditionalist” opera fans.

The opera’s ending even reads like Mao’s preemptive answer to the controversy she knows the show will provoke. “Who’s afraid?” she asks, echoing a line from Su’s celebrated poem “Calming the Waves.”

In this interview, Mao discusses the new show, its reception, and the broader struggle to revive Chinese opera without losing its essence. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Su Dongpo ranks among China’s greatest cultural icons. What inspired you to create a show based on his life?

Mao: Su Dongpo’s life was full of dramatic turns. He once rode high in his prime, then suddenly hit rock bottom and was driven from place to place in exile. Yet he always remained at ease with himself — he had a natural gift for dealing with hardship. As I see it, he kept his feet in the mud while flowers bloomed in his heart.

At my age, with so many years of stage and life experience, I need a role with exactly this kind of depth, dramatic expressiveness, and tension. Ten years ago, I probably couldn’t have played him. Now, the timing feels just right. My looks may not be what they were, and my voice is no longer as clean as it was — but that heavier, thicker texture happens to suit the role.

Honestly, I think I’m quite like Su Dongpo — “an incorrigible optimist.” When I run into difficulties, I get a good night’s sleep, have a good meal, and my troubles pass. A while ago, when we performed in (the eastern city of) Nanjing, I bumped into a good friend, the writer Bi Feiyu. He asked me, “If Su Dongpo were a woman, what do you think she’d be like?” I answered with one word: “Me.”

Sixth Tone: Your emotional resonance with Su is clear onstage. But is it true that the creation of this show was also a difficult process?

Mao: It was. At the lowest point — when we were rehearsing the passage built around his most famous work, “Charm of a Maiden Singer: Memories of the Past at Red Cliff,” I found I simply could not go on. I had no idea how the music should be presented, how the vocals should sound, or how it should be performed.

But this impasse ended up handing me the key to a breakthrough. I thought of the rankou technique — a tradition of using stylized false beards to highlight a character’s personality and emotional state — and decided to turn to that ancient craft for help.

Yue opera doesn’t use the rankou, so I traveled to (the northern province of) Shanxi to study beard technique under Li Yuexian, the celebrated female performer of male roles in Jin opera. What I picked up was only the basics of the art — but it mattered enormously. I had found the key that unlocked the door to Su Dongpo. I knew how to play him.

Sixth Tone: That section is particularly powerful. It’s rare to see the rankou used that way — not hanging quietly, but torn off and wielded in a fierce dance. It became more than a marker of gender and age, instead signifying Su Dongpo’s creative, social standing – and something else that resists being put into words.

Mao: I was indeed trying to transform the rankou technique into a “second face” for building the character — a vehicle for Su Dongpo’s complex emotions and the shifts in his attitude towards life. This kind of artistic grafting across opera genres is also an exploration of what might be possible when Yue opera kunsheng portray middle-aged and elderly men.

That said, although the rankou solved one of my biggest creative problems, the production was still extremely difficult to rehearse — we halted rehearsals three times before it finally premiered. That process itself was very “Su Dongpo.” The hardships I went through in rehearsals helped build the character. The closer I drew to Su’s spiritual world, the more it nourished me. Every performance I give is a process of self-growth. Playing Su Dongpo has made me grow once again.

Sixth Tone: You have said more than once that playing Su Dongpo was a healing process.

Mao: Yes — and not only was I healed; I think the audience was, too. I have been thinking a lot about one question recently: China has so many celebrated literati; why is Su Dongpo so especially beloved?

We revere the unyielding passion of Qu Yuan — who drowned himself in the Miluo River after the fall of the capital of Chu, the ancient kingdom where he served as a loyal minister — and admire Tao Yuanming’s return to a pastoral life. But we cannot live the way they did: those paths are impossible to replicate in contemporary society.

Su Dongpo’s attitude toward life, by contrast, offers practical wisdom that remains useful for anyone living today. His life went through peaks and troughs, yet he never sank. He forged a path forward through adversity and kept his composure even amid the storms. And he loved life: he loved cooking, he loved making friends.

These qualities may be exactly what comforts people today. The fast pace of life, emotional exhaustion, uncertainty — everyone suffers some degree of anxiety. And Su Dongpo’s answer is neither escape nor resistance, but acceptance.

From this perspective, I believe this play can be embraced not only by Chinese audiences today, but by international audiences as well. How can Yue opera go global? I have thought about that question for many years, and I have done a great deal of experimenting. In my view, this production can go global, because Su’s spiritual state has the power to resonate with audiences of different countries and cultures.

Foreign viewers may not understand the conventions of Yue opera, may not be familiar with Song dynasty history, may never even have heard of Su Dongpo — but they can understand how a person faces the vicissitudes of fate and maintains dignity and gentleness in adversity.

Sixth Tone: Speaking of going global, the lighting, movement, stage design, and even some of the music all feel very modern. Were international audiences on your mind while you were rehearsing?

Mao: Not at all. Our first consideration was still the domestic audience. Today’s audiences have seen so much. The traditional “one table and two chairs” staging is fine as far as it goes, but it may no longer satisfy people’s aesthetic needs when it comes to how stories are told and opera is experienced. What we have been exploring all along is how a comprehensive stage aesthetic can connect with contemporary audiences and deliver the emotional value that modern people are looking for.

Sixth Tone: You have always been a “reformer” of Yue opera. In your mind, is there anything about Yue opera that must absolutely never change?

Mao: Sure. First, the dialect of Yue opera must not change. Its language and phonology are Yue opera’s most distinctive artistic markers and a living embodiment of eastern China’s Jiangnan culture. Pronunciation gives rise to melody, and melody gives rise to vocal style; the soft, lilting local accents carry Yue opera’s original spirit and warmth. To abandon the dialect would be to lose the soul of the genre.

Second, performance style centered on all-female Yue opera troupes must not change. Since the first women’s training school was founded in 1923 and all-female Yueju opera went on to become mainstream, this uniquely captivating aesthetic has shaped the genre’s grace and vitality, and set Yue opera apart from every other form of Chinese opera. We must keep passing down and developing this distinctive artistic character.

Third, the aesthetic centered on xieyi — suggestive, imagistic expression — must not change. Xieyi is not only the aesthetic hallmark of Yue opera; it is the aesthetic hallmark of all traditional Chinese art. This beauty of suggestion runs through every detail of vocal design, performance, and stage setting, and is core to traditional Chinese art. We should always hold fast to this essence of Eastern aesthetics, and find a new national style that belongs to the present moment

(Header image: Mao Weitao (center) stars in the premiere of the Yue opera “Su Dongpo” in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, Dec. 29, 2025. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019116/On the Table at Shanghai Mayor Meet: AI, Sports, Tourism
World.title: On the Table at Shanghai Mayor Meet: AI, Sports, Tourism
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019116/On the Table at Shanghai Mayor Meet: AI, Sports, Tourism
World.content:
SHANGHAI — The 38th annual International Business Leaders’ Advisory Council for the Mayor of Shanghai (IBLAC) convened on Sunday, with global industry leaders recommending the city build a stronger global brand through AI deployment, sports, and cultural tourism.

Founded in 1989, IBLAC brings together international business leaders annually to discuss the city’s economic development. It has grown from 12 members from eight countries to 42 members from 15 countries, working in industries ranging from sports and consumer goods to health care and finance.

In 2025, the added value of Shanghai’s service industry reached 4.5 trillion yuan ($620 billion), ranking first among Chinese cities and accounting for nearly 80% of the city’s GDP. By 2030, that figure is expected to reach roughly 6 trillion yuan, with service imports and exports exceeding $300 billion.

“Shanghai’s service industry plays a pivotal role in driving economic growth, stimulating consumption and fostering,” John Waldron, president and chief operating officer of Goldman Sachs, said in his keynote speech.

He urged Shanghai to expand its cross-border data transfer framework and give greater priority to financial institutions and applicants.

Next, Jason Furman, an economics professor at Harvard University, advised Shanghai against chasing bigger AI models and instead to leverage its service sector — financial institutions, hospitals, and law firms, among other operations — to lead AI deployment. He also recommended attracting global scientists while training Chinese workers in skills that machines cannot replicate.

“AI will not take a city’s place in the world economy, but a city that uses AI better will,” Furman said during the event’s keynote speech.

Elliott Hill, president and chief executive officer of international footwear brand Nike, said that Shanghai should increasingly capitalize on signature events like the Shanghai Marathon and F1 Chinese Grand Prix. Each event should become a citywide celebration that connects sport with commercial districts, public spaces, culture, and retail, driving greater economic impact across the city, he said.

Hill also suggested making exercise part of everyday life by creating more community sports-related gatherings, from school programs to community runs. He called for deeper collaboration among government, business, and universities to expand access, attract world-class events, and develop talent, cementing Shanghai’s status as a global sports capital.

Manny Maceda, partner and chairman at global consultancy Bain & Company, urged the city to shift tourism toward experiences over attractions, centering tourist experiences around Shanghai cultural features such as its Art Deco architecture, jazz-related history, food, and riverfront customs to strengthen the city’s global cultural brand and sharpen its identity as the place “where East meets West.”

At a Sunday afternoon press conference, Shanghai Mayor Zhu Zhongming said attendees offered many pertinent, forward-looking recommendations. “We will work to turn this global wisdom into a ‘Shanghai solution’ for expanding and upgrading the service industry,” he said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019108/China Drafts Landmark Gig Worker Labor Rights Rules
World.title: China Drafts Landmark Gig Worker Labor Rights Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019108/China Drafts Landmark Gig Worker Labor Rights Rules
World.content:
China has drafted its first departmental rules on gig workers’ labor rights, strengthening protections for platform-based flexible employees such as food delivery riders.

The draft, released by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security on Oct. 8, is open for online public feedback until Nov. 8.

The proposal comes as flexible employment grows in China, with the number of people in flexible employment — including those who rely on internet platforms to earn a living — projected to reach 320 million this year, according to the China New Employment Research Center. Gig work has also come under fire for subjecting workers to excessive hours, opaque algorithms, and gaps in social security coverage.

In 2021, China introduced its first guidelines clarifying platforms’ responsibilities toward gig workers regarding employment, remuneration, social security, and workplace safety. In 2024, the country issued related guiding cases, and this July, it expanded occupational injury insurance for gig workers.

Under the new draft, platforms and their partner businesses must sign labor contracts with workers that meet the legal criteria for employment relationships, such as full-time employees. It excludes people who use online platforms to run their own businesses independently or offer freelance services on their own terms.

For workers in more flexible arrangements, such as part-time work or work across multiple platforms, platforms must sign written employment agreements specifying pay, labor protections, and liability for breaking the agreement, among others. When platform companies and partner businesses jointly manage workers, all three parties must sign a written agreement.

The draft also clarifies dispute resolution procedures. Platforms bear primary responsibility for overseeing partner businesses’ employment practices, and workers involved in legal disputes may name both the platform and its partner as parties to a case. When workers challenge pay, working hours, performance reviews, or account bans, companies must investigate and respond within 48 hours.

Platforms must also build reasonable task-allocation systems and performance metrics into their algorithms, avoid encouraging excessive work through targets or incentives, and explain relevant algorithmic rules to workers and authorities.

Decisions with “significant consequences for workers,” including suspending work assignments or banning accounts, must also undergo human review.

The draft further states that employers will face legal responsibilities and penalties for violations under existing legislation. For instance, employers may be required to pay outstanding wages, overtime pay, or economic compensation. If wages fall below the local minimum wage, employers must pay the difference.

“The draft’s biggest breakthrough is placing workers who are under the management of platforms but do not fully fit into an employment relationship under protections, and applying past traditional labor laws to flexible platform-based work,” Wang Tianyu, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Law, wrote in a related commentary.

“At the same time, it establishes mechanisms to hold companies accountable and prevent them from evading employment obligations, such as through subcontracting or inducing workers to register as individual businesses,” he said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019032/In China’s Universities, Students Are Majoring in Second Chances
World.title: In China’s Universities, Students Are Majoring in Second Chances
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019032/In China’s Universities, Students Are Majoring in Second Chances
World.content:
Until this spring, Weng Yujia was studying management because of its supposed job prospects. At the same university in Shanghai, Lin Yuanhao studied international relations and public affairs, presented as the best option based on her college entrance exam score.

Today, both now study Chinese language and literature.

Within weeks of starting university, Weng had soured on management and its math- and science-heavy coursework. “I just plain disliked” many required classes, she said, adding that she struggled to see some of their educational value.

Lin had wanted to study Chinese language and literature from the start, but her college entrance exam score fell short of the cutoff. By the time she switched majors, a sixth of the roughly 120 students enrolled in her international relations course had moved to other fields, mostly economics, management, or law.

“Changing majors is like giving students a second chance to choose,” she told Sixth Tone.

Across China, more students are making that choice as universities give them greater freedom to reconsider majors they picked under pressure from college entrance exams, parental expectations, or worries about future employment.

For years, changing majors was difficult, with universities limiting transfers or requiring students to meet strict grade and class-rank thresholds. It wasn’t until 2005 that, for the first time at the national level, the Ministry of Education issued a new regulation allowing students to change majors if their universities agreed.

National rules were further loosened in 2017, when students with an “interest or particular strength in another field” were explicitly allowed to apply for transfers.

This June, several schools nationwide eased transfer caps and academic requirements, while Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, in the southwestern Sichuan province, has allowed 2026 entrants to earn a degree in a different major by taking its required courses. At Wuhan University, in central China’s Hubei province, more than 600 undergraduates switched majors in 2025 and over 70% of cross-college applications were approved, a record high.

As transfers become more common, more students will have to decide whether starting over is worth the trade-offs. Changing course can still mean entrance exams, lost credits, extra years of study, and difficult conversations with parents, all before they know whether the new major will prove a better fit.

Take two

On her college applications, Weng initially ranked management as her top major — a factor universities consider alongside cutoff scores when granting admission — because of its solid job prospects. In contrast, Lin listed Chinese language and literature as her top choice, but her score on China’s national college entrance exam, the gaokao, did not meet the cutoff.

At Weng and Lin’s university, transfer requirements differ by department. The Chinese department, which both transferred into, weighs GPA at a relatively high 70%, alongside an admissions interview, partially in English, with department faculty at 30%. To prepare for the transfer, Lin also self-studied traditional Chinese characters and took courses in the Chinese department.

After the two were notified of their own transfer acceptances this spring, they watched as others in their circles followed the trend. Several of Weng’s friends at other Chinese schools changed majors: one switched from French to chemistry, while another went from civil engineering to biological sciences.

Chen, a 22-year-old tourism management major at Jiaying University, in the southern Guangdong province, initially majored in English education because her parents told her to.

But by the end of her first semester, she felt the major was a bad fit. “I don’t like teaching, and I’m not interested in psychology or education either,” she said.

She decided to transfer to tourism management after a friend in the department told her about it. Chen felt the major would fit her personality: describing herself as “outgoing” and “drawn to challenges,” she said her dream is to travel the world.

She consulted others who had transferred to tourism management about the GPA requirement and the pressure to catch up on the curriculum. Some told her the major was a bad choice, while others were incredulous as to why she’d want to transfer. Chen’s parents were also initially opposed, but later came around after she explained her rationale.

To transfer majors, Chen had to take an entrance exam and undergo an interview with department faculty — both of which she passed. Now a senior in the tourism management department, she has no regrets and is preparing to take the entrance exam to pursue a master’s in the same field.

A philosophy faculty member involved in major transfers at a top Shanghai university, who asked to remain anonymous, sees the trend growing because students want to have more choices.

He said he supports universities offering major transfers, noting that gaokao score cutoffs keep students out of fields that might suit them and that they know what they like and what fits them better after taking courses in college.

However, he cautioned that transferring majors is not a decision to be taken lightly. “Students shouldn’t see it as a way to obtain better prospects or a better way out,” he said. “That leads them to (transfer majors) for utilitarian reasons rather than their own ideas.”

Long road

But switching majors can come with its own set of challenges.

Wu Wenjun, another student in Shanghai, was accepted as a transfer student from history into her dream major, law — something she hadn’t gotten into originally due to her gaokao score. The law school had a steep requirement, however: to earn her degree, Wu would have to drop down a grade and spend four years on top of the year she had already completed as a history major.

Wu was prepared to make that time sacrifice — even if it meant future employers might assume she had delayed graduation and look down on her application, a common phenomenon in China. If the transfer fell through, she was also prepared to delay graduation by a year to finish her original history degree, since she had taken only law by that point.

Now a senior in law school, Wu said she sometimes struggles with how much she has to memorize. She also said she finds law especially competitive. And when she switched majors as a sophomore, Wu felt she trailed her classmates, many of whom had already begun interning at prestigious law firms.

But being a transfer student has had upsides too. Wu said the five-year graduation requirement brought unexpected benefits, including lighter course loads each term, since she had already completed various general graduation requirements during her first year as a history student.

Wu has also found internship interviewers to be fairly understanding once they learned she had transferred rather than delayed graduation. She notes that personal advantages also matter greatly to law firms, not just how long it took to graduate. Her English proficiency, for example, gives her an edge at foreign firms. “In law, you don’t have to stand at the top of the pyramid and be number one to find a job,” Wu said.

The Shanghai philosophy instructor noted that students who transfer majors often have one more year of experience than their peers, richer résumés, and greater freedom in course arrangements.

He observed that many students who transfer into philosophy are more enthusiastic and motivated than students who have been in the program longer. He attributed this to transfer students’ “second choice” feeling like a “rebirth” in learning, and they cherish their opportunities more.

Looking back, Wu said her transfer gave her more room for error, but added that as another one-time option, it also carries risk.

She hopes the transfer process will eventually look different: students take courses in a certain major, discover they are suited to or interested in it, and then decide to transfer. “It’s best to go with what suits you and what you like,” she said.

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo; editors: Marianne Gunnarsson and Apurva.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019103/Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.title: Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019103/Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.content:
Two books translated into English from Chinese have been shortlisted for the 2026 U.S. National Translation Awards, which recognize excellence in both original and translated literary works.

The shortlist, announced Tuesday by the American Literary Translators Association, includes two originally written in Chinese: Chinese author Shuang Xuetao’s short story collection “Hunter,” translated by Jeremy Tiang, and Hong Kong writer Hon Lai Chu’s “Mending Bodies,” translated by Jacqueline Leung, among a total of 11 poetry and prose works translated from nine languages.

“The Ruins,” an anthology by Chinese poet Ye Hui and translated by Li Dong, was longlisted among 23 works across prose and poetry on Sept. 3 but did not make the shortlist. Ye is known for his spare, understated poems that draw on everyday life and nature and explore questions of time, memory, and existence.

Established in 1998, the awards rank among the world’s top professional accolades for literary translation. Winning translators in both categories — poetry and prose — each receive a $4,000 prize. Translations of Chinese works have previously been listed for the prize, including works by contemporary writers Xu Zechen and Yan Lianke, as well as Qing dynasty (1644–1911) novelist and playwright Li Yu.

Shuang Xuetao, author of “Hunter,” one of the two shortlisted Chinese works, was born in 1983 in Shenyang, capital of the northeastern Liaoning province. He is widely considered a leading figure in the “Dongbei Renaissance,” a cultural movement emerging from northeast China, or Dongbei. Known for his use of local dialect, Shuang often portrays the lives of ordinary people in the region, long dismissed as a cultural backwater and rust belt. Several of his works have been adapted into films.

“Hunter” features 11 standalone stories, some of which were originally written in Dongbei dialect: from provincial ambulance drivers searching for a hospital in the middle of the night, to a legendary knife fighter working in a factory. In a note about their selection published alongside the announcement, the competition’s judges wrote that Shuang’s stories “paint a portrait of a region marked by gritty pragmatism, dark humor, and magical realism.”

The work was translated by Shuang’s long-term collaborator Jeremy Tiang — a novelist in his own right. The judges wrote that Tiang “expertly translated Shuang’s often inventive, utterly unique description; his English texts are layered and witty.”

The second book nominated for the prize, “Mending Bodies” by Hong Kong writer Hon Lai Chu, is a work of speculative fiction and follows a young woman adjusting to life after surgically binding her body to a partner, in a future where people are encouraged to do so. Hon has previously drawn praise for her surreal, introspective fiction, which often explores the fragility of the body, memory, and human relationships.

According to the judges, Jacqueline Leung, the book’s Hong Kong-based translator, “flawlessly translates the between-the-lines subtleties of the languages.”

“The shortlisting of these works carries substantial significance for the overseas circulation of Sinophone literature and its greater visibility within global professional literary circuits, representing, in a sense, a multifaceted retelling of Chinese stories across fiction and poetry,” Shao Dong, an assistant professor of creative writing at Hong Kong Metropolitan University, told Sixth Tone.

The overall award winners will be announced on Oct. 23 as part of the American Literary Translators Association’s annual conference.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Covers of “Hunter,” “Mending Bodies,” and “The Ruins,” by Shuang Xuetao, Hon Lai Chu, and Ye Hui, respectively. Reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.title: ‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.content:
The thieves came in the dead of night in late August — seven ghostly figures illuminated only by the glow of their flashlights and burning cigarettes. When they left, tucked under their arms were 10 chickens and two geese.

The next day, watching footage of the theft recorded by a security camera, Xu Lingni’s heart sank. It was the end of a dream.

The poultry had been kept overnight in a hilltop coop at the bucolic Huxi campus of the Sichuan Fine Arts Institute (SCFAI), in the southwestern megacity of Chongqing, and belonged to the Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative, a student-led club aimed at rebuilding the bonds between humans and nature.

The group had intended to use the project to promote interest across campus and beyond in food-waste conversion, community-supported agriculture, plastics consumption, and other sustainability issues.

For Xu, the club’s leader, those plans vanished along with those 12 birds. Yet worse was to come.

After a brief investigation, the Chongqing police discovered that several workers hired by SCFAI for a summer construction project had taken the poultry and eaten them. Their crew manager agreed to pay 7,000 yuan ($1,040) to compensate for the financial loss and the students’ emotional distress.

However, the theft drew widespread attention and sparked fresh criticism over raising animals on campus. Facing mounting pressure, the school’s leadership decided to ban the practice. The cooperative was over.

Hatching a plan

The Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative was a key part of the Healing Garden Project, which inhabits a patch of land on campus once piled high with construction waste. Seven years ago, Jin Lipeng, an associate professor in SCFAI’s School of Experimental Art, led students in repurposing the debris to pave paths and build planting beds. He envisioned an area that could restore nature and nurture people.

At the time, the campus cafeteria was sending hundreds of kilograms of food scraps — often mixed with unsorted plastic waste — to an incinerator dozens of kilometers away. Jin and his students began to use these leftovers as compost, converting roughly 40 tons of food waste into fertilizer over the years.

The idea for the cooperative stemmed from a graduate student’s thesis project in spring 2025 that looked at permaculture and the role of foraging chickens in loosening soil, eating pests, clearing weeds, and providing eggs. To test a theory, the student purchased five chickens of a local breed with red combs and black skin. They were allowed to roam freely through campus and returned at night to their hilltop coop.

Xu, an undergraduate majoring in sculpture, was already involved in the garden project and began informally caring for the chickens, buying them grain and taking them to the veterinarian.

In summer last year, as temperatures soared above 40 degrees Celsius, one bird died of heatstroke, and three others disappeared. Fearing that the sole survivor would get lonely, Xu bought a new one from the market. Then one of the escapees returned.

A few days later, Xu found six new adolescent chickens in the coop. A school janitor, who had bought them to raise for their meat, agreed to sell the birds to the students. These were soon joined by a common chicken brought from a roadside stall, a Plymouth Rock chicken, a new hatchling, and a wuhei black-boned chicken. (Two birds died before the theft — one from hypothermia, the other from a wild animal attack. The wuhei chicken was the only one left behind by the thieves; its dark plumage likely made it hard to spot at night.)

As the flock grew, the birds began producing more eggs than the students could eat. Jin, whose research area includes labor issues, proposed creating the cooperative as a student club and asked Xu to lead it. Soon, the students were dividing up their responsibilities: caring for the animals, sourcing and selling merchandise, writing articles, and managing social media channels. In June this year, several attended an international conference to introduce the cooperative’s work.

Those who joined the project felt that caring for the chickens brought them “healing energy.” Xu recalls one classmate who would often hold the birds and cry. “The theft this summer hit her especially hard, and she wasn’t the only one,” Xu says, adding that the cooperative not only fostered friendships but also helped some members find meaning.

While she doesn’t exactly share Jin’s grand ideals, Xu believes that through her work she came to understand seemingly distant but deeply personal issues such as permaculture and climate change.

“Most university students have no idea where eggs come from, what happens to food waste, or why rubbish gets incinerated,” she said in a speech at a climate change forum in May. “Dorm rooms are piled with takeout plastic. Delivery workers risk heatstroke in extreme temperatures. Yet few students have enough awareness to connect these to drought, heat, and carbon emissions.

“Our work lets people feel the pressure and causes of climate change firsthand,” she added, “and shows that through campus community-supported agriculture we can mount a small resistance.”

Making a mess

The cooperative began selling eggs for about 2 yuan each to residents on and around campus this March. The chickens laid two to eight eggs a day. Xu stored them in her apartment’s refrigerator, took orders through an online group chat, and delivered them to customers on her electric bike. She calculates that this brought in just over 500 yuan in total.

Fans of the project were kept up to date through the club’s channel on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, which has more than 6,300 followers. In addition, the cooperative sold themed merchandise including fridge magnets, tote bags, and silk scarves, which brought in about 2,000 yuan.

Not everyone was supportive, though. The most common complaint was that the free-roaming chickens often defecated on the pathways and at the entrance to the student dormitories. To prevent this, this summer the birds were fenced in on the hillside.

In 2022, Chongqing introduced regulations prohibiting the raising of livestock and poultry in urban areas. However, the restrictions apply only to commercial-scale farming, while exceptions can be made for educational purposes and scientific research.

While the number of chickens at SCFAI was far below commercial scale, the activity fell outside the definition of “backyard rearing,” putting it in a gray area. As such, the school took an open-minded approach, requiring only proper fencing and separation, despite repeated objections from others in the campus community.

The cooperative used old bamboo posts and tall netting to enclose the poultry on the hilltop. But the gate was never locked. “This is a public welfare project. Anyone was welcome to come in to spend time with the chickens,” Xu explains.

For security, the group installed an infrared camera to watch the flock at night and raised two goslings to guard the coop. “Geese bite hard. Once I went up the hill in a raincoat, and they didn’t recognize me, so they bit me,” Xu adds. “We’d thought the intruders would be stray cats or weasels — never thieves.”

Ruffling feathers

The theft sparked an outpouring of grief online. “Come home, little ones” and “My babies are gone” were typical comments posted by students in the aftermath.

In the coming weeks and months, Xu and her classmates had planned to step up marketing and sales, offer egg-based food delivery services, and write a handbook on community supported agriculture that could inspire other schools and universities.

That’s now all been scrapped. This fall, the school’s leadership announced a ban on keeping poultry on campus.

In a statement, it also said that officials had learned during mediation that the maintenance workers who took the birds had endured long hours of intense labor in hot weather, with limited food and lodging. Some students strongly objected to this version of events, arguing that chicken meat is cheap and widely available — and that the workers weren’t “desperate,” they just wanted to taste free-range birds.

“Pioneering ecological practice is inherently accompanied by trial and error and waiting,” the statement read. “We will review and consolidate, continue deepening our existing work, and wait for the right conditions to restart explorations.”

The cooperative maintained that its activities “filled a gap” in the school’s labor education by giving students hands-on experience as well as teaching responsibility and empathy. But there was no overturning the decision.

The sole survivor of the theft, the wuhei chicken, was moved to a student’s home for safekeeping and has quickly adapted to her new environment. Xu says the bird is even laying eggs again.

(Due to privacy concerns, Xu Lingni is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Kong Lingyu.

A version of this article originally appeared in FoodThink. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.
