The first concerns the non-use of force. The Geneva International Discussions were established after the August 2008 war, and security and non-use of force have remained permanent items on the agenda.

However, Tbilisi and Moscow fundamentally disagree over who should make the relevant commitments. Russia demands guarantees regarding Sukhumi and Tskhinvali, thereby placing responsibility on Tbilisi. Georgia, by contrast, insists that the main security problem is Russia’s military presence and occupation.

The second issue is even more serious. By demanding the delimitation of so-called state borders, Moscow treats Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region as states independent of Georgia.

This contradicts the principle of Georgia’s territorial integrity, which the overwhelming majority of the international community recognises.

Expert Teona Akubardia sees these two demands as part of Russia’s broader political strategy.

In her assessment, Moscow is trying to formalise its influence over Georgia in legal and political terms. “Its ultimate goal is to formalise its strategic control over Georgia — control that Russia already exercises in practice, even though it has not been legally formalised,” she said.

Akubardia believes that Russia’s economic restrictions, the issue of the occupied regions and Georgia’s deteriorating relations with the West should not be viewed as isolated developments.

In her view, opening a transit corridor through Abkhazia may also be linked to Moscow’s demands.

Giorgi Rukhadze has also pointed to this possibility.

Georgia’s parliamentary speaker, Shalva Papuashvili, offers a different interpretation. He notes that Russia’s demands are not new and that Moscow has raised them at the Geneva talks for many years.

“There is nothing new in this statement. At every meeting within the Geneva format, Russian representatives raise exactly the same issue. We, in turn, raise the questions of the return of displaced people, the withdrawal of Russian occupation forces and other matters,” he said.

Nevertheless, experts believe this does not rule out the possibility that Moscow is using new economic levers to pursue its long-standing objectives.

Gia Khukhashvili: ‘Dependence on the Russian market carries the risk of constant pressure’

Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili describes Russia’s decision as a familiar form of economic coercion.

“This is Russia’s brazen ‘sledgehammer’ approach,” he said.

Khukhashvili believes Moscow’s actions could have two consequences: increased pressure on Georgia’s government and business sector, and conditions that encourage informal deals and corruption.

He argues that companies may try to cultivate ties with influential figures in Russia to circumvent the restrictions. However, he has provided no specific evidence of corrupt deals.

Khukhashvili is particularly critical of business models that rely heavily on the Russian market.

“The problem is that our businesses — constantly chasing short-term gains and worrying about how to please the authorities — have still failed to understand that they cannot tie themselves to the market of an enemy country. They should have done everything possible to diversify these risks,” he said.

In his view, short-term profits from operating in Russia could ultimately lead to much greater losses.

“I would tell winemakers this: you cannot ‘reach an agreement’ with Russia. Today, you may make a few pennies, but tomorrow you could lose ten times as much. Leave the Russian market alone. Find people who speak English and target other markets. Forget Russia and explore new opportunities — otherwise, you will remain trapped in this situation forever,” he said.

Khukhashvili’s recommendation draws directly on economic data showing just how heavily Georgia’s wine industry depends on the Russian market.

Russia accounts for almost two-thirds of Georgian wine exports

Between January and August 2026, Georgia exported $102.2 million worth of wine to Russia. Total Georgian wine exports over the same period amounted to approximately $163.6 million.

Russia therefore accounted for around 62.5% of the total value of Georgian wine exports. By volume, its share stood at approximately 66.6%.

Russia remains the largest export market for Georgian wine, despite a decline in sales compared with the previous year.

Poland ranks second, with Georgian wine exports worth around $10.7 million. Ukraine, China, Kazakhstan and Germany follow, but export volumes to these countries remain far below those to Russia.

Losing the Russian market would affect producers differently. Tbilvino offers a clear example.

According to the company’s chief executive, Zurab Margvelashvili, who spoke to BM.ge, Tbilvino exports wine to around 30 countries and has relatively little dependence on the Russian market. A potential ban would therefore cause some financial losses, but the company does not expect serious damage.

Margvelashvili also notes that the company exports to markets with strict quality standards, while the Russian side has provided no detailed information about any specific violations.

Energy dependence: a more powerful lever than wine

Roman Gotsiridze, an opposition politician and former head of Georgia’s National Bank, has highlighted natural gas imports in the context of the current developments.

According to figures he cited, Russia accounted for 1.7% of Georgia’s natural gas consumption in 2018. That share rose to 20% in 2023 and 25% in 2024. Estimates put it at around 28% in 2025.

Gotsiridze believes this growing dependence gives Russia an additional lever for economic pressure.

Unlike wine exports, natural gas supplies directly affect energy security, industrial operations and people’s everyday needs.

Gotsiridze has therefore warned the government about possible scenarios involving more severe pressure from Russia.

Could Russia expand the embargo?

Mamuka Pipia, leader of the openly pro-Russian party Solidarity for Peace, says the ban on Georgian beverages represents only the first wave of restrictions.

In his view, further measures will target other companies and product categories.

His prediction deserves particular attention because Pipia represents a political force that takes a favourable view of Russia.

Teona Akubardia also points to an earlier statement by Pipia. She notes that he mentioned a list of Georgian companies accused of supporting anti-Russian activity as early as June.

If such a list did exist, it would be important to establish whether the companies named on it overlap with those now facing restrictions.

Georgian experts also consider it possible that Russia will expand its measures.

Gia Khukhashvili believes Moscow could use new restrictions to pressure Georgian businesses into exercising political caution. Giorgi Rukhadze suggests that the initial decision may be intended to demonstrate Russia’s capacity to exert economic pressure.

These assessments point to several possible scenarios. The restrictions could remain limited to the seven companies and be lifted following negotiations. They could spread to other producers. Alternatively, Russia could make the use of trade restrictions a permanent instrument of pressure.

How is Georgian Dream responding, and has its strategy worked?

The Georgian government insists that maintaining economic ties with Russia serves the country’s interests and that businesses should not give up profitable markets for political reasons.

Georgian Dream also argues that other countries have economic leverage over Georgia.

Commenting on Russia’s latest restrictions, parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili also raised the risks associated with trade relations with the European Union. He pointed to issues involving sanctions, tariffs and the port of Kulevi.

The Georgian Dream government justified its decision not to join international sanctions against Russia by arguing that it needed to protect the Georgian economy. Kobakhidze described the decision as correct and pragmatic.

However, Georgian Dream’s opponents ask what additional security Georgia has gained by maintaining economic ties with Russia.

The restrictions introduced on 9 October have shown that economic relations with Russia do not guarantee Georgian companies unrestricted access to the Russian market. Moscow continues to demand the establishment of so-called state borders with the occupied regions. At the same time, Russia’s sanitary watchdog has restricted imports of products from Georgian companies.

Opposition politician Shalva Kereselidze, a member of the For Georgia party founded by Giorgi Gakharia, links the situation to Georgian Dream’s foreign policy. He argues that the government has damaged relations with the European Union while failing to protect Georgia’s economic and political interests in its dealings with Russia.

“Do not think that the more you concede to Russia, the more favourably it will view you or the sooner it will take your interests into account. No — the outcome will be even worse,” he said.

World.title: Turkmenistan's mobile banking transactions rise 140.7% to $20.3M
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The volume of non-cash bank card transactions through mobile banking in Turkmenistan reached 71.1 million manat ($20.3 million) in the period from January through August 2026, up 140.7% year-on-year.

The figure was calculated by Trend based on data published by the Central Bank of Turkmenistan.

According to the calculations, Rysgal JSCB recorded the highest growth in mobile banking transaction volume, increasing by 632.5% compared with the same period of 2025. This represents more than a sevenfold increase.

Turkmenistan State Commercial Bank (SCBT) and the State Bank for Foreign Economic Affairs followed, with increases of 92.5% and 82.7%, respectively.

At the same time, Turkmenbashi JSCB recorded growth of 19.7%, while Dayhanbank SCBT and Senagat JSCB posted increases of 16.8% and 4.3%, respectively.

According to Trend’s calculations, mobile banking transaction volumes declined by 9.6% at Turkmen-Turkish JSCB and by 91.2% at Halkbank.

For reference, the Central Bank of Turkmenistan launched cashless payments in 2001 with the introduction of the domestic Altyn Asyr card scheme. While the initial infrastructure was developed in the 2000s, broader adoption gained momentum in the mid-2010s as part of government efforts to digitalize the economy.

In August 2020, the government announced the launch of the Halkbank Terminal mobile application, developed by JSCB Halkbank to allow merchants to accept cashless payments directly through NFC-enabled smartphones, replacing traditional POS terminals. The initiative was presented as a step toward expanding cashless payments and introducing contactless payment technologies across the country.

Alongside payment terminals, Turkmen banks have expanded digital banking services, including Internet Banking, Mobile Banking, e-commerce payment platforms and specialized applications such as Senagat Töleg, while continuing to develop the national Altyn Asyr bank card payment system. These services enable customers to pay for utilities, telecommunications, transport, taxes and other public services electronically.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s daily oil output reaches 448,000 b/d in September
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Azerbaijan's crude oil production averaged 448,000 barrels per day in September 2026, compared with 442,000 barrels per day in August, OPEC says in its Oil Market Report.

According to Trend's calculations, Azerbaijan's daily crude oil production increased by 1.36% month on month.

The September rebound followed a decline in Azerbaijan's oil production from 455,000 barrels per day in July to 442,000 barrels per day in August, a decrease of 2.9%.

OPEC estimates that on a quarterly basis, Azerbaijan produced 454,000 b/d in Q1, 456,000 b/d in Q2 and 449,000 b/d in Q3.

Meanwhile, the latest data from Azerbaijan's State Statistics Committee show that 17.692 million metric tons of crude oil, including gas condensate, were produced in the country from January through August 2026.

According to Trend’s estimates, this figure decreased by 698,800 metric tons, or 3.8%, compared to the same period last year.

During the reporting period, marketable crude oil accounted for 17.648 million metric tons of the total crude oil production, which is 701,100 metric tons, or 3.8%, less than the figure for the same period of the previous year.

According to the latest report from the State Customs Committee, in the period from January through August 2026, Azerbaijan exported 14.678 million metric tons of crude oil and petroleum products derived from bituminous rocks, worth $9.282 billion.

According to Trend’s calculations based on the agency’s data, this figure increased by $886 million, or 10.6%, in value terms compared to the same period last year, while it decreased by 1.247 million metric tons, or 7.8%, in physical terms.

World.title: Iran’s production-sector financing rises nearly 12-fold
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The value of financing instruments supporting Iran’s production sector increased nearly 12-fold during the period from March 21 through September 22, 2026, compared with the period from March 21 through September 22, 2025.

According to Trend’s analysis of statistics from the Central Bank of Iran, the total value of these financing instruments reached 3.03 quadrillion rials (about $1.68 billion) during the reporting period, compared with 254 trillion rials (about $141 million) during the corresponding period in 2025.

The value of credit-guarantee securities supporting production growth reached 596 trillion rials (about $331 million), compared with 124 trillion rials (about $69.1 million) during the corresponding period in 2025.

The value of electronic promissory notes used in the production chain totaled 2.25 quadrillion rials (about $1.25 billion), compared with 127 trillion rials (about $70.5 million) during the corresponding period in 2025.

The value of welfare cards linked to the credit-guarantee securities system for production growth amounted to about 149 trillion rials (about $82.6 million), compared with 2.5 trillion rials (about $1.4 million) during the corresponding period in 2025.

Factoring, or the financing of receivables, amounted to 35.4 trillion rials (about $19.6 million) during the reporting period.

World.title: Azerbaijan denies reports of hijab ban in medical institutions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The Azerbaijan Audiovisual Council and the Ministry of Health have issued a joint statement following the circulation of a fake document on social media and messaging platforms claiming that restrictions had been introduced on wearing the hijab in medical institutions.

The statement notes that the letter being circulated and attributed to the Ministry of Health is fake. The ministry has neither issued such a document nor given medical institutions any relevant instructions.

Presenting the fake letter as an official document misleads the public and constitutes disinformation.

The Azerbaijan Audiovisual Council called on media outlets and social media users to verify information through official sources, refrain from presenting the fake document as authentic, and avoid contributing to the spread of disinformation.

World.title: Iran’s East Azerbaijan customs exports rise 27% in value
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Exports of goods through the customs offices of Iran’s East Azerbaijan Province rose by 27% in value and 4% in volume during the period from March 21 through September 22, 2026, compared with the same period in 2025.

Ali Asghar Abbaszadeh, head of East Azerbaijan Province customs, announced the figures, according to the Iranian Customs Administration.

"During the reporting period, 1.7 million tons of goods worth $1.08 billion were exported through the province’s customs offices," he said.

Abbaszadeh said the main exports included iron and steel products worth $211 million, copper and copper products worth $192 million, petrochemical and rubber products worth $107 million, mineral fuels and various types of bitumen worth $74 million, and grain and flour products worth $62 million.

According to the customs official, the goods were exported to 80 countries, primarily Türkiye, Iraq, Armenia, Afghanistan and Georgia.

During the same period, 278,000 tons of goods worth more than $688 million were imported into Iran through the province’s customs offices. Import value increased by 8%, while import volume rose by 25% compared with March 21–September 22, 2025, Abbaszadeh said.

He added that the main imports included machinery and equipment worth $113 million, tobacco products worth $91 million, vehicles and spare parts worth $53 million, petrochemical and rubber products worth $43 million, and red meat worth $29 million.

The goods were imported from 54 countries, including Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates, China, Germany and India, he said.

Abbaszadeh also reported that approximately 429,000 tons of transit cargo entered Iran through the province’s customs offices during the reporting period, an increase of 35% compared with the same period in 2025. Meanwhile, 878,000 tons of transit cargo left Iran through the province’s customs offices, up by 19% year-on-year.

According to Trend’s analysis of Iranian Customs Administration statistics, during the period from March 21, 2025, through January 20, 2026, East Azerbaijan Province’s customs offices handled exports totaling 2.8 million tons worth $1.47 billion and imports totaling 395,000 tons worth $1.29 billion.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 15, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

World.title: Yass Valley Council residents facing possible 76pc rate rise
World.content:
Residents in Yass, Murrumbateman and Sutton are facing a 76 per cent increase in their rates, following a Yass Valley Council decision to take the measure to public consultation.

The motion passed 5-4 after the council called an extraordinary meeting on Wednesday to address its financial issues.

Independent consultants have found the council would need to generate an extra $8.3 million from operations each year by 2027-28 to maintain its financial and infrastructure position.

The council has put a special rate variation to the community for feedback. (ABC News)

The motion means the council will spend six weeks in community consultation, taking three financial options to the public.

All three would result in a cumulative 76 per cent increase in rates, but the different models would stage the increases differently over the four years.

Mayor Jasmin Jones stressed this did not mean council had decided to approve the rate hike.

"It was a decision to go out to our community for the next six weeks to put our boots on the ground, to get that really robust feedback from our community," she said.

Mayor says 'structural problem' with NSW council funding

Ultimately the council would also need the special rate variation to be approved by the NSW Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal.

Speaking to 666 ABC Canberra, Cr Jones agreed 76 per cent sounded like "a lot".

"But that is the structural financial correction that is happening across New South Wales right now," she said.

" Yass Valley Council is certainly not alone in the need to go for a special rate variation at least once every 10 years. "

Yass Valley Council mayor Jasmin Jones has defended its financial management. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

She pushed back against suggestions the council had mismanaged its finances.

"I think it's fair to say that if every rural council is going for a special rate variation every 10 years, that tells you that there's a structural problem in how councils are funded," she said.

"Our rate peg only allows us to put up rates every year — for example, 3.4 per cent or 3.7 or 3.9 — when the cost of materials skyrocketed, for example, during the diesel crisis."

Asked about the decision to invest in a new council building, which has drawn some ire in the community, Cr Jones said it had been necessary.

"The workplace wasn't fit for purpose — we had people's chairs actually falling through the floor, it was beyond redeeming that particular building," she said.

Cr Jones also conceded they were struggling to keep up with roads maintenance.

"I can totally accept that in terms of roads, that when we say we're going to come and grade that road three times a year and we're struggling to do even once, that they'd be dissatisfied," she said.

The extraordinary meeting led to a vote to put the three financial options to the public. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

'There's not a lot that we can do'

The near three-hour meeting was passionate at times with members of the public having their say.

Malcolm Bamford, who lives in the council area, said he did not feel confident after leaving the meeting.

"The decision had to be made, OK, but the biggest concern ... was how are they going to do it?" he said.

"They've got an increase before, and then we've another one, nothing really came out of it that makes you confident.

"If we need the money, there's not a lot that we can do.

"We've got to get out of the trouble that we're in."

Yass Valley Council chief executive Gayleen Burley said it was an "emotive" issue for people struggling to keep up with costs.

"We have compassionate debt recovery services," she said.

"But also we want to engage early with our residents, so that if there is an issue with meeting the demand for an increase in rates, that they're able to engage with council and we can come to a workable solution."

Yass Valley Council chief executive Gayleen Burley says compassionate financial assistance is available. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Renters urged to have their say too

The issue of financial sustainability in local government is not new, and a federal inquiry into their viability is currently underway.

In 2024, the Australian Local Government Association (ALGA) called for a greater cut of federal tax revenue.

In November last year, the Yass Valley Council deferred a vote on a rate increase of between 40 and 58 per cent.

Cr Jones urged all residents to have their say on the proposal.

She said the variation would not apply to services such as rubbish collection, water or sewerage.

"And I just want to emphasise that everyone can have a say, you don't need to be receiving a rates bill to have a say on this.

"So if you're a renter, we still need to hear from you because these are costs that get passed on to you.

"We need to hear from community and sporting organisations, young people, families, older residents across not just Yass and Murrumbateman, but also our villages."

World.title: Conroy targets 'rot' in Defence after $15.6m bungle unmasked
World.content:
Defence officials behind Australia's flagship missile program racked up at least $15.6 million in financial and procurement blunders, a freedom of information document shows, including paying out $13.3 million before securing basic legal sign-off.

The defence file exposes a pattern of basic accounting and administrative failures within the Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Group (GWEO), the $36 billion initiative designed to manufacture and stockpile advanced weapons and ammunition on Australian soil.

The federal government acknowledged the errors exposed in the document, with Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy telling the ABC: "We agree the rot has to stop."

The defence document shows the administrative errors included two payments of $8.1 million and $5.2 million, which were made in June 2023.

Officials paid out the money to cover contract price hikes before getting the mandatory legal approval required to increase the contract's value.

A further four transactions broke basic rules when staff went out to market to get quotes before getting required sign-off from their managers.

In another instance, officials broke spending rules on a $631,365 order by approving a bill that was higher than the allowed spending limit, then mistakenly filing the paperwork in Australian dollars instead of the foreign currency, distorting the exchange rate used.

The money represents a tiny fraction of the multi-billion-dollar defence procurement budget but it raises concerns about how the funds are handled.

There is no suggestion any of the money was lost, but Defence records make it clear the funds were spent "contrary to Defence procurement policy".

More breaches redacted from document

An unknown number of additional breaches and their costs were redacted from the document.

However, "yes" boxes confirm corrective action was required on at least eight additional occasions.

The paperwork also highlights broader procedural lapses across the program, including an August 2025 breach where staff relied on outdated spending rules, missing a policy change that dropped the manager sign-off threshold from $200,000 to $80,000.

Pat Conroy and South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas pictured last year touring a missile assembly factory. (Supplied: Kym Smith, Defence)

The errors were only identified when a new contract management team conducted a review of previous transactions.

"The personnel involved in processing the escalation payment are no longer within the Contract Management Team," the Defence document says, explaining the current team reviewed the arrangement, identified the non-compliance, and formally reported it.

Officials ultimately granted retrospective approval to the $13.3 million in payments on July 10, 2025, roughly two years after the cash went out the door.

Do you know more? If you know more about this story, contact Olivia Caisley at oliviacaisley.journo@proton.me

Mr Conroy used the ABC's revelations to justify the Albanese government's creation of the newly minted Defence Delivery Group to improve oversight, enforce tighter controls on contracts and get "more bang for the buck for taxpayers".

He also laid blame at the feet of the former Liberal government.

"The management of this contract, a legacy of the former government that outsourced important work to a legion of consultants and contractors, was just not good enough," he said.

" We agree the rot has to stop. That's why since coming to office, we have acted to ensure that the management of this contract is now done by Defence public servants. "

"That's why we have ramped up investment in GWEO and made it a priority, which includes greater oversight of management of this contract."

The FOI document shows the unauthorised price-hike payments occurred in June 2023 — more than a year after the Albanese government first took office.

Greens want accountability

Greens leader David Shoebridge, who is also the party's spokesperson on defence, said the issue highlighted deep issues with defence procurement.

"GWEO is one of the government's big-ticket items on defence spending. Questions need to be asked about who was held to account here," he said.

"The documents only say the 'personnel involved' have been moved on.

"In most cases in Defence, 'moved on' is code for promoted away from a problem.

"What is 100 per cent clear is that no one in a leadership position has even been held to account."

David Shoebridge says Defence should not "promote away the problem". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A Defence spokesperson told the ABC the department took issues of non-compliance and transparency seriously.

"[It has] demonstrated this through proactive referrals, stronger controls, and increased oversight," they said.

Audit office looks into domestic munitions

The internal disclosures come amid an extensive, two-part investigation by the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) into Defence's domestic munitions contracts.

The national audit body first exposed severe probity gaps and sole-sourcing failures in June 2024, before handing down a damning second report in July 2026 that criticised the GWEO enterprise for delivering "limited assurance" on value-for-money.

The GWEO division will be consolidated into the new Defence Delivery Agency. (Supplied: Defence/Rodney Braithwaite)

The government has committed between $26 billion and $36 billion over the next decade under the Integrated Investment Program (IIP) to accelerate the GWEO enterprise.

GWEO is among the divisions set to be consolidated into the new Defence Delivery Agency, which will manage Australia's $56 billion annual defence spending from July 2027.

The initiative aims to curb costly project blowouts on major military assets.

World.title: RSL going bush to connect with veterans from Afghanistan
World.content:
Afghanistan war veteran Josh Donnelly straddles two worlds: being a father of six living on the NSW mid-north coast, and a former soldier confronting his own isolating battles.

The 39-year-old was medically discharged with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after serving in the army from 2006 to 2013 and being deployed to Afghanistan from 2012.

With his PTSD making it difficult to work, Mr Donnelly gets to make up for lost time with his three youngest children.

"It's hard; all of them could come and see Dad, and I could be the happiest bloke in the world," Mr Donnelly said.

"And they can come and see me, and I can be an angry bastard, basically.

"It's hard for them, having a dad with PTSD, but at the same time, it's all they've ever known."

Younger veterans needing support

The Royal Commission into Veteran and Defence Suicide found there was a clear need for members transitioning out of Defence to access ongoing support and rebuild their identities as civilians.

Approximately 30,000 Australians were deployed across the Middle East from 2001 to 2021.

NSW RSL president Vincent Williams says the organisation is making inroads in encouraging younger veterans to join. (Supplied: NSW RSL )

While the national average age of an RSL member is 69, NSW RSL president Vincent Williams said the youngest possible veteran from the first deployment to Afghanistan in 2001 would now be only 43.

"At the age of 43, you've still got commitments to work, and you've got commitments to your family," he said.

"It's important for us to provide activities which will allow them to engage with other veterans because the camaraderie and the connectivity are very important."

Emma Palmer at the Uruzgan Medical Center while on tour in Afghanistan with the Australian Army. (Supplied: Emma Palmer)

Bellinger River RSL sub-branch president Emma Palmer has been working to attract younger veterans to her RSL branch to help build that connection among those who served.

She was deployed as a nurse to the Uruzgan Medical Centre, where she treated all patients impacted by the conflict.

"It was a life-defining experience," she said.

"I was only there for a short time, but the impact of that has been lifelong."

Emma Palmer is an Afghanistan veteran. She told the ABC they treated anyone injured by the war, including the enemy. (Supplied: Emma Palmer)

When Ms Palmer came home, the staff who worked alongside her in a civilian hospital at home asked where her compassion had gone.

It was only at the end of last year that she was diagnosed with PTSD.

" It doesn't stop affecting you and you need somewhere to talk about it. "

Finding a new place for mateship

Ms Palmer said Afghanistan veterans had been missing a place to settle in the returned service person community.

"Afghanistan is the longest running conflict, so some people did like seven tours," Ms Palmer said.

"[We're] trying to give people a place where they can feel connected, where they can share their experiences with someone who understands, so they don't have to explain."

Emma Palmer has organised a retreat for Afghanistan and Iraq veterans to help them connect. (ABC Coffs Coast: Caitlan Charles )

This weekend, to mark 25 years since Australian troops were first deployed to Afghanistan, veterans like Matt Foster will go camping and fishing together with their families on a property nicknamed "Chora Valley Resort" in the Bellinger Valley.

Mr Foster, who served in Afghanistan in 2009, said he wanted a chance to reconnect with those who understood what it was like to be there.

"It could be nerve-wracking outside the bases and even inside the bases, due to indirect rocket fire," he said.

" The thing that gets everyone through is the mateship and the guys and girls that you're there with. "

Matt Foster is a veteran originally from Ebor. (Supplied: Matt Foster)

Mr Donnelly said the trip would give veterans a chance to commemorate and connect in an informal way.

"If it's sitting around having a beer, or a chat with people around a fire," he said.

"That is what I find most exciting about what we're doing."

Ms Palmer said it was important to include the families of veterans because their lived experience was different to that of other families.

"No veteran has served alone; their family serves alongside them," she said.

World.title: Breaking: Unemployment rate sits at post-COVID high after revision
World.content:
Australia's unemployment rate remained at 4.7 per cent in September, after August's jobless rate was revised upwards.

It means the national unemployment rate remains at its highest level in the post-COVID era, in seasonally adjusted terms.

An estimated 39,300 fewer Australians were in work last month, and the number of officially unemployed people increased by 8,900.

Inflation lower than expected The odds of the Reserve Bank lifting interest rates in November have fallen sharply after the latest consumer price index (CPI) came in lower than expected, with headline inflation up 4 per cent in the year to August.

The proportion of people in work or actively looking for work, the "participation rate", also surprisingly fell to 66.8 per cent, from 67 per cent.

It means the average unemployment rate in the September quarter was 4.63 per cent, well above (and ahead of) the Reserve Bank's forecast of 4.5 per cent for the December quarter this year.

However, the Bureau of Statistics data show that, in trend terms, things remained steady last month.

The trend unemployment rate remained at 4.6 per cent, the participation rate at 66.9 per cent, hours worked remained steady, and the employment-to-population ratio held at 63.8 per cent.

World.title: Wallaroos lose star but regain experience for historic 'quadruple header'
World.content:
The Wallaroos have been forced to leave out star fullback Caitlyn Halse for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Halse is unavailable for the WXV Global Series Test due to concussion symptoms.

The 20-year-old's withdrawal is a blow but the Wallaroos have regained experienced winger Maya Stewart, who returns to the starting XV.

Stewart, a 27-Test veteran with the Wallaroos, was named after recovering from an Achilles tendon injury.

Her inclusion sees Desiree Miller move from the wing to fullback in place of Halse.

Wallaroos 'got some work to do' Ending a run of six straight defeats was not enough to leave the Wallaroos satisfied with their 30-10 win over Scotland in Edinburgh this morning.

In the forward pack, captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona and Pia Tapsell swap positions in the back row, starting at blindside flanker and number eight respectively.

Eva Karpani and Cecilia Smith have returned to the match-day squad on the reserves bench, which also features fresh faces Allana Sikimeti and Piper Simons.

"We have maintained considerable selection consistency throughout the WXV, strategically strengthening our cohesion and combinations," Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance, Tim Walsh, said in a statement.

"During the WXV we have layered specific areas of our game to build stronger performances each Test.

"We have selected a balanced 23 armed with leadership, power, strength and speed."

Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona will play at blindside flanker against Scotland. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The Wallaroos are chasing back-to-back wins over Scotland.

In their most recent Test, the Wallaroos triumphed 30–10 in Edinburgh late last month.

The two sides meet in Sydney and Canberra (October 23) to conclude their WXV Global Series campaigns.

Saturday's match is part of a rugby "quadruple header" at Stadium Australia.

The Wallabies meet the All Blacks in the final Bledisloe Cup Test, while the Australian women's and men's sevens teams are also appearing.

The world champion Australian women's team plays arch rivals New Zealand, while the men's squad faces two-time Olympic champions Fiji.

It is the first time all four national rugby teams will be playing on the same match-day schedule.

Wallabies squad (1-15): Brianna Hoy, Brittany Merlo, Faliki Pohiva, Kaitlan Leaney, Michaela Leonard, Siokapesi Palu Sekona (c), Piper Duck, Pia Tapsell, Samantha Wood, Waiaria Ellis, Amelia Whitaker, Faitala Moleka, Georgina Friedrichs, Maya Stewart, Desiree Miller

Reserves: Tania Naden, Allana Sikimeti, Eva Karpani, Jemma Bemrose, Emily Chancellor, Lily Bone, Piper Simons, Cecilia Smith

World.title: Patients struggling with rising costs and long waits for healthcare refunds
World.content:
Victoria's Labor government and the opposition have promised $53.6 million for the Victorian Patient Transport Assistance Scheme (VPTAS) if successful at next month's state election.

The scheme provides financial assistance to eligible Victorians who need to travel long distances to access specialist medical treatment.

Under proposed changes to the program, accommodation subsidies would increase from $45 to $125 a night and fuel reimbursements from 21 cents per kilometre to 35 cents.

Mildura woman Lara Hamilton is one of almost 30,000 regional Victorians who use the VPTAS.

She regularly visits Melbourne for appointments and mostly relies on flights for her travel.

Lara Hamilton uses a mobility scooter and relies on flights and one-way lifts from family members. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

She called the announcement a "bandaid" solution and said her budget would still be tight, as reimbursements could take months to hit her account.

Currently, she is waiting on claims for thousands of dollars.

"With the cost-of-living crisis at the moment, no-one can afford to wait for $4,500," she said.

"I have to choose to basically not drive my own motor vehicle locally to try to save money, catch a bus or walk when I can."

The standard processing time for a claim is six to eight weeks, but Ms Hamilton said she had been waiting much longer.

"I lodge paper forms and it's taking an excess of six months for any type of reimbursement," she said.

"If you're lucky, you may receive an email approximately four months post-lodgement."

'Impossible' wait times

Mildura couple Wendy and Eddie Rushforth access VPTAS to cover the cost of travel for medical treatment across the state.

Ms Rushforth said the couple had also cut back on their spending to save up for appointments.

"[We] cut down on our food, turn everything off for the electricity and don't drive anywhere," she said.

Ed and Wendy Rushforth have to budget to afford travel to doctor and specialist appointments. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

Ms Rushforth said even the estimated wait times were too long.

"Six to eight weeks is a long time without having money, and to not be able to shop because you have to save up for so long," she said.

Funding increase

To access the scheme, Australian citizens, permanent residents or refugees must travel 100 kilometres one way or 500km within seven days.

The service must be from the closest eligible specialist service within Victoria.

Ingrid Stitt says the increase will make a "real difference". (ABC News)

"We don't want people to have to worry about money as well as everything else that they're dealing with," Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said.

Ms Stitt said the government had introduced measures to decrease wait times, including the launch of an online portal.

"We've also put some additional resources into the team that process those claims because we do want to see people get reimbursed a lot quicker," she said.

Georgie Crozier says the Coalition has been advocating for an increase to accommodation and petrol reimbursement rates. (AAP: James Ross)

Shadow Health Minister Georgie Crozier said Labor had 12 years to fix issues with VPTAS yet waited until a few weeks out from the election.

"The Coalition has long been advocating on behalf of regional Victorians for an increase in the accommodation and petrol rates under the VPTAS, which are the lowest in the country under Labor," Ms Crozier said.

End of 'postcode penalty'

According to the Leukaemia Foundation's National Patient Travel Scorecard, Victoria has the worst reimbursement options in the country.

Under the new funding, Victoria would move to equal first alongside South Australia.

Chris Tanti says the foundation's focus would now turn to how the funding is delivered. (ABC News)

"Victorians facing cancer [treatment] now have something they have not had before: a clear, costed promise to end the postcode penalty," CEO Chris Tanti said.

Mr Tanti said bipartisan support was a "significant milestone", but it had come after more than a decade of pushing for change.

The funding change is expected to roll out on July 1, 2027 if either Labor or the Coalition forms government.

World.title: Brisbane City Council floats trialling licensed bars on CityCats
World.content:
Brisbane's CityCats could soon become floating bars, with the council exploring options to add alcohol licensing to the city's ferries.

Brisbane City Council (BCC) has confirmed it is looking into a pilot program that would see ten double-decker CityCat ferries outfitted with licensed bars.

A spokesperson for BCC said the idea was inspired by Sydney ferry services that serve alcohol.

Councillor Andrew Wines told ABC Radio Brisbane the plan was in its early stages.

"We're having a look at an idea where, on a small number of ferries … to see whether we can have a food and beverage offering on our ferries to allow people the option to be able to buy a drink if they wish on the ferry on the way home," he said.

BCC says the idea was inspired by Sydney ferry services that serve alcohol, such as the Manly Ferry. (ABC News: Dean Caton)

Cr Wines said Saturdays were more popular for CityCat patronage than weekdays, and that the council was looking for ways to "make living in Brisbane even more enjoyable".

"We thought we would have a discussion both with the public and with a range of people about whether this was something people were interested in."

The idea has drawn some criticism from local residents, with one caller describing it as "a ridiculous idea".

"What's next, beers on the bus?" Gavin said.

"You've got families using those things, kids there. People are going to get intoxicated.

" What happens if they have an accident because they're drunk and they slip getting off the ferry? "

Cr Wines said BCC would take licensing requirements into account, including serving food and practising responsible service of alcohol.

"We are absolutely going to stay on the right side of all licensing and RSA requirements on this," he said.

"This is not going to be a party boat, this is going to be an opportunity to have a drink here and there, not dissimilar to Straddie … and not dissimilar to Manly Ferry in Sydney."

Cr Wines says licensing laws would be taken into account, including serving food and practising responsible service of alcohol. (ABC News)

He said matters like opening hours and product offerings were still being worked through.

Deputy leader of the Labor council opposition Lucy Collier said the council had the "wrong priorities".

"Brisbane's LNP Lord Mayor thinks it's fine for CityCat staff to be overworked and underpaid, and now he wants them to become bartenders and clean up intoxicated people's vomit," Cr Collier said.

Pay negotiations still ongoing

The plan comes at a fraught moment for CityCat operator RiverCity Ferries, which is still working through a new pay deal with Brisbane ferry staff.

Ferry staff's refusal to work on Riverfire night on September 5 was the latest episode in a long-running pay dispute between the Maritime Workers Union and RiverCity Ferries.

Pay negotiations between MUA and the operator have been ongoing since October last year, with workers conducting industrial action intermittently since July 30.

Cr Wines said he would work with RiverCity Ferries to determine how bar staffing might be accomplished but said he wasn't certain how pay negotiations were progressing.

"I believe that negotiations have been progressing and that the two groups … my understanding is that things have been improving and I remain optimistic."

World.title: Calls for stronger warnings on iron infusion risks
World.content:
Kate Russell thought getting an iron infusion would help alleviate her fatigue, but instead she says the treatment led to a condition that landed her in an induced coma.

The 46-year-old said she was not warned about the potential risks and the 12 months since her admission to Toowoomba Hospital's intensive care unit (ICU) had been "devastating".

Ms Russell said she was diagnosed with severe hypophosphataemia, where phosphate levels in the blood become dangerously low, which can occur following an iron infusion.

"[I had] countless specialist appointments and medications, as well as using up all my personal leave and having to give up parts of my role [as a teacher]," Ms Russell said.

"It's taken a huge financial toll on my family."

Kate Russell says she was active before getting an iron infusion. (Supplied: Kate Russell)

She said the only risk associated with having an iron infusion she was informed about was iron staining on her arm where the intravenous needle was inserted.

But Ms Russell said she started experiencing muscle weakness and heart palpitations after her treatment in October last year, and she continued to deteriorate for a month before she collapsed in a doctor's surgery and was rushed to hospital.

"I just could not continue to breathe, so they decided that they needed to take over my breathing and intubate me," she said.

She said when the cause of her illness was identified, she was given phosphate replacement therapy.

Iron infusion risk becoming more common

Women of reproductive age are getting iron infusions at an increasingly high rate. (ABC: Emily Bryan)

Medical experts say hypophosphataemia is a complication that can occur with the use of ferric carboxymaltose, an intravenous iron preparation commonly administered in Australia.

Recent data shows it is becoming more common as the use of iron infusions surges across Australia, particularly among women of reproductive age.

There were 46 reports of hypophosphataemia associated with ferric carboxymaltose in 2025, compared with 17 cases in 2020 according to the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA).

Bond University assistant professor and general practitioner Kieran Le Plastrier said several patients had presented to his practice feeling "generally unwell" after receiving an iron infusion this year and blood tests had shown they all had low phosphate.

Hypophosphataemia is becoming more common as the use of iron infusions rises. (Supplied: Queensland Health)

"They felt really, really terrible at a time when they're expecting to feel really great because we've done the iron infusion," he said.

Dr Le Plastrier said ferric carboxymaltose caused hypophosphataemia by preventing the breakdown of a hormone, which in turn signalled the kidneys to excrete more phosphate than usual.

"All versions of infusions can do it, but this particular product has a high rate because it blocks the conversion of certain cofactors in the gut and in the blood from being able to recycle and absorb phosphate," he said.

" Phosphate turns over every day; we excrete it in our kidneys and in our stool and this product can actually cause that to increase significantly. "

He said patients experiencing low phosphate levels were treated with an oral replacement and usually returned to regular health within a few months in mild cases.

Kieran Le Plastrier says iron infusions can cause the kidneys to waste phosphate. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

US strengthens warnings

Last month, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) brought in its strongest safety warning, a boxed warning, for ferric carboxymaltose due to the risks of hypophosphataemia.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) said it was "aware of and currently evaluating" the move in the United States, but did not say whether Australia would adopt the same warning.

The organisation said it routinely monitored safety information and added that action taken by overseas regulators did not automatically result in the same action in Australia.

Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) co-deputy chair Aadhil Aziz said Australian regulators should consider following the US to ensure patients and healthcare professionals were better informed about the potential risk.

"Having a warning doesn't mean that you don't do this," Dr Aziz said.

" It just means that you're paying more attention to the phosphate, and I don't think that's a bad thing. "

He said patients should discuss dietary changes or oral iron tablets with their regular doctor before opting for an iron infusion.

For patients who required intravenous iron, he said checking phosphate levels before treatment could also help identify potential risk factors.

"We want our Australian patients to be safe and by focusing on safety first, making sure that this doesn't happen and what can be prevented is prevented," Dr Aziz said.

Kate Russell urges others to be aware of symptoms. (Supplied: Kate Russell)

Meanwhile, Ms Russell said it had taken her almost a year to recover, and she had only recently returned to work full-time as a physical education teacher.

She urged anyone thinking about getting iron infusions to do their research before getting the treatment.

"Look out for these symptoms post-iron infusion. If you experience it, go straight back to your GP," she said.

"I don't think anyone should have to experience this."

World.title: Tame Impala’s spectacular show a kaleidoscope of colour and controlled chaos
World.content:
CultureLive reviewsMelbourne live reviews Tame Impala’s spectacular show a kaleidoscope of colour and controlled chaos Marcus Teague , Vyshnavee Wijekumar, Tony Way Andrew Fuhrmann and Updated October 15, 2026 — 12:17pm ,first published October 11, 2026 — 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Key points DANCE: The Stuttgart Ballet bring The Sleeping Beauty to Regent Theatre

MUSIC: Isata Kanneh-Mason peforms at the Melbourne Recital Centre

MUSIC: Pekka Kuusisto performs with the ACO at Legends and Luminaries

MUSIC

Tame Impala ★★★★

Rod Laver Arena, October 14 Kevin Parker loves a laser. In a 2015 Rolling Stone interview with the Tame Impala doyen, it’s revealed that a bedroom in his Fremantle home – the same house in which he’s then just self-made his brilliant third LP Currents – is filled with dozens of automated stage lights on stands. Parker explains that instead of complaining about a light show he’s not happy with, he decided to teach himself how to design his own. Kevin Parker’s meticulousness is all over the spectacular Tame Impala live experience. Richard Clifford Checks out. Parker’s meticulousness is all over the spectacular Tame Impala live experience. While he presents as the chill savant who’s wandered onto the spaceship stage at the rave, armed with a casual jumper, floppy hair and a selection of monster hits etched into the universal songbook, an enormous rig of tessellated lights and lasers unfolds in increasingly eye-boggling configurations. It all makes the springy house chords of Breathe Deeper, arena-singalong melody of Feels Like I Only Go Backwards, and mirror-maze of groove feints that propel guitar stomper Elephant feel like the apex of the live music experience. A bedroom producer’s fantasy in full flight. Grittier electronic tracks from new LP Deadbeat are offset by the sweet tenor of Parker’s voice. Dracula and Afterthought – both with nods to Michael Jackson’s Thriller – are fun highlights, Parker stepping off-stage in pop star mode to slap hands with fans. The squealing crowd skews much younger than the 40-year-old Parker, suggesting his arc from airy psych-rock into a signature DIY-brand of mainstream pop has energised new generations of fans.



Parker’s spectacular Rod Laver Arena show is a bedroom producer’s fantasy in full flight. Richard Clifford Mid-set, Parker ambles backstage, followed by a cameraman who films him appearing to urinate in a bathroom. He re-emerges by the mixing desk on a lamp-lit stage to sip from a can of Melbourne Bitter and sing insular Deadbeat tracks Ethereal Connection and Not My World, surrounded by 14,000 people waving phone torches. In the shadows, his longtime band chug away in service to a set list that rarely changes and a frontman who lets his lasers do the talking. Where I’m sitting, the sound mix is overwhelmed by shuddering bass frequencies – a disappointment for enjoying the production of a famously meticulous sound nerd. But the annoyance fades as we cascade into mass singalongs Let It Happen, Eventually, and The Less I Know the Better, each exploding with a kaleidoscope of confetti, colour and controlled chaos around this clever Peter Pan from Perth at the centre of it all.

Reviewed by Marcus Teague MUSIC

Macy Gray ★★★

The Encore Tour

Hamer Hall, October 13 Someone in the crowd calls out “Macy!” – another yells “Where are you?” The crowd is getting impatient by this point, starting to clap to entice Macy Gray on to the stage. It’s understandable, given they’ve been waiting for more than an hour, including a 15-minute late start to the event and a dynamic performance from support act Emi Secrest.



Macy Gray performs at Melbourne’s Hamer Hall. Martin Philbey Eventually the band walks out, all of them wearing a similar afro wig (perhaps it’s a nod to her signature hair?). Gray finally strolls on stage in a bright orange summer dress and red fingerless gloves, launching into her signature raspy tones to cheers. Related Article Take 7 Macy Gray was dumped by her record label while pregnant. Then her career really took off Gray returns to Australia following a successful 2024 run that celebrated the 25th anniversary of her debut album, On How Life Is. The 2026 The Encore Tour is even more expansive, covering metro and regional venues nationally. Tuesday’s show was a postponed session from September 11 due to a 24-hour strike by Arts Centre Melbourne staff. Instead of a soulful evening of live music, the public were met with a picket line and public rally. (The industrial dispute has since been resolved after staff accepted an improved pay offer.)



The cancelled performance didn’t seem to faze Gray, as she made no mention of it. She continued to swish her skirt, side step and clap her hands to the funky beat. She encouraged the audience to sing and dance along, stating “this ain’t no library”. She reiterates to the audience that she and the band have come all the way from Los Angeles “to hear you sing to us”. Gray with members of her band, who bring a more jazz-inspired approach to her original songs, on stage at Hamer Hall. Martin Philbey The band brings a more jazz-inspired approach to her original tracks, including shifting up the island groove in Witness. She changes the lyrics, encouraging the audience to repeat “and I wish I was Jesus” followed by “I’ll fix it for ya”. Alongside other originals, such as I’ve Committed Murder, she sings covers of Radiohead’s Creep, Boney M.’s Sunny and Fred Said Right’s I’m Too Sexy. A disgruntled couple leaves early, complaining that they didn’t pay to hear cover songs. The set finishes at 10.50pm – late for a school night. But Gray doesn’t leave without singing her most well-known song, I Try, which gets fans to their feet, and joining in the chorus.



DANCE

The Sleeping Beauty ★★★★

Regent Theatre, until October 18 The Stuttgart Ballet is in town, offering a rare chance to see a major European company dance one of its signature storybook ballets – with all the old-world charm and seriousness you could want. It’s also a chance to see a handful of genuine international ballet stars. First among them is Elisa Badenes, who danced Aurora on opening night, a dancer with exceptional composure and the silkiest of turns. The Stuttgart Ballet is in town. Kate Longley Her Prince Désiré was Henrik Erikson: neat as a folded napkin in everything he does. His partnering with Badenes was compelling throughout, culminating in an exquisite grand pas de deux during the marriage festivities. The highlight was a diagonal of supported turns and plunging fish dives where, for one blissful moment, the two dancers appeared so connected, so entirely at one, that it was unclear who was supporting who. The wicked fairy Carabosse was danced by Jason Reilly, a veteran dramatic dynamo. He has a distinctive presence: quick, harassed, mocking, but earnest even when parodying the classical steps of the others.



Carabosse has an elevated significance in Marcia Haydée’s version of the ballet. Haydée has transformed the contest between Carabosse and the Lilac Fairy into a sort of epic contest between good and evil. It can seem a little absurd – too much drama for the fey conceit – but this is a production that is very much of its time. Created in 1987, it’s essentially a Cold War fairy tale, showing a world dominated by two great powers. Mizuki Amemiya of The Stuttgart Ballet. Kate Longley Abigail Willson-Heisel brought unflappable presence to the Lilac Fairy, while among the other dancers, Riccardo Ferlito drew the eye with the height and energy of his leaps as the bare-chested Ali Baba. It’s a long way to travel just to perform The Sleeping Beauty, even if it is a defining production. Once upon a time, they might have brought a second ballet to show another side of their repertoire. But visits by international companies of this stature – any stature, really – are few and far between these days.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann



MUSIC

Isata Kanneh-Mason ★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, October 9 Navigating a journey from darkness to light, pianist Isata Kanneh-Mason’s Australian debut recital offered plenty of familiar music. Bookended by two of Beethoven’s most popular sonatas, the “Moonlight” and the “Waldstein”, it also included Ravel’s astoundingly imaginative but fiendishly difficult Gaspard de la nuit. Two works by Bulgarian-English composer Dobrinka Tabakova provided a contrasting contemporary aesthetic. Isata Kanneh-Mason performs at Melbourne Recital Centre on October 9, 2026 Laura Manariti In Beethoven’s famous moonlit opening, Kanneh-Mason’s striking ability for extremely restrained dynamics and tone colour might have suggested a burgeoning sense of drama, yet this remained unrealised. The blazing finale displayed her prodigious technique, even if greater detail could have been revealed with lighter pedalling. In Ravel’s brightly hued triptych, the water sprite Ondine splashed around in a luxurious aqueous soundscape while Kanneh-Mason’s trademark restraint lent the scene of the scaffold appropriate eeriness. She also convincingly captured Scarbo’s caprice, mischief and malevolence.



After a symbolic change from dark evening gown to shorter pale blue dress, Kanneh-Mason turned to two works by Tabakova, containing the nucleus of the program. Nocturne, an attractive minimalist miniature summoned up night. Using harmonics and repeated notes, Halo effectively evoked a lunar halo which becomes increasingly bright. Editor's pick Melbourne live reviews Jealousy, friendship and love take centre-stage in this story Clearly close to her heart, Kanneh-Mason played the “Waldstein” with great devotion, ensuring that the finale’s beginning did point to the dawn (an alternative nickname for the work). The blazing sunshine of the closing pages, however, were clouded over by some heavy pedalling. Impressive as Kanneh-Mason’s playing is, trading some technical brilliance for a wider tonal palette and greater emotional abandon would have taken the performance to a higher level. An over-the-top arrangement of the 1960s hit I Say a Little Prayer for You provided a buoyant encore for the enthusiastic audience.

Reviewed by Tony Way



MUSIC

Pekka Kuusisto: Legends and Luminaries ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, October 10 Ebullience is at the heart of Pekka Kuusisto’s artistic DNA. Joy, passion, commitment and a sense of fun are among the enviable qualities the Finnish violinist and composer brought to his latest collaboration with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Pekka Kuusisto (left) performs with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Nic Walker As guest leader, Kuusisto helmed the orchestra through a program of contrasting styles, all with their own aural appeal. In Kuusisto’s thoughtful arrangement of excerpts from Mozart’s The Magic Flute, a little messiness was the price paid for an overture that ran at bullet train speed. Once the high-octane excitement subsided, beautifully shaped lyrical moments emerged before leading into the Queen of the Night’s aria. Written for Kuusisto and premiered with the ACO Collective in 2019, American composer Nico Muhly’s Shrink: Concerto for Violin and Strings is a tour de force that is a perfect fit for the dedicatee’s mercurial personality.



Across the work’s 22 minutes, Muhly weaves an intricate, compelling tapestry of textures, while the soloist jumps through every technical hoop imaginable. Kuusisto clearly thrives on such challenges, bringing unflagging zeal and a wealth of colour and emotion to the cleverly constructed score that exploits narrowing intervals alluded to in the title. Editor's pick Melbourne Fringe Festival Not just red noses and creepy characters: Why it’s time to give clowning another chance Receiving its first Australian performances on this tour, Pulitzer Prize-winning composer Ellen Reid’s “paean to the Californian landscape”, West Coast Sky Eternal elicited an empathetic performance. Its shifting textural perspectives are intriguing at first before an extended pizzicato passage tends to unbalance its structure. Clearly revelling in Kuusisto’s leadership, an arrangement of Mendelssohn’s String Quintet No. 2 in B-flat, Op. 87 received classic ACO treatment. Ebullience certainly radiated through the outer movements, while an elegant second-movement scherzando preceded an exquisite, heart-tugging slow movement. A superbly judged encore came with Reger’s arrangement of one of Bach’s most intimately rhapsodic works for organ, the chorale prelude O Mensch, bewein’.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing King hopes Green Spaces on best behaviour to provide another debut win Craig Kerry October 15, 2026 — 12:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Rachel King believes “naughty teenager” Green Spaces is getting his mind back on the job in time for the Caulfield Cup (2400m) as the star Sydney jockey chases another Victorian first. King won the Caulfield Guineas at her first attempt last Saturday when Bjorn Baker-trained colt Warwoven backed up his Golden Rose victory at Rosehill with another dominant group 1 performance. The English-born jockey became the first female rider to win those races. Rachel King salutes on Green Spaces in the Australian Derby in April. Getty Images She will aim for another first-attempt win next week when she partners Warwoven in the Cox Plate at Flemington. In between, she heads to Caulfield on Saturday for a first ride in the $6 million staying feature. “My first-ever ride at Caulfield won, Manicure, a few years ago,” King said.



“James [Cummings] sent me down to ride Deprive in a group 1 [2019 Sir Rupert Clarke] and he chucked something in earlier in the day, so I could have a look around the track, and it was Manicure. She came out and won, and I thought, this is easy. “My first winner down the straight was in the [2023] Coolmore [Stud Stakes with Ozzmosis], so hopefully I can keep it going in group 1s.” Godolphin entire Green Spaces, which took King to a first Australian Derby win for a female jockey in April, has been set for the Caulfield and Melbourne Cups, but his form has been mixed. The Baker-trained stayer was off the pace two starts ago when 11th in the Kingston Town Stakes (2000m) after steady runs in the Winx and Chelmsford Stakes. Rachel King after winning the Australian Derby on Green Spaces. Getty Images



King was encouraged by Green Spaces’ most recent effort when fourth in the Metropolitan as he stepped out to 2400m. She hoped Baker could again have him primed for his target race, although his draw in 18 was a concern. “They timed it well for a grand final last prep, so I think they can do the same again,” she said. “The preparation has been designed especially around this race. “His first couple of runs were really good. Two runs ago was probably a bit fair, but it was a day where it was probably tricky to make ground. That last run was a tick back in the right direction, definitely, and his work since then has been a lot better. “I was describing him as a colt that’s getting a bit like a naughty teenager. Just starting to have a little think about things and stuff like that, but since his last run, he’s been a lot more on the ball, mind on the job.



“He’s obviously got the ability there. We know that because he’s a group 1 winner, but he’s just got to do things right, which I think he will on Saturday, although it’s a tricky gate. “Over that kind of distance, it probably evens it out a little bit. We’ll sort of see how the track’s playing and things like that. There’ll be enough pressure, there always is in a group 1. “I think it was only a month ago, he was still favourite for the race, so he has got the form there for it. That was part of the reason why I was alway going to try to follow him down there.” Rachel King celebrates winning the Caulfield Guineas on Warwoven for trainer Bjorn Baker. Getty Images King also has chances at Caulfield with NSW-trained runners Dance To The Boom ($13) in the Alinghi Stakes, Williadow ($10) in the Harry White Stakes and Hidden Motive ($9) in the group 2 sprint.



She won twice early in the career of Baker-trained mare Dance To The Boom, which has gate two. “She’s been a little bit in and out of form, I guess, but I galloped her on Tuesday and she was really good,” King said. “I’m really happy with the trials and she’s drawn soft. “Willaidow, I had to sit on him the other day. He seemed like he was going well.”

World.title: Locksley fires up copper growth push across NSW heartland
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Locksley fires up copper growth push across NSW heartland Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS October 15, 2026 — 12:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Locksley Resources has set its sights on becoming a serious player in Australia’s copper sector, stitching together a sprawling 1000-square-kilometre copper-gold district in central New South Wales following its move to secure an option over the nearby Iron Duke project. The company’s newly minted Greater Tottenham Copper project packs an impressive starting punch, led by its existing Tottenham resource of 9.86 million tonnes grading 0.73 per cent copper, 0.22 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 2g/t silver. The historic Carolina mine at Locksley Resources’ Tottenham project near Cobar sits within its Greater Tottenham copper district, covering more than 1000 square kilometres in NSW’s prolific Lachlan Fold Belt. Adding further muscle to the copper play is Iron Duke’s historical 1.3-million-tonne resource grading one per cent copper and 0.6g/t gold, giving Locksley two established mineralised centres and a vast stretch of prospective ground to chase further discoveries. The option over Iron Duke, acquired from Sky Metals, looks a particularly savvy move. The project boasts a history of high-grade results, with rock chip and mine dump sampling reportedly returning values up to a spectacular 26.1 per cent copper. Previous drilling also delivered multiple wide, high-grade intercepts, including a hefty 13m grading 1.56 per cent copper and 4.48g/t gold from just 37m.



‘The greater Tottenham project hosts an established copper-gold mineral resource supported by brownfields growth and a substantial legacy dataset.’ Locksley Resources technical director Ian Stockton Notably, Locksley has laid out a two-pillar strategy for the new district-scale play. The first pillar will focus on resource growth through targeted drilling of extensions to known copper-gold systems at Tottenham, such as the high-grade Carolina deposit, while testing a suite of brownfields and greenfields targets. These targets include extensions of the Mt Royal and Orange Plains prospects, alongside a re-evaluation of the Bogan River prospect. The second pillar aims to increase the economic viability of each resource tonne through technical studies covering metallurgy, mineability and processing pathways. As part of the fresh copper move, Locksley has also initiated an integrated exploration strategy, compiling and reprocessing more than 20 years of geophysical, geochemical and geological data. A key near-term goal will be to complete a nearly finished independent mineral resource estimate, providing an updated technical foundation for the entire Greater Tottenham district. Locksley Resources technical director Ian Stockton said: “The Greater Tottenham project hosts an established copper-gold mineral resource supported by brownfield growth centres and a substantial legacy dataset. The independent mineral resource estimate will provide a contemporary technical baseline to guide targeted drilling and supporting studies toward potential development options. Ongoing integration of drilling, reprocessed geophysics and geochemistry is improving geological confidence and defining high-priority exploration targets expected to be part of the near-term exploration programs.”



The combined Greater Tottenham project sits within the Girilambone Basin of the well-known Lachlan Fold Belt, a region that hosts some of NSW’s most significant copper and gold operations. With neighbours including the Cobar mining district and the Tritton and Mineral Hill operations, Locksley finds itself in a postcode with a serious mining pedigree. The renewed copper push follows Locksley’s recent decision to pull the pin on further exploration at its Mojave critical minerals project in California, where a sharp 57 per cent collapse in antimony prices and disappointing geological continuity prompted a rethink. Rather than pouring more money into its Desert Antimony Mine and El Campo rare earths prospects, the company has opted to preserve its US claims at minimal cost and redirect its firepower towards opportunities with greater commercial potential. With its Australian copper ambitions now firmly in the spotlight, Locksley has traded the uncertainty of early-stage US exploration for an established NSW copper resource, a swag of promising drill targets and a sizeable stretch of largely underexplored ground. If the next round of drilling can turn some of those targets into additional tonnes, Greater Tottenham could provide the company with a compelling springboard into Australia’s copper development ranks. World.title: RBA on notice to hold off on rate rises as jobless rate hits 5-year high
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalJobs RBA on notice to hold off on rate rises as jobless rate hits 5-year high Shane Wright October 15, 2026 — 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Reserve Bank is facing pressure to hold off on any further interest rate rises after unemployment reached its highest level in almost five years. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed the jobless rate reached 4.7 per cent in September, with a 39,000 drop in the number of people holding down a job. Unemployment is now at its highest level since October 2021. Loading There was a 9000 increase in the total number of unemployed which reached 732,000, its highest level since April 2021. The jobless rate would have been higher but for a 0.2 percentage point drop in the participation rate, which measures the number of people in work or looking for it.



Economists had been expecting the unemployment rate to remain steady after it lifted in August. The result was driven by NSW where the unemployment rate jumped by 0.4 percentage points to 4.7 per cent. NSW shed 35,000 jobs during the month, while its jobless rate has now reached a near-5 year high. In June, the state’s jobless rate was just 4 per cent. Unemployment eased in Victoria, by 0.1 per cent to 5.1 per cent, and in South Australia where it dropped by half a percentage point to 4.2 per cent. Total employment in Queensland eased slightly, but the state has put on 37,700 jobs over the past 12 months, compared to 34,700 in Victoria and 51,900 in NSW.



Loading The bureau’s head of labour statistics, Sean Crick, said the employment to population ratio had also fallen in September. “This September a higher proportion of people remained unemployed compared to recent years,” he said. The figures had an immediate impact on interest rate expectations. The Australian dollar fell almost a quarter of a cent against its US counterpart on expectations that interest rates may not climb much higher in Australia. Oxford Economics Australia economist Oscar Guth said the figures confirmed the overall softening in the nation’s jobs market which had become evident over recent months.

World.title: Online safety laws to penalise platforms promoting gender-based violence
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSocial media Online safety laws to penalise platforms promoting gender-based violence Nick Newling October 15, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Labor’s flagship online safety bill will penalise platforms that allow users to advocate gender-based violence, but Communications Minister Anika Wells has removed the promotion of illicit-drug use from its expanded list of harmful online content. Greens communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young, who has emerged as the sole gatekeeper for the legislation’s passage by the end of the year, has said major changes are necessary for her party to support the bill following a Senate inquiry reporting back next month. Minister for Communications Anika Wells. Alex Ellinghausen After weeks of backlash from the Coalition and the Greens over the use of ministerial discretion in the draft legislation to say what is and isn’t online harm, three additional categories have been added to the list, and powers taken away from the minister. The creation of fake nude material without a person’s consent; the posting, or threat of posting, an intimate image of another person without their consent; and the encouragement, promotion or incitement of gender-based violence will now all fall under the legislation.



Alongside the removal of ministerial discretion, material or conduct that “encourages, promotes, urges or instructs illicit drug use” has also been removed from the list of harms. The reason for this removal was not discussed in the bill’s explanatory documents nor Wells’ introductory speech to parliament. Loading Speaking in the House of Representatives on Thursday morning, Wells said: “The core of the digital duty of care is to provide a safe online environment where all Australians are protected from seriously harmful and illegal content. It moves the safety net upstream to the people who design the product to stop the harm before it ever reaches an Australian user. “It is not about controlling adults online; it is about getting illegal and seriously harmful material offline, and giving adults choice. Like when you buy a new appliance, the government sets minimum safety standards, but ultimately, what you choose to buy is up to you, as long as it’s legal and safe.” While the Coalition has all but ruled itself out of supporting the bill’s passage through the Senate, Liberal senator Sarah Henderson’s demands of carveouts for journalists have been heeded.



An entirely new section of the bill, listing “excluded material” has been added. The list protects news, entertainment, artistic and professional research content from the bill, among other narrow categories deemed in the public interest. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news LIVE: Unemployment jumps to highest level in nearly five years; Wells introduces Digital Duty of Care, pushes back on censorship criticism Hanson-Young said the bill needed to be significantly strengthened to put “the fear of god” into big tech companies, as she demanded penalties be tied to social media platforms’ global revenue. The Greens also want individuals have the capacity to sue platforms for causing harm. “We are sick and tired as Australians and as consumers of big tech running our lives, we’re sick and tired of having material shoved into our children’s feeds that is dangerous and harmful,” Hanson-Young said. The senator will also ask the government to crack down on the addictive elements of social media, including infinite scrolling features.



Wells said the changes would face a 12-month “transitional period” in which platforms would be able to prepare, and reaffirmed the ability for users to “opt in” to algorithms through a notification sent to all account holders.
