World.title: The damage Trump has inflicted on America is spreading
World.content:
BusinessThe economyInflation Opinion The damage Trump has inflicted on America is spreading Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 15, 2026 — 11:59am

October 15, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

With less than three weeks to go before the US midterm elections, the latest inflation data shows that the US inflation rate is not just accelerating, but that the impact on prices is broadening. Given that the core issue in the election is affordability, the headline rise in the rate in September of 0.6 per cent – a material increase on the 0.4 per cent rise in August – and the year-on-year increase in prices of 3.7 per cent (3.4 per cent previously) couldn’t have come at a worse time for Donald Trump and the Republicans. With the midterms looming, the inflation shock could scarcely have come at a worse time for Trump and the Republicans. Bloomberg Economists had expected the rate to nudge up, not generate the biggest rise since April. While the biggest contributor to the swelling inflation rate was energy prices, which accounted for more than half the overall rise, even on a “core” basis, which excludes energy and food costs, there was a 0.3 per cent increase in September and a 2.6 per cent increase from September last year.



The disparity between the headline and core rates suggests something quite unsettling for Trump; the Republicans facing election and Americans more generally: it’s not just the war in Iran and higher oil prices driving higher consumer prices. Related Article Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war The Putin ‘solution’: Donald Trump’s strange deal is destined to fail Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Trump’s war in the Middle East has driven the oil price up from around $US70 a barrel to more than $US106 a barrel, with flow-on effects to the prices of gasoline and diesel, which have soared by 45 per cent and 70 per cent respectively from the levels before the February 28 attacks on Iran. It appears that those increases in energy costs are now feeding into the wider economy as transport, travel, heating costs are rising. They have yet to hit groceries, where prices rose only 1.8 per cent last month, but US food companies are saying increasing costs in the agricultural sector and the impact on their transport costs of the huge price spike for diesel is inevitably going to result in higher prices.



Even if the war Iran were to end soon, the shortages of diesel – caused by the damage done to Middle Eastern refinery infrastructure and the success Ukraine has had in targeting Russian refineries – mean, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday, that prices could start rising again. The world will remain short of diesel until the middle of next year, it said. Affordability concerns are top of mind for American voters heading into the US midterm elections. Getty Images The IEA also said that the controversial deal Trump announced this week to ease sanctions on Russia and allow it to export diesel was “unlikely to materially affect” the amount of the fuel in the market – because of Russia’s dearth of operational refineries. In any event, the volumes involved in that deal are too small to make much difference to prices. Trump has, unsurprisingly, overstated its potential. While energy might be the biggest contributor to the lift in the inflation rate, it’s not, as indicated, the only one.



Prices for computers and related equipment are up almost 10 per cent over the past 12 months and software prices are up more than 28 per cent. That’s attributable to the boom in the artificial intelligence sector. More disconcerting are rises in the cost of basic consumer goods like appliances, toys and apparel. Toys, for instance, were up 4.2 per cent in September. (Either consumers have ignored Trump’s advice to buy one doll rather than 30, or that one doll and other playthings have become a lot more expensive). Related Article Explainer

US election ‘A referendum on the president’: What’s at stake in these US midterms? The spread of inflationary pressures into a broader range of goods and services may be partly a function of increased transport costs, but it may also be an indication that the delayed effects of Trump’s tariffs on the rest of the world are increasingly showing through. The New York Federal Reserve Bank last week produced research that concluded that it could take up to 12 months for the full impact of increases in tariffs – including cost increases for US companies reliant on imported raw materials or components – to flow through to end prices.



The erratic way in which Trump’s raft of tariffs have been introduced, delayed, withdrawn (after being deemed illegal by the Supreme Court) and then replaced in July by yet another global suite, made it likely that their full impact would take time to emerge. That now seems to be happening. The electoral damage of surging inflation is compounded by another data set released this week, which showed real hourly wages declining, relative to the same months last year, for the sixth successive month. In September, they were down 0.7 per cent from September last year, adding to the sense of a “K-shaped” economy, where the wealthy have benefited from Trump’s big tax cuts and a buoyant stockmarket while average Americans are doing it increasingly hard. The inflation data comes at an awkward time for the Federal Reserve Board, whose Open Market Committee – the body that sets the Fed’s policy rate – meets on the 27th and 28th of this month. The Fed raised the federal funds rate 25 basis points last month, the first increase in more than three years.



Before the release of the inflation numbers, Fed officials had been talking down the prospect of an October rate rise, arguing that the impact of the war in the Middle East and Trump’s tariffs would fade, and the rate would approach the Fed’s 2 per cent target some time next year. Financial markets, which had factored in the near certainty of another rate hike in the immediate response to last month’s decision and the “hawkish” language that accompanied it from the Fed’s chair, Kevin Warsh, had been progressively lowering the probability of an increase this month to negligible levels as it became clear from the minutes of the September meeting that the officials were less hawkish than Warsh’s commentary might have suggested. Loading After Wednesday’s data release, the odds on a rate rise priced into bond futures shot back up above 50 per cent, before subsiding to around 40 per cent. The proximity to the elections probably argues against another rise, with the December meeting now looking far more likely.



The Fed has had enough run-ins with Trump, who wants it to force rates down to one per cent or below and has launched unprecedented legal attacks on board members in an attempt to wrest control of its decision-making, without provoking another. Warsh, appointed by Trump with an expectation (or at least Trump’s expectation) that he would lower rates, could find himself, like his predecessor, Jerome Powell, targeted by Trump if the president thinks he has harmed Republicans’ electoral prospects and put him in personal jeopardy from a Democrat-controlled Congress. The erratic way in which Trump’s raft of tariffs have been introduced, delayed, withdrawn and then replaced in July by yet another global suite, made it likely that their full impact would take time to emerge. That now seems to be happening. While an October rate rise might be unlikely, barring something out of left field it makes a near-certainty of one before the end of the year. The US sharemarket fell and yields at the shorter end of the bond market rose in response to the inflation data. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index, which reflects the performance of the big chip designers and manufacturers that are central to the AI boom, fell 4.3 per cent on the news, taking its decline over the past 10 days to more than 11 per cent. The Nasdaq index was down almost 2 per cent.



Tech stocks, particularly those directly engaged in the AI frenzy, are very sensitive to movements in interest rates because an increase in rates shrinks the current value of their future revenues and profits, if any. Related Article Opinion

Inflation Don’t blame Ukraine: Prices go up and up, thanks to Trump’s wars Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist A rising rate environment – which is near-certain unless the inflation rate reverses its trajectory – is a significant threat to the AI boom, as it is to the Republicans’ Congressional majorities and Trump’s ability to do as he likes in a second half of his term that would likely be studded with impeachment threats against him and the family his first two years in the White House have enriched. World.title: One Nation candidate called to ‘decolonise’ Muslim lands
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election One Nation candidate called to ‘decolonise’ Muslim lands Patrick Hatch Updated October 15, 2026 — 11:46am ,first published 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One Nation’s candidate for Melbourne has a history of promoting far-right rhetoric about waging religious war against Muslims, using misogynistic language and spreading COVID-19 conspiracy theories. Matthew Collins has deleted or locked his social media accounts since being selected as a candidate – one of 112 running for Pauline Hanson’s party at next month’s state election. In his X profile photo, Matthew Collins poses as a knight on a horse. But The Age has obtained a catalogue of his X (Twitter) posts captured before he shut down his account, and has verified them using data-scraping tools which archived some of his almost 17,000 posts made over the previous decade. His posts display a fixation with a perceived clash of civilisations between Christians and Muslims, which an extremism researcher said was a preoccupation of extreme right-wing figures that should be rejected.



One Nation refused to answer detailed questions about Collins’ posts, including his calls to “decolonise” parts of the Muslim world and his frequent references to the Christian crusades. The candidate did not respond to attempts to contact him through his election campaign Facebook page this week. The party’s candidate profile for Collins says the 35-year-old works in sales and is running in the Greens-held seat to restore community safety and government responsibility, and to ease cost-of-living pressures. One Nation is currently polling at a 23 per cent primary vote, according to the latest Resolve Political Monitor conducted for this masthead, suggesting the party will for the first time have a significant presence in the next Victorian parliament. Collins, whose profile picture on X portrays himself as a knight, posted in November last year: “If you thought the crusades ended with Richard the Lionheart, you’ve got another thing coming.” In another post, he suggests that The World Decolonization Forum – an academic event that examines the legacy of colonisation – should “decolonise constantiople [sic]… and syria and kurdistan”.



Another post in August features a picture of the Battle of Clavijo in 884AD captioned “RECONQUISTA” – a reference to the Christian military campaigns to retake what is now Spain and Portugal from Muslim rule. Expelling Muslims from the Turkish capital Istanbul – previously called Constantinople when it was the capital of the Christian Byzantine Empire – is a tenet of some extreme far-right ideologies. Matthew Collins is running for One Nation in the Greens-held seat of Melbourne. Brenton Tarrant, the Australian man who murdered 51 Muslims in the 2019 Christchurch shootings, referred in his manifesto to “coming for Constantinople” and making it “Christian owned once more”. Tarrant also inscribed “Clavijo 844” on his weapon before opening fire. Anders Breivik, who killed 77 people in a terrorist attack in Norway in 2011 and inspired Tarrant, referred to the “Reconquista” several times in his manifesto and also adopted crusader iconography.



There is no suggestion Collins endorses violent extremism, only that his online posts closely align with elements of some of those ideologies. Deakin University political extremism researcher Josh Roose said Collins was using the language of elements of the extreme right which was preoccupied with the idea of launching a modern Crusade against Muslims. Matthew Collins (waving the flag) with One Nation members during the Nepean byelection earlier this year. Wayne Taylor “It’s the idea of the need for a modern great crusade to take on global Islam aggressively, to fight it. He’s talking about decolonising Constantinople, which means effectively to rid it entirely of its Muslim population,” Roose said. “You can only imagine how that would be read by Muslim communities in Australia but more broadly the wider Australian community.



Related Article Victorian Parliament Inside the world of the self-described conspiracy theorist anointed One Nation’s Victorian leader “It actually speaks to the violent rhetoric that underpins a lot of the extreme right. If One Nation wants any claim to be developing into and becoming a mass political party, they would do well to reject rhetoric of religious conquest and exclusion associated with elements of the extreme right.” In other X posts, Collins sent images of the September 11 terrorist attacks to New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, and referred to Mamdani, who is Muslim, as having a “jihad face”. In one post Collins also uses the term “foid”, a term taken from the misogynistic “manosphere” subculture. A glossary compiled by the United Nation defines “foid” as a dehumanising word for women meaning “female humanoid organism”. Collins’ selection as a One Nation candidate has exercised support for the party from members of banned neo-Nazi group, the National Socialist Network, with prominent member Michael Nelson – who attended One Nation’s campaign launch earlier this month – describing Collins on X as a “patriot”.

World.content:
CultureLive reviewsMelbourne live reviews Tame Impala’s spectacular show a kaleidoscope of colour and controlled chaos Marcus Teague , Vyshnavee Wijekumar, Tony Way Andrew Fuhrmann and Updated October 15, 2026 — 12:17pm ,first published October 11, 2026 — 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Key points DANCE: The Stuttgart Ballet bring The Sleeping Beauty to Regent Theatre

MUSIC: Isata Kanneh-Mason peforms at the Melbourne Recital Centre

MUSIC: Pekka Kuusisto performs with the ACO at Legends and Luminaries

MUSIC

Tame Impala ★★★★

Rod Laver Arena, October 14 Kevin Parker loves a laser. In a 2015 Rolling Stone interview with the Tame Impala doyen, it’s revealed that a bedroom in his Fremantle home – the same house in which he’s then just self-made his brilliant third LP Currents – is filled with dozens of automated stage lights on stands. Parker explains that instead of complaining about a light show he’s not happy with, he decided to teach himself how to design his own. Kevin Parker’s meticulousness is all over the spectacular Tame Impala live experience. Richard Clifford Checks out. Parker’s meticulousness is all over the spectacular Tame Impala live experience. While he presents as the chill savant who’s wandered onto the spaceship stage at the rave, armed with a casual jumper, floppy hair and a selection of monster hits etched into the universal songbook, an enormous rig of tessellated lights and lasers unfolds in increasingly eye-boggling configurations. It all makes the springy house chords of Breathe Deeper, arena-singalong melody of Feels Like I Only Go Backwards, and mirror-maze of groove feints that propel guitar stomper Elephant feel like the apex of the live music experience. A bedroom producer’s fantasy in full flight. Grittier electronic tracks from new LP Deadbeat are offset by the sweet tenor of Parker’s voice. Dracula and Afterthought – both with nods to Michael Jackson’s Thriller – are fun highlights, Parker stepping off-stage in pop star mode to slap hands with fans. The squealing crowd skews much younger than the 40-year-old Parker, suggesting his arc from airy psych-rock into a signature DIY-brand of mainstream pop has energised new generations of fans.



Parker’s spectacular Rod Laver Arena show is a bedroom producer’s fantasy in full flight. Richard Clifford Mid-set, Parker ambles backstage, followed by a cameraman who films him appearing to urinate in a bathroom. He re-emerges by the mixing desk on a lamp-lit stage to sip from a can of Melbourne Bitter and sing insular Deadbeat tracks Ethereal Connection and Not My World, surrounded by 14,000 people waving phone torches. In the shadows, his longtime band chug away in service to a set list that rarely changes and a frontman who lets his lasers do the talking. Where I’m sitting, the sound mix is overwhelmed by shuddering bass frequencies – a disappointment for enjoying the production of a famously meticulous sound nerd. But the annoyance fades as we cascade into mass singalongs Let It Happen, Eventually, and The Less I Know the Better, each exploding with a kaleidoscope of confetti, colour and controlled chaos around this clever Peter Pan from Perth at the centre of it all.

Reviewed by Marcus Teague MUSIC

Macy Gray ★★★

The Encore Tour

Hamer Hall, October 13 Someone in the crowd calls out “Macy!” – another yells “Where are you?” The crowd is getting impatient by this point, starting to clap to entice Macy Gray on to the stage. It’s understandable, given they’ve been waiting for more than an hour, including a 15-minute late start to the event and a dynamic performance from support act Emi Secrest.



Macy Gray performs at Melbourne’s Hamer Hall. Martin Philbey Eventually the band walks out, all of them wearing a similar afro wig (perhaps it’s a nod to her signature hair?). Gray finally strolls on stage in a bright orange summer dress and red fingerless gloves, launching into her signature raspy tones to cheers. Related Article Take 7 Macy Gray was dumped by her record label while pregnant. Then her career really took off Gray returns to Australia following a successful 2024 run that celebrated the 25th anniversary of her debut album, On How Life Is. The 2026 The Encore Tour is even more expansive, covering metro and regional venues nationally. Tuesday’s show was a postponed session from September 11 due to a 24-hour strike by Arts Centre Melbourne staff. Instead of a soulful evening of live music, the public were met with a picket line and public rally. (The industrial dispute has since been resolved after staff accepted an improved pay offer.)



The cancelled performance didn’t seem to faze Gray, as she made no mention of it. She continued to swish her skirt, side step and clap her hands to the funky beat. She encouraged the audience to sing and dance along, stating “this ain’t no library”. She reiterates to the audience that she and the band have come all the way from Los Angeles “to hear you sing to us”. Gray with members of her band, who bring a more jazz-inspired approach to her original songs, on stage at Hamer Hall. Martin Philbey The band brings a more jazz-inspired approach to her original tracks, including shifting up the island groove in Witness. She changes the lyrics, encouraging the audience to repeat “and I wish I was Jesus” followed by “I’ll fix it for ya”. Alongside other originals, such as I’ve Committed Murder, she sings covers of Radiohead’s Creep, Boney M.’s Sunny and Fred Said Right’s I’m Too Sexy. A disgruntled couple leaves early, complaining that they didn’t pay to hear cover songs. The set finishes at 10.50pm – late for a school night. But Gray doesn’t leave without singing her most well-known song, I Try, which gets fans to their feet, and joining in the chorus.



DANCE

The Sleeping Beauty ★★★★

Regent Theatre, until October 18 The Stuttgart Ballet is in town, offering a rare chance to see a major European company dance one of its signature storybook ballets – with all the old-world charm and seriousness you could want. It’s also a chance to see a handful of genuine international ballet stars. First among them is Elisa Badenes, who danced Aurora on opening night, a dancer with exceptional composure and the silkiest of turns. The Stuttgart Ballet is in town. Kate Longley Her Prince Désiré was Henrik Erikson: neat as a folded napkin in everything he does. His partnering with Badenes was compelling throughout, culminating in an exquisite grand pas de deux during the marriage festivities. The highlight was a diagonal of supported turns and plunging fish dives where, for one blissful moment, the two dancers appeared so connected, so entirely at one, that it was unclear who was supporting who. The wicked fairy Carabosse was danced by Jason Reilly, a veteran dramatic dynamo. He has a distinctive presence: quick, harassed, mocking, but earnest even when parodying the classical steps of the others.



Carabosse has an elevated significance in Marcia Haydée’s version of the ballet. Haydée has transformed the contest between Carabosse and the Lilac Fairy into a sort of epic contest between good and evil. It can seem a little absurd – too much drama for the fey conceit – but this is a production that is very much of its time. Created in 1987, it’s essentially a Cold War fairy tale, showing a world dominated by two great powers. Mizuki Amemiya of The Stuttgart Ballet. Kate Longley Abigail Willson-Heisel brought unflappable presence to the Lilac Fairy, while among the other dancers, Riccardo Ferlito drew the eye with the height and energy of his leaps as the bare-chested Ali Baba. It’s a long way to travel just to perform The Sleeping Beauty, even if it is a defining production. Once upon a time, they might have brought a second ballet to show another side of their repertoire. But visits by international companies of this stature – any stature, really – are few and far between these days.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann



MUSIC

Isata Kanneh-Mason ★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, October 9 Navigating a journey from darkness to light, pianist Isata Kanneh-Mason’s Australian debut recital offered plenty of familiar music. Bookended by two of Beethoven’s most popular sonatas, the “Moonlight” and the “Waldstein”, it also included Ravel’s astoundingly imaginative but fiendishly difficult Gaspard de la nuit. Two works by Bulgarian-English composer Dobrinka Tabakova provided a contrasting contemporary aesthetic. Isata Kanneh-Mason performs at Melbourne Recital Centre on October 9, 2026 Laura Manariti In Beethoven’s famous moonlit opening, Kanneh-Mason’s striking ability for extremely restrained dynamics and tone colour might have suggested a burgeoning sense of drama, yet this remained unrealised. The blazing finale displayed her prodigious technique, even if greater detail could have been revealed with lighter pedalling. In Ravel’s brightly hued triptych, the water sprite Ondine splashed around in a luxurious aqueous soundscape while Kanneh-Mason’s trademark restraint lent the scene of the scaffold appropriate eeriness. She also convincingly captured Scarbo’s caprice, mischief and malevolence.



After a symbolic change from dark evening gown to shorter pale blue dress, Kanneh-Mason turned to two works by Tabakova, containing the nucleus of the program. Nocturne, an attractive minimalist miniature summoned up night. Using harmonics and repeated notes, Halo effectively evoked a lunar halo which becomes increasingly bright. Editor's pick Melbourne live reviews Jealousy, friendship and love take centre-stage in this story Clearly close to her heart, Kanneh-Mason played the “Waldstein” with great devotion, ensuring that the finale’s beginning did point to the dawn (an alternative nickname for the work). The blazing sunshine of the closing pages, however, were clouded over by some heavy pedalling. Impressive as Kanneh-Mason’s playing is, trading some technical brilliance for a wider tonal palette and greater emotional abandon would have taken the performance to a higher level. An over-the-top arrangement of the 1960s hit I Say a Little Prayer for You provided a buoyant encore for the enthusiastic audience.

Reviewed by Tony Way



MUSIC

Pekka Kuusisto: Legends and Luminaries ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, October 10 Ebullience is at the heart of Pekka Kuusisto’s artistic DNA. Joy, passion, commitment and a sense of fun are among the enviable qualities the Finnish violinist and composer brought to his latest collaboration with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Pekka Kuusisto (left) performs with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Nic Walker As guest leader, Kuusisto helmed the orchestra through a program of contrasting styles, all with their own aural appeal. In Kuusisto’s thoughtful arrangement of excerpts from Mozart’s The Magic Flute, a little messiness was the price paid for an overture that ran at bullet train speed. Once the high-octane excitement subsided, beautifully shaped lyrical moments emerged before leading into the Queen of the Night’s aria. Written for Kuusisto and premiered with the ACO Collective in 2019, American composer Nico Muhly’s Shrink: Concerto for Violin and Strings is a tour de force that is a perfect fit for the dedicatee’s mercurial personality.



Across the work’s 22 minutes, Muhly weaves an intricate, compelling tapestry of textures, while the soloist jumps through every technical hoop imaginable. Kuusisto clearly thrives on such challenges, bringing unflagging zeal and a wealth of colour and emotion to the cleverly constructed score that exploits narrowing intervals alluded to in the title. Editor's pick Melbourne Fringe Festival Not just red noses and creepy characters: Why it’s time to give clowning another chance Receiving its first Australian performances on this tour, Pulitzer Prize-winning composer Ellen Reid’s “paean to the Californian landscape”, West Coast Sky Eternal elicited an empathetic performance. Its shifting textural perspectives are intriguing at first before an extended pizzicato passage tends to unbalance its structure. Clearly revelling in Kuusisto’s leadership, an arrangement of Mendelssohn’s String Quintet No. 2 in B-flat, Op. 87 received classic ACO treatment. Ebullience certainly radiated through the outer movements, while an elegant second-movement scherzando preceded an exquisite, heart-tugging slow movement. A superbly judged encore came with Reger’s arrangement of one of Bach’s most intimately rhapsodic works for organ, the chorale prelude O Mensch, bewein’.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: King hopes Green Spaces on best behaviour to provide another debut win
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing King hopes Green Spaces on best behaviour to provide another debut win Craig Kerry October 15, 2026 — 12:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Rachel King believes “naughty teenager” Green Spaces is getting his mind back on the job in time for the Caulfield Cup (2400m) as the star Sydney jockey chases another Victorian first. King won the Caulfield Guineas at her first attempt last Saturday when Bjorn Baker-trained colt Warwoven backed up his Golden Rose victory at Rosehill with another dominant group 1 performance. The English-born jockey became the first female rider to win those races. Rachel King salutes on Green Spaces in the Australian Derby in April. Getty Images She will aim for another first-attempt win next week when she partners Warwoven in the Cox Plate at Flemington. In between, she heads to Caulfield on Saturday for a first ride in the $6 million staying feature. “My first-ever ride at Caulfield won, Manicure, a few years ago,” King said.



“James [Cummings] sent me down to ride Deprive in a group 1 [2019 Sir Rupert Clarke] and he chucked something in earlier in the day, so I could have a look around the track, and it was Manicure. She came out and won, and I thought, this is easy. “My first winner down the straight was in the [2023] Coolmore [Stud Stakes with Ozzmosis], so hopefully I can keep it going in group 1s.” Godolphin entire Green Spaces, which took King to a first Australian Derby win for a female jockey in April, has been set for the Caulfield and Melbourne Cups, but his form has been mixed. The Baker-trained stayer was off the pace two starts ago when 11th in the Kingston Town Stakes (2000m) after steady runs in the Winx and Chelmsford Stakes. Rachel King after winning the Australian Derby on Green Spaces. Getty Images



King was encouraged by Green Spaces’ most recent effort when fourth in the Metropolitan as he stepped out to 2400m. She hoped Baker could again have him primed for his target race, although his draw in 18 was a concern. “They timed it well for a grand final last prep, so I think they can do the same again,” she said. “The preparation has been designed especially around this race. “His first couple of runs were really good. Two runs ago was probably a bit fair, but it was a day where it was probably tricky to make ground. That last run was a tick back in the right direction, definitely, and his work since then has been a lot better. “I was describing him as a colt that’s getting a bit like a naughty teenager. Just starting to have a little think about things and stuff like that, but since his last run, he’s been a lot more on the ball, mind on the job.



“He’s obviously got the ability there. We know that because he’s a group 1 winner, but he’s just got to do things right, which I think he will on Saturday, although it’s a tricky gate. “Over that kind of distance, it probably evens it out a little bit. We’ll sort of see how the track’s playing and things like that. There’ll be enough pressure, there always is in a group 1. “I think it was only a month ago, he was still favourite for the race, so he has got the form there for it. That was part of the reason why I was alway going to try to follow him down there.” Rachel King celebrates winning the Caulfield Guineas on Warwoven for trainer Bjorn Baker. Getty Images King also has chances at Caulfield with NSW-trained runners Dance To The Boom ($13) in the Alinghi Stakes, Williadow ($10) in the Harry White Stakes and Hidden Motive ($9) in the group 2 sprint.



She won twice early in the career of Baker-trained mare Dance To The Boom, which has gate two. “She’s been a little bit in and out of form, I guess, but I galloped her on Tuesday and she was really good,” King said. “I’m really happy with the trials and she’s drawn soft. “Willaidow, I had to sit on him the other day. He seemed like he was going well.”

World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Locksley fires up copper growth push across NSW heartland Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS October 15, 2026 — 12:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Locksley Resources has set its sights on becoming a serious player in Australia’s copper sector, stitching together a sprawling 1000-square-kilometre copper-gold district in central New South Wales following its move to secure an option over the nearby Iron Duke project. The company’s newly minted Greater Tottenham Copper project packs an impressive starting punch, led by its existing Tottenham resource of 9.86 million tonnes grading 0.73 per cent copper, 0.22 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 2g/t silver. The historic Carolina mine at Locksley Resources’ Tottenham project near Cobar sits within its Greater Tottenham copper district, covering more than 1000 square kilometres in NSW’s prolific Lachlan Fold Belt. Adding further muscle to the copper play is Iron Duke’s historical 1.3-million-tonne resource grading one per cent copper and 0.6g/t gold, giving Locksley two established mineralised centres and a vast stretch of prospective ground to chase further discoveries. The option over Iron Duke, acquired from Sky Metals, looks a particularly savvy move. The project boasts a history of high-grade results, with rock chip and mine dump sampling reportedly returning values up to a spectacular 26.1 per cent copper. Previous drilling also delivered multiple wide, high-grade intercepts, including a hefty 13m grading 1.56 per cent copper and 4.48g/t gold from just 37m.



‘The greater Tottenham project hosts an established copper-gold mineral resource supported by brownfields growth and a substantial legacy dataset.’ Locksley Resources technical director Ian Stockton Notably, Locksley has laid out a two-pillar strategy for the new district-scale play. The first pillar will focus on resource growth through targeted drilling of extensions to known copper-gold systems at Tottenham, such as the high-grade Carolina deposit, while testing a suite of brownfields and greenfields targets. These targets include extensions of the Mt Royal and Orange Plains prospects, alongside a re-evaluation of the Bogan River prospect. The second pillar aims to increase the economic viability of each resource tonne through technical studies covering metallurgy, mineability and processing pathways. As part of the fresh copper move, Locksley has also initiated an integrated exploration strategy, compiling and reprocessing more than 20 years of geophysical, geochemical and geological data. A key near-term goal will be to complete a nearly finished independent mineral resource estimate, providing an updated technical foundation for the entire Greater Tottenham district. Locksley Resources technical director Ian Stockton said: “The Greater Tottenham project hosts an established copper-gold mineral resource supported by brownfield growth centres and a substantial legacy dataset. The independent mineral resource estimate will provide a contemporary technical baseline to guide targeted drilling and supporting studies toward potential development options. Ongoing integration of drilling, reprocessed geophysics and geochemistry is improving geological confidence and defining high-priority exploration targets expected to be part of the near-term exploration programs.”



The combined Greater Tottenham project sits within the Girilambone Basin of the well-known Lachlan Fold Belt, a region that hosts some of NSW’s most significant copper and gold operations. With neighbours including the Cobar mining district and the Tritton and Mineral Hill operations, Locksley finds itself in a postcode with a serious mining pedigree. The renewed copper push follows Locksley’s recent decision to pull the pin on further exploration at its Mojave critical minerals project in California, where a sharp 57 per cent collapse in antimony prices and disappointing geological continuity prompted a rethink. Rather than pouring more money into its Desert Antimony Mine and El Campo rare earths prospects, the company has opted to preserve its US claims at minimal cost and redirect its firepower towards opportunities with greater commercial potential. With its Australian copper ambitions now firmly in the spotlight, Locksley has traded the uncertainty of early-stage US exploration for an established NSW copper resource, a swag of promising drill targets and a sizeable stretch of largely underexplored ground. If the next round of drilling can turn some of those targets into additional tonnes, Greater Tottenham could provide the company with a compelling springboard into Australia’s copper development ranks. World.title: RBA on notice to hold off on rate rises as jobless rate hits 5-year high
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalJobs RBA on notice to hold off on rate rises as jobless rate hits 5-year high Shane Wright October 15, 2026 — 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Reserve Bank is facing pressure to hold off on any further interest rate rises after unemployment reached its highest level in almost five years. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed the jobless rate reached 4.7 per cent in September, with a 39,000 drop in the number of people holding down a job. Unemployment is now at its highest level since October 2021. Loading There was a 9000 increase in the total number of unemployed which reached 732,000, its highest level since April 2021. The jobless rate would have been higher but for a 0.2 percentage point drop in the participation rate, which measures the number of people in work or looking for it.



Economists had been expecting the unemployment rate to remain steady after it lifted in August. The result was driven by NSW where the unemployment rate jumped by 0.4 percentage points to 4.7 per cent. NSW shed 35,000 jobs during the month, while its jobless rate has now reached a near-5 year high. In June, the state’s jobless rate was just 4 per cent. Unemployment eased in Victoria, by 0.1 per cent to 5.1 per cent, and in South Australia where it dropped by half a percentage point to 4.2 per cent. Total employment in Queensland eased slightly, but the state has put on 37,700 jobs over the past 12 months, compared to 34,700 in Victoria and 51,900 in NSW.



Loading The bureau’s head of labour statistics, Sean Crick, said the employment to population ratio had also fallen in September. “This September a higher proportion of people remained unemployed compared to recent years,” he said. The figures had an immediate impact on interest rate expectations. The Australian dollar fell almost a quarter of a cent against its US counterpart on expectations that interest rates may not climb much higher in Australia. Oxford Economics Australia economist Oscar Guth said the figures confirmed the overall softening in the nation’s jobs market which had become evident over recent months.

World.title: Online safety laws to penalise platforms promoting gender-based violence
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSocial media Online safety laws to penalise platforms promoting gender-based violence Nick Newling October 15, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Labor’s flagship online safety bill will penalise platforms that allow users to advocate gender-based violence, but Communications Minister Anika Wells has removed the promotion of illicit-drug use from its expanded list of harmful online content. Greens communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young, who has emerged as the sole gatekeeper for the legislation’s passage by the end of the year, has said major changes are necessary for her party to support the bill following a Senate inquiry reporting back next month. Minister for Communications Anika Wells. Alex Ellinghausen After weeks of backlash from the Coalition and the Greens over the use of ministerial discretion in the draft legislation to say what is and isn’t online harm, three additional categories have been added to the list, and powers taken away from the minister. The creation of fake nude material without a person’s consent; the posting, or threat of posting, an intimate image of another person without their consent; and the encouragement, promotion or incitement of gender-based violence will now all fall under the legislation.



Alongside the removal of ministerial discretion, material or conduct that “encourages, promotes, urges or instructs illicit drug use” has also been removed from the list of harms. The reason for this removal was not discussed in the bill’s explanatory documents nor Wells’ introductory speech to parliament. Loading Speaking in the House of Representatives on Thursday morning, Wells said: “The core of the digital duty of care is to provide a safe online environment where all Australians are protected from seriously harmful and illegal content. It moves the safety net upstream to the people who design the product to stop the harm before it ever reaches an Australian user. “It is not about controlling adults online; it is about getting illegal and seriously harmful material offline, and giving adults choice. Like when you buy a new appliance, the government sets minimum safety standards, but ultimately, what you choose to buy is up to you, as long as it’s legal and safe.” While the Coalition has all but ruled itself out of supporting the bill’s passage through the Senate, Liberal senator Sarah Henderson’s demands of carveouts for journalists have been heeded.



An entirely new section of the bill, listing “excluded material” has been added. The list protects news, entertainment, artistic and professional research content from the bill, among other narrow categories deemed in the public interest. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news LIVE: Unemployment jumps to highest level in nearly five years; Wells introduces Digital Duty of Care, pushes back on censorship criticism Hanson-Young said the bill needed to be significantly strengthened to put “the fear of god” into big tech companies, as she demanded penalties be tied to social media platforms’ global revenue. The Greens also want individuals have the capacity to sue platforms for causing harm. “We are sick and tired as Australians and as consumers of big tech running our lives, we’re sick and tired of having material shoved into our children’s feeds that is dangerous and harmful,” Hanson-Young said. The senator will also ask the government to crack down on the addictive elements of social media, including infinite scrolling features.



Wells said the changes would face a 12-month “transitional period” in which platforms would be able to prepare, and reaffirmed the ability for users to “opt in” to algorithms through a notification sent to all account holders. World.title: The damage Trump has inflicted on America is spreading
World.content:
BusinessThe economyInflation Opinion The damage Trump has inflicted on America is spreading Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 15, 2026 — 11:59am

October 15, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

With less than three weeks to go before the US midterm elections, the latest inflation data shows that the US inflation rate is not just accelerating, but that the impact on prices is broadening. Given that the core issue in the election is affordability, the headline rise in the rate in September of 0.6 per cent – a material increase on the 0.4 per cent rise in August – and the year-on-year increase in prices of 3.7 per cent (3.4 per cent previously) couldn’t have come at a worse time for Donald Trump and the Republicans. With the midterms looming, the inflation shock could scarcely have come at a worse time for Trump and the Republicans. Bloomberg Economists had expected the rate to nudge up, not generate the biggest rise since April. While the biggest contributor to the swelling inflation rate was energy prices, which accounted for more than half the overall rise, even on a “core” basis, which excludes energy and food costs, there was a 0.3 per cent increase in September and a 2.6 per cent increase from September last year.



The disparity between the headline and core rates suggests something quite unsettling for Trump; the Republicans facing election and Americans more generally: it’s not just the war in Iran and higher oil prices driving higher consumer prices. Related Article Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war The Putin ‘solution’: Donald Trump’s strange deal is destined to fail Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Trump’s war in the Middle East has driven the oil price up from around $US70 a barrel to more than $US106 a barrel, with flow-on effects to the prices of gasoline and diesel, which have soared by 45 per cent and 70 per cent respectively from the levels before the February 28 attacks on Iran. It appears that those increases in energy costs are now feeding into the wider economy as transport, travel, heating costs are rising. They have yet to hit groceries, where prices rose only 1.8 per cent last month, but US food companies are saying increasing costs in the agricultural sector and the impact on their transport costs of the huge price spike for diesel is inevitably going to result in higher prices.



Even if the war Iran were to end soon, the shortages of diesel – caused by the damage done to Middle Eastern refinery infrastructure and the success Ukraine has had in targeting Russian refineries – mean, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday, that prices could start rising again. The world will remain short of diesel until the middle of next year, it said. Affordability concerns are top of mind for American voters heading into the US midterm elections. Getty Images The IEA also said that the controversial deal Trump announced this week to ease sanctions on Russia and allow it to export diesel was “unlikely to materially affect” the amount of the fuel in the market – because of Russia’s dearth of operational refineries. In any event, the volumes involved in that deal are too small to make much difference to prices. Trump has, unsurprisingly, overstated its potential. While energy might be the biggest contributor to the lift in the inflation rate, it’s not, as indicated, the only one.



Prices for computers and related equipment are up almost 10 per cent over the past 12 months and software prices are up more than 28 per cent. That’s attributable to the boom in the artificial intelligence sector. More disconcerting are rises in the cost of basic consumer goods like appliances, toys and apparel. Toys, for instance, were up 4.2 per cent in September. (Either consumers have ignored Trump’s advice to buy one doll rather than 30, or that one doll and other playthings have become a lot more expensive). Related Article Explainer

US election ‘A referendum on the president’: What’s at stake in these US midterms? The spread of inflationary pressures into a broader range of goods and services may be partly a function of increased transport costs, but it may also be an indication that the delayed effects of Trump’s tariffs on the rest of the world are increasingly showing through. The New York Federal Reserve Bank last week produced research that concluded that it could take up to 12 months for the full impact of increases in tariffs – including cost increases for US companies reliant on imported raw materials or components – to flow through to end prices.



The erratic way in which Trump’s raft of tariffs have been introduced, delayed, withdrawn (after being deemed illegal by the Supreme Court) and then replaced in July by yet another global suite, made it likely that their full impact would take time to emerge. That now seems to be happening. The electoral damage of surging inflation is compounded by another data set released this week, which showed real hourly wages declining, relative to the same months last year, for the sixth successive month. In September, they were down 0.7 per cent from September last year, adding to the sense of a “K-shaped” economy, where the wealthy have benefited from Trump’s big tax cuts and a buoyant stockmarket while average Americans are doing it increasingly hard. The inflation data comes at an awkward time for the Federal Reserve Board, whose Open Market Committee – the body that sets the Fed’s policy rate – meets on the 27th and 28th of this month. The Fed raised the federal funds rate 25 basis points last month, the first increase in more than three years.



Before the release of the inflation numbers, Fed officials had been talking down the prospect of an October rate rise, arguing that the impact of the war in the Middle East and Trump’s tariffs would fade, and the rate would approach the Fed’s 2 per cent target some time next year. Financial markets, which had factored in the near certainty of another rate hike in the immediate response to last month’s decision and the “hawkish” language that accompanied it from the Fed’s chair, Kevin Warsh, had been progressively lowering the probability of an increase this month to negligible levels as it became clear from the minutes of the September meeting that the officials were less hawkish than Warsh’s commentary might have suggested. Loading After Wednesday’s data release, the odds on a rate rise priced into bond futures shot back up above 50 per cent, before subsiding to around 40 per cent. The proximity to the elections probably argues against another rise, with the December meeting now looking far more likely.



The Fed has had enough run-ins with Trump, who wants it to force rates down to one per cent or below and has launched unprecedented legal attacks on board members in an attempt to wrest control of its decision-making, without provoking another. Warsh, appointed by Trump with an expectation (or at least Trump’s expectation) that he would lower rates, could find himself, like his predecessor, Jerome Powell, targeted by Trump if the president thinks he has harmed Republicans’ electoral prospects and put him in personal jeopardy from a Democrat-controlled Congress. The erratic way in which Trump’s raft of tariffs have been introduced, delayed, withdrawn and then replaced in July by yet another global suite, made it likely that their full impact would take time to emerge. That now seems to be happening. While an October rate rise might be unlikely, barring something out of left field it makes a near-certainty of one before the end of the year. The US sharemarket fell and yields at the shorter end of the bond market rose in response to the inflation data. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index, which reflects the performance of the big chip designers and manufacturers that are central to the AI boom, fell 4.3 per cent on the news, taking its decline over the past 10 days to more than 11 per cent. The Nasdaq index was down almost 2 per cent.



Tech stocks, particularly those directly engaged in the AI frenzy, are very sensitive to movements in interest rates because an increase in rates shrinks the current value of their future revenues and profits, if any. Related Article Opinion

Inflation Don’t blame Ukraine: Prices go up and up, thanks to Trump’s wars Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist A rising rate environment – which is near-certain unless the inflation rate reverses its trajectory – is a significant threat to the AI boom, as it is to the Republicans’ Congressional majorities and Trump’s ability to do as he likes in a second half of his term that would likely be studded with impeachment threats against him and the family his first two years in the White House have enriched. World.title: One Nation candidate called to ‘decolonise’ Muslim lands
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election One Nation candidate called to ‘decolonise’ Muslim lands Patrick Hatch Updated October 15, 2026 — 11:46am ,first published 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One Nation’s candidate for Melbourne has a history of promoting far-right rhetoric about waging religious war against Muslims, using misogynistic language and spreading COVID-19 conspiracy theories. Matthew Collins has deleted or locked his social media accounts since being selected as a candidate – one of 112 running for Pauline Hanson’s party at next month’s state election. In his X profile photo, Matthew Collins poses as a knight on a horse. But The Age has obtained a catalogue of his X (Twitter) posts captured before he shut down his account, and has verified them using data-scraping tools which archived some of his almost 17,000 posts made over the previous decade. His posts display a fixation with a perceived clash of civilisations between Christians and Muslims, which an extremism researcher said was a preoccupation of extreme right-wing figures that should be rejected.



One Nation refused to answer detailed questions about Collins’ posts, including his calls to “decolonise” parts of the Muslim world and his frequent references to the Christian crusades. The candidate did not respond to attempts to contact him through his election campaign Facebook page this week. The party’s candidate profile for Collins says the 35-year-old works in sales and is running in the Greens-held seat to restore community safety and government responsibility, and to ease cost-of-living pressures. One Nation is currently polling at a 23 per cent primary vote, according to the latest Resolve Political Monitor conducted for this masthead, suggesting the party will for the first time have a significant presence in the next Victorian parliament. Collins, whose profile picture on X portrays himself as a knight, posted in November last year: “If you thought the crusades ended with Richard the Lionheart, you’ve got another thing coming.” In another post, he suggests that The World Decolonization Forum – an academic event that examines the legacy of colonisation – should “decolonise constantiople [sic]… and syria and kurdistan”.



Another post in August features a picture of the Battle of Clavijo in 884AD captioned “RECONQUISTA” – a reference to the Christian military campaigns to retake what is now Spain and Portugal from Muslim rule. Expelling Muslims from the Turkish capital Istanbul – previously called Constantinople when it was the capital of the Christian Byzantine Empire – is a tenet of some extreme far-right ideologies. Matthew Collins is running for One Nation in the Greens-held seat of Melbourne. Brenton Tarrant, the Australian man who murdered 51 Muslims in the 2019 Christchurch shootings, referred in his manifesto to “coming for Constantinople” and making it “Christian owned once more”. Tarrant also inscribed “Clavijo 844” on his weapon before opening fire. Anders Breivik, who killed 77 people in a terrorist attack in Norway in 2011 and inspired Tarrant, referred to the “Reconquista” several times in his manifesto and also adopted crusader iconography.



There is no suggestion Collins endorses violent extremism, only that his online posts closely align with elements of some of those ideologies. Deakin University political extremism researcher Josh Roose said Collins was using the language of elements of the extreme right which was preoccupied with the idea of launching a modern Crusade against Muslims. Matthew Collins (waving the flag) with One Nation members during the Nepean byelection earlier this year. Wayne Taylor “It’s the idea of the need for a modern great crusade to take on global Islam aggressively, to fight it. He’s talking about decolonising Constantinople, which means effectively to rid it entirely of its Muslim population,” Roose said. “You can only imagine how that would be read by Muslim communities in Australia but more broadly the wider Australian community.



Related Article Victorian Parliament Inside the world of the self-described conspiracy theorist anointed One Nation’s Victorian leader “It actually speaks to the violent rhetoric that underpins a lot of the extreme right. If One Nation wants any claim to be developing into and becoming a mass political party, they would do well to reject rhetoric of religious conquest and exclusion associated with elements of the extreme right.” In other X posts, Collins sent images of the September 11 terrorist attacks to New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, and referred to Mamdani, who is Muslim, as having a “jihad face”. In one post Collins also uses the term “foid”, a term taken from the misogynistic “manosphere” subculture. A glossary compiled by the United Nation defines “foid” as a dehumanising word for women meaning “female humanoid organism”. Collins’ selection as a One Nation candidate has exercised support for the party from members of banned neo-Nazi group, the National Socialist Network, with prominent member Michael Nelson – who attended One Nation’s campaign launch earlier this month – describing Collins on X as a “patriot”.

World.title: Casino operators bid $15 million for online licences
World.content:
Eleven entities have successfully bid to apply for the 15 licences available to operate online casinos in New Zealand.

The final auction price reached $15 million per licence.

Audio player for " Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/1924049%2Fcasino-operators-bid-15-million-for-online-licences

Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 17m

A new regulatory system is being implemented that sets out rules for operators providing online casino gambling in this country.

Minister of Internal Affairs Brooke van Velden said earlier this year the operators that obtained licenses would need to comply with a set of criteria, and it would be illegal for unlicensed operators to offer services to New Zealanders.

"Licensing is how we regulate most forms of gambling domestically. This is not intended to increase the amount of gambling New Zealanders do but to ensure operators meet requirements for consumer protection and harm minimisation, as well as paying tax."

Licences will last three years.

The bidders that won the right to apply included SkyCity, TAB and Christchurch Online.

The Department of Internal Affairs said a successful bid did not guarantee that a licence would be granted and they would all need to go through a detailed application and assessment process.

"While the successful auction operators are being announced, the brands that may ultimately operate under a licence are not being published at this stage. Operators may make changes throughout the application process, and approved brands will be published on a public register owned by the Department of Internal Affairs once their licence has been granted."

It said the auction was carried out in "ascending clock" format.

The price changed in steps and at each step participants were offered the option of staying in or dropping out.

From 1 December, providers must stop offering online casino gambling in New Zealand if they have not applied for a licence.

World.title: Case of woman stuck in Cook Islands may be hot to handle, immigration lawyer says
World.content:
An immigration lawyer says a woman stuck in the Cook Islands for three years is a case which may be "too hot to handle" for decision-makers.

Immigration New Zealand will not allow her to travel here because it doubts her stated intention to fly straight to her home country, which is reportedly in south Asia.

The 49-year-old woman told the Cook Islands News her situation was a psychological nightmare.

Despite assistance from Cook Islands Immigration, neither New Zealand nor Australia has approved a transit visa for her return home.

Cook Islands principal immigration officer Chere Arthur wrote to Immigration New Zealand on 11 April 2025, offering assistance by having someone escort the South Asian national to Auckland Airport until she boarded her connecting flight to Singapore.

Richard Small, who is not the woman's lawyer, said his practice had dealt with similar cases.

He said Immigration seemed to fear she would claim asylum when she landed in New Zealand, because she had before.

"Here there is a suggestion of a past refugee claim and that would have triggered all kinds of alarm bells, unfortunately those alarm bells can drown out the individuals circumstances of the case."

World.title: Heavy rain causes flooding in Awakino Gorge
World.content:
One lane has been left open through State Highway 3 through Awakino Gorge, following heavy rainfall and flooding.

Stop/go traffic management is in place where flooding is.

Road users should expect delays, follow all traffic management and instructions from onsite staff, and drive to the conditions.

MetService says a cold front continues to trudge over the North Island.

"Today is a wet day for the majority of Aotearoa New Zealand. A frontal rainband continues to move over the North Island today, bringing bouts of heavy rain as it passes," Metservice said in an update.

World.title: NZ risks squandering digital, economic potential, tech leaders say
World.content:
Technology leaders are again warning New Zealand risks squandering its digital and economic potential if political leaders continue to reset the nation's technological direction every three years.

The Tech Users Association set out a strategic direction at this week's summit, which needs investment, and long-term cross-party alignment.

"What's urgently needed is certainty, coordination, and commitment across political lines to deliver a joined-up national strategy," TUANZ chief executive Craig Young said.

Digital services contributed about $17 billion in annual exports, with potential to generate $76b through artificial intelligence and other technologies.

However, the outlook was seen as severely constrained by fragmented, short-term political cycles and piecemeal party policies.

TUANZ board member Haley Mortimer said three strategic themes included empowering people, building resilience, and earning trust through innovation.

However, Mortimer highlighted significant equity gaps across the country, with about one in 10 households lacking internet access.

Other concerns were increasing digital security risks as New Zealanders were already losing $200 million a year to online scams, while 35 percent of small businesses also suffered from insufficient cyber resilience.

"While New Zealand will never be the largest tech market in the world, we can become one of the most trusted places in the world to innovate," Mortimer said.

"Human oversight, data sovereignty, and digital inclusion must be designed into our systems so that technology supports better decisions without removing human accountability."

Young said technology was a driver of productivity, but needed a long-term view at the highest level of government.

He said there was some agreement on taking a long-term view on infrastructure.

"What we haven't seen is something put in the in the ground that says we're going to put some money into technology," Young said.

World.title: AI, Japan and the other tough national security choices New Zealand faces
World.content:
A geopolitical analyst says New Zealand faces tough and costly choices on national security and defence but they're barely being debated on the election trail.

Associate professor Reuben Steff is visiting from Mendel University in the Czech Republic for the Aspen New Zealand Security Forum in Queenstown on Friday.

He said informed people he talks to say defence spending would have to keep going up beyond its already rising trajectory, of an extra $9 billion up to 2029.

"We could go completely neutral, we could say, 'Hey, reject all this stuff'. I don't think it's going to happen," Steff told a NZ Institute of International Affairs forum in Wellington on Wednesday.

Higher defence spending was just one among the big choices ahead that political leaders were not talking much about even though polling showed New Zealanders cared about it, he said.

"We're very good in New Zealand kicking the can down the road, but we have these imminent decision points.

"What are we going to do about the frigates and the renewal of the entire navy? How are we going to fund that?"

What about joining AUKUS Pillar Two - where had that got to, Steff asked.

Smart moves he proffered could include moving closer to a newly militarily awakened Japan perhaps in a trilateral with Australia, and appointing a national security adviser like many countries had.

Attracting expensive AI military technology by offering the country's unique geography as a testbed for other countries was another option.

The tech tide could not be stopped but had to be tapped.

"We don't want to be passively dependent on this coming to us and others setting the terms for us."

Building datacentres, and gaining some sovereignty while spreading them out of their huge and vulnerable concentration in Auckland, was another example.

"If we don't do this, others countries are going to do it."

New Zealand was already more a giver than a taker on space launch. On military drones, it was not a question if the country bought them, but where from "and whether we can build a system around them" of doctrine, data, people and industry, Steff said, who recently published a 60-page report on AI and defence.

Inaction was one handicap; lack of speed was another, Steff said in a joint note with retired army officer John Howard put out by the NZ Initiative.

"The problem is not what New Zealand knows but how it decides."

Steff gave the Wellinton forum a picture of New Zealand where, instead of a slide into a steady loss of autonomy amid the Great Power competition of US versus China, the country assumed the US would always be around in the Pacific, but hedged by focusing on partners and sources of tech - say, frigates from Japan - close to home and strategic zone of Australia and the Pacific islands.

World.title: Tertiary Education Commission defends its decision to limit nurse training enrolments
World.content:
Audio player for " TEC defends limits on nursing student enrolments " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/1923349%2Ftertiary-education-commission-defends-its-decision-to-limit-nurse-training-enrolments

TEC defends limits on nursing student enrolments Morning Report Download MP3 7m

The Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) is defending its decision to limit the number of people training to be a nurse.

It has written to tertiary providers asking them to limit nursing enrolments next year to 2025 levels, because there are not enough student placement spots available in hospitals.

Health New Zealand said student nurses need experienced clinicians available to provide appropriate supervision for their placement.

But nurse educators have told RNZ the TEC directive made no sense with the pressure on the workforce. It comes as an election-year battle between Labour and National rages on over how many nurses have been hired.

TEC chief executive Tim Fowler told Morning Report that the number of nursing enrolments had increased by 30 percent in the last six years - jumping from around 8000 enrolments to just over 11,000.

"We really are now at a point where we've got to manage the key rate limiting step for further enrolments which is the availability of clinical placements."

It was not an issue of cost but of "the availability of clinical placements in a variety of different settings to be able students the access they need to complete their studies." he said.

Health New Zealand had worked with the commission and education providers to look at how to manage that, he said.

The Tertiary Education Commission would be comfortable with the number of nursing enrolments being increased next year but only if providers could find additional placements off their own accord and get the agreement of the district chief nurse, he said.

Fowler rejected that the request was a cap on nursing enrolment numbers.

"It is a management tool and we're asking providers to limit their enrolments and manage those within the scope that we've given them."

He would not speculate on how many fewer nurses would be trained next year as a result of the policy but said the number of enrolments for 2025 was roughly 700 fewer than for 2026.

"We've been managing this particular issue with providers and Health New Zealand for at least two years ... I'm moderately surprised it's become an issue now."

He said enrolment numbers had been pushing up against the capacity of the clinical placement system in the last two years.

"We are definitely now at a point where some careful and intentional planning around further increases is required to be able to manage those clinical placements."

Health NZ national chief nurse Nadine Gray said intentional planning was needed to ensure everyone enrolled had access to clinically safe quality placements.

World.title: Hollywood actor Cliff Curtis excused from court, recovering from internal injuries
World.content:
Iconic New Zealand actor Cliff Curtis has missed his day in court, recovering from internal injuries after an alleged drunk driving crash.

The actor has been charged with reckless driving and driving with excess breath alcohol causing injury.

He is yet to enter a plea.

Curtis was not in the Auckland District Court on Thursday, as he is excused for medical reasons.

Police prosecutor Karamvir Talwar requested Curtis' bail conditions include not contacting the victim and not driving.

Judge Ajit Swaran Singh granted the conditions, remanding Curtis on bail.

The maximum sentence for the excess breath alcohol charge is five years in prison or a fine of $20,000 alongside a mandatory disqualification from driving for a at least 12 months.

Driving recklessly carries a maximum sentence of three months imprisonment or a $4500 fine and disqualification for six months or more.

Curtis released a statement on Wednesday ahead of his court date.

"I made a devastating mistake, and I'll have to live with the consequences and do what I can to address the harm caused," he said.

"I am deeply sorry. My thoughts are with the injured taxi driver and his family."

In a statement from last month, Curtis said he was deeply saddened by what happened.

"My thoughts are with those who were hurt, and their families at this time."

Curtis had helped the injured driver after the crash, his statement said.

Curtis has appeared in a number of movies both locally and overseas including Once Were Warriors and more recently James Cameron's Avatar franchise.

He teamed up with fellow actor Jason Momoa and director Taika Waititi to acquire the Auckland-based film studio Studio West in a bid to bring more jobs and Polynesian-led storytelling to New Zealand.

World.title: What we learnt from a rough and tumble finance debate
World.content:
Audio player for " Six parties clash over the economy at Queenstown debate " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/1905390%2Fwhat-we-learnt-from-a-rough-and-tumble-finance-debate

Six parties clash over the economy at Queenstown debate Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Analysis - National's Nicola Willis and Labour's Barbara Edmonds turned up to Queenstown ready for a bit of rough and tumble on Wednesday evening.

The ASB Great debate featuring cross-party finance spokespeople has a history of getting a bit rowdy, and while it's often the large audience responsible for a lot of that, this year it was the panelists leading the charge.

In addition to Willis and Edmonds the 800-strong southern crowd got served up Act's David Seymour, New Zealand First's Shane Jones, the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick, and newcomer Qiulae Wong of the Opportunity party.

Stood side-by-side in the middle of the panel of five, Willis and Edmonds scrapped it out about the government's Investment Boost and Labour's plan to scrap it and replace it with a policy that targets small businesses.

Audio player for " National’s panic and pivot as it tries to win back its fractured base " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/1905390%2Fwhat-we-learnt-from-a-rough-and-tumble-finance-debate

National’s panic and pivot as it tries to win back its fractured base Caucus Download MP3 46m

Debate moderator TVNZ's Jack Tame asked Edmonds what a business like Coronet Peak, which has benefitted from Investment Boost's tax support for businesses would do without it, Edmonds fired back "I don't have to copy Nicola, we are two very different people" to huge applause from the crowd.

In an unusual twist, Swarbrick and Jones paired up regularly throughout the debate, and were highly amused by the scrap playing out in the middle of the panel, leading Jones to pipe up and suggest the Green co-leader "offer some clarity".

Edmonds held her ground against Willis however, saying in her opening remarks she would be the next finance minister: "Not Chlöe Swarbrick and not Nicola Willis - Barbara Edmonds the MP for Kenepuru will be."

Seymour summarised the Willis and Edmonds showdown saying: "It's like two bald men fighting over a comb in the middle there."

Jones also received some big laughs in his opening remarks when he detailed how slow and clogged up the economy had become, shouting: "Look at my beloved fast-track, it's turned into a constipated beast."

Tax was also a big talking point with Wong, Edmonds, and Swarbrick given a shot at pitching their respective land, capital gains, and wealth tax proposals to the audience.

The debate descended into sledges and lots of shouting as Willis and Seymour took their turns picking holes in them all.

Swarbrick revved up at Willis, who said Labour would introduce a capital gains tax (CGT) and Swarbrick who wants a wealth tax would "kick the door wide open" and expand it.

Given an opportunity to respond, Swarbrick harked back "to a time even I can remember" when National criticised the international visitor levy, only to then increase it when in government.

Seymour was highly amused by that, quipping: "I love how Chlöe said she was old enough to remember something that happened in 2018."

A new coalition also came out of the tax debate when Wong, Edmonds, Jones and Swarbrick were all asked whether they would support a bed tax for Queenstown if in government, and it was a unanimous yes from them all, much to the delight of the crowd.

Another big laugh came when Willis and Seymour were in the thick of a debate on breaking up the supermarkets and Jones interrupted to say: "Now you know what our Cabinet meetings are like."

Seymour - not one to miss an opportunity - replied: "One person has to bring the basic economics to Cabinet, that's exactly what it's like!"

One of the final topics rounding out the debate was the issue of superannuation and how the country will afford it in years to come.

All of the politicians were asked if they supported being part of a cross-party review on the country's retirement future.

Seymour said he would entertain it with a yes, but noted he was disappointed it wasn't a big feature of the debate overall, given what a significant issue it is.

Wong was supportive, saying Opportunity needed to be in Parliament and in the room "to be the broker in a heated environment where people don't agree and have proven not to hold themselves accountable to long-term plans".

Edmonds acknowledged Willis who had agreed to the idea with her at the weekend. Willis returned that and said she too wanted to celebrate Edmonds on that front but added she was disappointed the conversation hadn't happened during this term, which she blamed on Labour.

Swarbrick was also in the 'yes' camp but said the "missing piece" in this election was also talking about investment in climate change adaptation and planning.

World.title: Australia is the monster that turns World Cup dreams to nightmares
World.content:
Almost a decade ago, the women's Rugby League World Cup final was the last day before everything changed.

Australia's cracking 23-16 win over New Zealand in 2017 didn't just deliver the team its first-ever World Cup final victory on home soil; it was the last major match before the women's game was transformed forever.

The following season, the interstate series moved under the NRL banner, the first NRLW season kicked off, and women's rugby league began to take giant strides.

Australia's 2017 World Cup win was the last game before the women's game changed forever. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe )

A few players from that watershed moment are still around for this year's Rugby League World Cup, which begins tomorrow in Parramatta, when Australia plays Samoa.

Isabelle Kelly, Kezie Apps and Simaima Taufa are still wearing green and gold; Zahara Temara has switched to New Zealand and will play for the Kiwi Ferns in their tournament opener against Fiji on Sunday alongside Raecene McGregor and Apii Nicholls.

These six exist in a different world from the one they came from, one where the players are now faster, stronger, fitter and more skilful; where pathways have improved, and player numbers have exploded; and where the game has evolved to the point where this should be the last World Cup held simultaneously with the men's tournament because the product is strong enough to stand alone.

The women's World Cup will again be held alongside the men's tournament. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

But the issue heading into the tournament is at the top end of the product, because Australia's dominance has become one of the growing pains the game must endure as everyone else tries to catch up.

Since that win in 2017, the Jillaroos have won 15 of 16 matches. They have not conceded more than two tries in a game since 2018.

In the last World Cup, they won their five matches by a cumulative scoreline of 312-12, including a 54-4 massacre of New Zealand in the final.

Unconventional coach out to extend the Jillaroos reign Jessica Skinner once doubted her coaching style was elite. Now she believes it's exactly what the top level needs, and her journey from rural NSW has shaped why.

The last time they played England, they won 90-4, and those four points mark the only try they've conceded to a team other than New Zealand in their past 16 games.

They won the Pacific Championship last year, scoring 110 points and conceding just 12 across three matches, with the Kiwi Ferns copping a 40-8 belting in the final.

State of Origin regulars like Jesse Southwell and Abbi Church, both overlooked for the match against Samoa, can't make this team. A living legend like Ali Brigginshaw can't even make the squad.

The Jillaroos have nine players from this year's NRLW Dally M Team of the Year. In Tamika Upton, Olivia Kernick, Tarryn Aiken, Isabelle Kelly and Jess Sergis, they have the best player, forward, halfback and centres in the world.
